label: Chapter 6 · Part B
title: The Nature of God II: Power, Knowledge, Goodness & God's Relation to the World
tagline: From pure actuality to an all-powerful, all-knowing, loving God who sustains every cause without being one of them
oneSentence: Starting from what the five proofs established (a purely actual, simple, necessary cause of all things) and applying proportionate causality, “action follows being,” and analogy, Feser derives that God is omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good, free, loving, and in the strictest sense incomprehensible, and then shows that he conserves the world at every instant, concurs with every genuine created cause without competing with it, and can work miracles that suspend rather than violate nature.
bigPicture:
The first five chapters each ended at the same summit by a different road: something purely actual, absolutely simple, subsistent existence itself, absolutely necessary. Chapter 6 asks what else we can know about that summit. Part A (the previous module) laid down the tools — the principle of proportionate causality, the principle that *action follows being* (agere sequitur esse), and the analogy of being — and derived unity, simplicity, immutability, immateriality, eternity. This module covers the second half of the chapter: the “personal” attributes of **power, knowledge, goodness, will, and love**, God's **incomprehensibility**, and then God's **relationship to the world**: conservation, concurrence, and miracles, closing with a short appendix on why God is called “he.”

What makes this stretch of the book distinctive is its method. Feser repeatedly shows that each attribute can be reached by **two routes**: *backward* from the world as God's effect (whatever is in the effect must somehow be in the cause) and *forward* from God's nature (what is pure actuality must act, know, and be good in the fullest way). When two independent routes converge, the result is much harder to dismiss as an artifact of one argument.

The section also does crucial defensive work. Nearly every popular objection to classical theism lives here: the paradox of the stone, foreknowledge versus free will, the claim that an unchanging God cannot love or choose, Leibniz's “best possible world,” the charge that analogy is obscurantism, deism, occasionalism, and Hume's definition of a miracle. Feser's recurring diagnosis is that the objector is treating God as **one more item in the world** — a very big, very smart agent alongside others — or is committing a **fallacy of accident**, mistaking what usually accompanies an activity in creatures (change, feeling, observation) for what is essential to it.

Finally, this module is where the God of the philosophers meets the world of everyday causes. The doctrine of **concurrence** explains how the sun really melts the ice while God is the source of every bit of its power, and the treatment of **miracles** explains why God does not “intervene” in nature — not because he has too little power, but because he is not a cause alongside the others at all. That idea, God as author rather than character, is the single most useful key for explaining this whole module to others.
objectives: Derive omnipotence by both the backward route (everything depends on God for existence and so for action) and the forward route (subsistent existence acts in the fullest way), and dissolve the paradox of the stone.

Reconstruct Feser's argument that God has an intellect and knowledge from proportionate causality, the reality of universals, and the rejection of Platonism, including how God meets each condition of the standard account of knowledge.

Explain why God knows the world by knowing himself as its cause rather than by observation, and use this to rebut the four-dimensionalism inference and the foreknowledge-versus-free-will objection (author vs. hypnotist).

State the privation account of badness with its triangle and tree examples, answer the four objections to it (reality of evil, pain, murderous intention, sadism), and show why it implies God is perfectly good but not the source of evil.

Argue that God has will and that it is free, and answer the objections from divine simplicity and from Leibniz/Rowe's best-possible-world reasoning, including the diamond reply to the ‘no most perfect being’ objection.
Explain why love is essentially an act of will rather than a passive feeling, and why an immutable God can therefore love.
Distinguish the loose sense in which God is comprehensible from the strict sense in which he is not, and explain why simplicity itself guarantees mystery without obscurantism.

Contrast occasionalism, mere conservationism, and concurrentism, give Feser's two arguments against each extreme, and illustrate concurrence with the chalk, moon, and father-guiding-the-hand examples.

Explain why a miracle is not a ‘violation of a law of nature,’ distinguish supernatural from preternatural and subnatural, describe additive vs. subtractive miracles (suspension, not breach), and explain the evidential role of miracles and why God is called ‘he.’

summary.heading: Omnipotence: two routes to an all-powerful God (pp. 205–208)
summary.body:
Power is the capacity to act or make, and since the five proofs concluded to a cause of the *existence* of things, there is obviously power in God. Feser argues he has *all* power, and he does so by two independent routes.

**Backward, from effects.** Everything other than God, actual or merely possible, would be composite, a mix of act and potency, something whose essence is distinct from its existence, and hence contingent. Such things can exist even for an instant only because the one purely actual, simple, necessary being is causing them to exist. Now add *agere sequitur esse*: what a thing does cannot outrun what it is, and existing is presupposed by acting. If a thing has no capacity even to *exist* on its own, it cannot have an independent capacity to *act*. So every created thing depends on God at every instant not only for its being but for every power it exercises. That which is the source of all power, with nothing outside the reach of its power, is omnipotent.

**Forward, from God's nature.** God just is subsistent existence, existing in the fullest possible way. To act or make is to actualize potential, so power is the capacity to actualize potential. By *agere sequitur esse*, what exists in the fullest way can act in the fullest way. Suppose there were some actualizable potential God could not actualize: what could possibly prevent him? Nothing could. So again God is omnipotent.

**Can God do absolutely anything?** If “anything” means anything that could in principle exist or occur, yes. If it means round squares or making 2 + 2 = 5, no — but this is not a limit on his power. There is no such thing as a *capacity* to actualize a round square, because the description is self-contradictory; it names nothing. The famous **paradox of the stone** (can God make a stone too heavy for him to lift?) dissolves the same way: since a stone's rising is something that can happen, God can always cause it, so “a stone too heavy for God to lift” is as incoherent as a round square. (A footnote adds Frankfurt's point: even if God could do contradictory things, he could make the unliftable stone and then lift it.) Likewise, God's inability to **sin** is no dent in omnipotence, since “perfectly good yet sinning” is also contradictory.
summary.plain: If everything that exists is being kept in existence by God at every moment, then everything it can do is borrowed from him too — you can't have your own power to act if you can't even exist on your own. That makes God the source of all power: all-powerful. Being all-powerful doesn't mean being able to do nonsense like drawing a square circle, because a ‘square circle’ isn't a real thing that anyone could fail to make.
summary.takeaway: God is omnipotent because every power anything has is borrowed from him at every instant — and his ‘inability’ to do the self-contradictory is no lack of power, since contradictions name nothing.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest move in this section is the jump from *God keeps everything in existence* to *God is the source of everything's power to act*. Why should one follow from the other?

Try a thought experiment. Suppose someone says: “My existence is on loan from God moment by moment, but my ability to lift this cup is entirely my own.” Ask: where would that ability live? A power is a feature *of* a thing. If the thing itself is on loan, every feature it has — its size, its shape, its powers — is on loan along with it. That is the principle *agere sequitur esse*, action follows being (step 4). And Feser adds a further observation: existing is presupposed by acting. Nothing acts without first being there to act. So a thing's capacity to act can be no more independent than its capacity to exist (step 5). Put that together with the conclusion of the proofs, that nothing exists for an instant without God (step 3), and you get step 6: nothing has any power that doesn't come from God, and nothing lies outside his power.

Feser then gets the same result from the other direction (steps 7–8). God just *is* existence, in the fullest possible way; power is the ability to actualize potential; so what exists in the fullest way can act in the fullest way. Try to name something that could block him — there is nothing outside him that isn't already dependent on him.

Two nuances. First, this does *not* mean creatures do nothing. That would be occasionalism, which Feser later rejects (step 44). Creatures really act; their power is simply derived, the way the moon really lights the night though its light comes from the sun. Second, omnipotence is defined as the power to cause whatever *could* exist or occur (step 9). People often think this makes logic a rule standing over God, as if God were straining against it. That's not Feser's picture. A ‘round square’ isn't a very difficult task; it isn't a task at all. The words cancel each other out.

That's why the paradox of the stone is a trick of grammar. A stone's rising is always possible, so God can always cause it; hence ‘a stone too heavy for God to lift’ describes nothing. Feser even notes (via Frankfurt) that if God *could* do contradictions, he could make the stone and then lift it anyway — so the paradox fails on either assumption.

checks.q: Why does Feser say that existing is more fundamental than acting?
options: Because acting presupposes existing, so a thing's capacity to act can't be more independent than its capacity to exist
Because existence is itself a kind of motion
Because God acts but does not exist
Because acting is ultimately an illusion
checks.explanation: Nothing acts without first being there to act. This is what turns dependence for existence into dependence for power (step 5). Option D is occasionalism, which Feser rejects.

checks.q: Someone asks: “Can God make a married bachelor?” What is Feser's answer?
options: Yes, because he is omnipotent
No, because logic is a law above God that limits him
No — but not from any lack of power: ‘married bachelor’ names nothing, so there is no capacity to lack
Only if he first decides to change the meaning of words
checks.explanation: Like a round square, the phrase is self-contradictory. Option B misreads Feser, who doesn't treat logic as an external limit on God.

checks.q: In the forward route, what grounds the claim that nothing could prevent God from actualizing any potential?
options: The paradox of the stone
The existence of evil
The analogy of attribution
God exists in the fullest way, so by agere sequitur esse he can act in the fullest way, and nothing outside him is independent enough to block him
checks.explanation: Steps 7–8: power follows being, and the fullest being has the fullest power. Everything else depends on God, so nothing could stand in his way.

summary.heading: Omniscience I: why there is an intellect in God (pp. 208–210)
summary.body:
Omniscience, too, can be reached backward or forward. The backward route starts from two claims already secured: everything that exists or could exist, and everything anything does, depends on God's causal action at every moment; and the **principle of proportionate causality** says whatever is in an effect must be in its total cause in some way (formally, virtually, or eminently). Therefore every feature of every actual or possible thing — colors, shapes, chemical make-up, nutritive and locomotive powers, and the features of minerals, plants, animals, humans, and angels — must somehow be in God.

They cannot be in him the way they are in things. Partly this is because he is immaterial, so he cannot literally be red or round. But Feser adds a deeper reason: even if God were material, if he merely *instantiated* redness and roundness, his own redness would be one more instance of a universal needing explanation, so he could not be the *ultimate* cause of red things. The same goes for the features angels might have.

Now bring in the results of chapter 3: universals are real (nominalism and conceptualism fail), and apart from existing in concrete instances they can exist only either as ideas in an intellect or in a Platonic “third realm” — and there is no such realm. Since the forms must be in God somehow, and not as instances, they must be in him as **concepts in an intellect**. So God has intellect.

Not only concepts but **propositions** must be there. God causes not just the cat and the mat to exist but the state of affairs of the cat's being on the mat. As a concept is the in-the-mind correlate of a universal, a proposition is the in-the-mind correlate of a state of affairs. So the proposition *that the cat is on the mat*, and the propositions for every state of affairs that does or could obtain, exist as thoughts in the divine intellect — including thoughts that particular propositions are true (the cat is on the mat) or false (unicorns exist).
summary.plain: A cause can't give what it doesn't have in some way, so everything found in the world — every color, shape, and kind of living thing — must be ‘in’ God somehow. It can't be there literally (God isn't red or round), and Feser has already argued there's no separate heaven of abstract ideas floating on its own. The only place left for the patterns of all things is in a mind, so God has something like a mind.
summary.takeaway: Because every feature of every possible thing must be in God, yet not as physical instances nor in a Platonic heaven, the patterns of things must exist in God as ideas — so God has an intellect.
summary.deepDive:
This is an argument by elimination, and the subtle part is the middle premise: why can't the features of things be in God simply as *instances*?

The obvious reason is that God is immaterial, so he can't literally be red, round, or made of carbon. But Feser gives a deeper reason that would hold even if God had a body. Suppose God were red. Then his redness would be one more red thing among red things, and the question “why is there any redness at all?” would still be unanswered — his redness would need explaining just as much as the apple's. An ultimate explanation of red things can't be another red thing.

Here's an analogy (a course illustration, not Feser's). Suppose you want to explain why thousands of copies of a novel all share the same words. Pointing to one more copy won't do; it has the same text and needs the same explanation. You need the text as it exists in the author's mind. Likewise, the ultimate source of all instances of a pattern must contain that pattern not as another instance but in the way a mind contains an idea.

Now the elimination (steps 13–15). Chapter 3 argued that universals — the patterns many things share — are real, not mere names (against nominalism) and not mere human concepts (against conceptualism, since they include truths no human has thought). Apart from concrete instances, a universal can exist only as a concept in an intellect or in a Platonic ‘third realm.’ Chapter 3 also rejected the third realm. Since the patterns must be in God somehow (step 12, from proportionate causality), and not as instances, and not in a separate realm, they are in God as concepts. So God has an intellect.

Feser then extends the point from concepts to propositions (step 16): God causes not just cats and mats but the cat's being on the mat, and a proposition is the thought-counterpart of a state of affairs.

The usual confusion: people hear “ideas in God” and picture God thinking about cats one after another, the way we do. Feser will correct this in the next sections: because God is simple, these ‘ideas’ are not a succession or collection of separate thoughts. Notice too that this argument depends on chapter 3; if you doubt realism about universals, that's the premise to examine.

checks.q: Why can't God be the ultimate cause of red things simply by being red himself?
options: Because his own redness would be one more instance of redness needing explanation
Because red is an unworthy property for God
Because a mind cannot have properties of any kind
Because colors are not real
checks.explanation: An ultimate explanation of all instances of a pattern can't itself be just another instance. That is Feser's reason beyond God's immateriality (step 13).

checks.q: Which three ways a universal might exist does Feser consider in this argument?
options: In God, in angels, or in humans
As words, as feelings, or as concepts
In space, in time, or in eternity
In concrete instances, as concepts in an intellect, or in a Platonic third realm
checks.explanation: With instances ruled out for God and the third realm rejected in chapter 3, only the intellect remains (step 15).

summary.heading: Omniscience II: from intellect to knowledge of everything (pp. 210–212)
summary.body:
Since every true or false proposition about creatures is true or false only because God makes the world such that it is, God is like an **author who conceives a whole story in one instantaneous flash**. Such an author cannot be wrong about whether a character is in the story, or about how he has framed it at that moment. A human author might later forget, but only because he is temporal, passes from one mental state to another, depends on a fallible brain, and is subject to outside forces — none of which applies to an eternal, immutable, incorporeal, omnipotent God.

Feser then applies the standard philosophical account of knowledge — someone knows *p* when (a) he thinks *p* is true, (b) *p* is true, and (c) he thinks so as the result of a reliable process — understood analogically. God meets (a), since the thought that the cat is on the mat is in his intellect; (b), since it really is true, precisely because he causes it; and (c), since there is no more reliable way to “find out” whether *p* is true than to be the one who makes it true (as an author knows a character is in the book because he put him there). So God has knowledge — of every proposition about what is or might be.

He also knows himself. An author cannot know less about his own creative act than about the story it produces. A human author may be ignorant of what is happening in his own digestive system, but only because he is composed of parts, his intellect distinct from his organs. God is simple: his intellect just is his power, which just is his existence. Knowing all propositions about himself and everything else, God has all knowledge: he is **omniscient**. The forward route to the same result was the chapter 3 argument that an infinite intellect must know everything (where Feser also answered Patrick Grim's objection to the very idea of omniscience).
summary.plain: Think of an author who dreams up a whole story in one flash: she can't be wrong about what's in it, because it's there only because she put it there. God knows the world the same way — things are true because he makes them true, and nothing is a more reliable way of knowing than that. Since he also knows himself completely, he knows everything: he is all-knowing.
summary.takeaway: God meets every condition for knowledge — he thinks p, p is true because he makes it true, and nothing is more reliable than making p true — and since he knows himself fully too, he knows everything.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is the third condition of knowledge: a belief must come from a *reliable process*. How could God satisfy that? Doesn't a ‘process’ take time and involve checking?

Feser's answer turns the usual picture around. We normally get reliable beliefs by being *affected* by the world — seeing, hearing, measuring. But there is another way to be reliably right: be the one who makes the thing so. Consider a game designer (a course illustration) who writes the rules of a simulated world. She doesn't need to run experiments to learn whether objects in her game fall when dropped; they fall because she wrote that rule. Her knowledge isn't less reliable than a tester's; it's more. That is Feser's point with the author: she knows a character is in the story because she put her there (step 18).

Notice the qualification Feser adds: the conditions apply to God only *analogically* (step 17). God doesn't literally ‘run a process’; what corresponds to reliability in him is that the truth of p depends on his causing it. This is the analogy of being at work, not a loophole.

The author analogy also has limits that Feser names himself. A human author can later forget, but only because he lives in time, passes from one mental state to another, depends on a fallible brain, and is exposed to outside forces. Remove all of those — as eternity, immutability, incorporeality, and omnipotence do — and the possibility of forgetting disappears.

Finally, self-knowledge (step 19). An author can't know less about her own creative act than about the story it produces. Yet a human author is ignorant of plenty about herself — her blood chemistry, say. Feser explains why this doesn't transfer: the human author is made of parts, her intellect distinct from her organs. God is simple, so his intellect just is his power, which just is his existence; there is no part of him standing outside his knowing.

The usual confusion: people imagine omniscience as a gigantic database that God consults. Feser's God doesn't look anything up; his knowing is his causing, and his knowing himself.

checks.q: Why can't God forget, as a human author might?
options: Because he has an unusually good memory
Because he records everything
Because he isn't temporal, doesn't pass between mental states, has no brain, and isn't subject to outside forces
Because forgetting would be a sin
checks.explanation: Feser traces human forgetting to features God lacks: being in time, changing, having a body, and being vulnerable to outside influences.

checks.q: Why does God have no ‘blind spots’ about himself, unlike an author who doesn't know what her digestive system is doing?
options: Because God's self-knowledge is acquired by careful introspection over eternity
Because God is simple: his intellect just is his power and existence, so nothing in him lies outside his knowing
Because God chooses to know only himself
Because God has a perfect nervous system
checks.explanation: The human author's ignorance comes from being composed of parts, with intellect distinct from organs. Simplicity removes that possibility (step 19).

summary.heading: Omniscience III: how God knows — self-knowledge, time, and free will (pp. 212–215)
summary.body:
An author does not know his characters by *observing* them; he knows them by knowing his own intentions as author. God knows the world the same way. He does not watch history unfold: he is not in time and need not wait for events; he has no sense organs, being incorporeal; and he learns nothing, since learning is change and he is immutable. In one timeless act he causes everything that was, is, and will be, and in **knowing himself as so acting** he knows it all. His knowledge of the world is a consequence of his self-knowledge.

**Four-dimensionalism does not follow.** Some infer that if God knows past, present, and future in one act, they must all somehow exist at once, so that time is a spacelike fourth dimension. That would follow only if God's knowledge were observational, since then everything would have to be there together to be observed together. But God knows from outside time that he causes, from outside time, a world with such-and-such a temporal history; it is a fallacy to infer that the world he knows is itself outside time. Compare a motionless hunter who knows in an instant that he has fired a bullet: it hardly follows that the bullet is motionless or present all along its path at once.

**Foreknowledge and free will.** The objection (Nelson Pike): if God infallibly knows I will go to work tomorrow, my not going would make God wrong, which is impossible, so I cannot freely refrain. Feser replies that knowing does not compel. If I know, however certainly, that you are sitting in the next room, that is compatible with your having freely chosen to sit there; and if I somehow knew you would sit there tomorrow (a promise, a crystal ball), why would *that* be incompatible? And why would it matter whether the knower is God?

The critic presses: God is not a mere knower but the *cause* of the present and the future, and he knows by causing. Feser answers with a **crime novel**. A character who carefully plots a murder for money commits it freely and is justly punished, and it would be silly to say he was not free because the author wrote it so. Contrast a plot twist in which another *character* hypnotized him — then we would say the act was not free. The hypnotist is a character alongside the others who interferes with them; the author is not. God is related to us as author, not as hypnotist, which is why his causality does not rival our freedom. The objection gains its force only when we speak of God's knowledge and action **univocally** rather than **analogically**.
summary.plain: God doesn't learn about the world by watching it, the way we watch a movie; he knows it the way an author knows her book, by making it. That's why his knowing everything doesn't mean the future is already ‘out there,’ and it doesn't turn us into puppets. An author who writes a character who freely commits a crime hasn't hypnotized that character — the author isn't in the story at all.
summary.takeaway: God knows the world by knowing himself as its timeless cause, not by watching it — which is why his knowledge implies neither a ‘block universe’ nor the loss of our freedom.
summary.deepDive:
Two objections are answered here, and both depend on the same insight: God's knowledge is an author's knowledge, not a spectator's (step 20).

**The block universe.** If God knows everything in one timeless act, must all times exist at once? Only if he knows by observing, because an observer needs the thing present in order to see it. But God knows by causing. Knowing, from outside time, that one causes a world with a history doesn't make that history happen all at once — just as a motionless hunter, knowing in an instant that he fired, doesn't make the bullet motionless. The timelessness belongs to the knower, not to what is known.

**Free will.** Here Feser answers in two layers, and it helps to keep them separate. *Layer one:* knowledge as such never compels. If I know you're sitting in the next room, you still chose to sit there; if a crystal ball told me you'd sit there tomorrow, you'd still choose it. (A course note: philosophers put this by saying “if God knows I'll do X, I'll do X” is necessary only because knowledge implies truth — the necessity attaches to the if-then, not to my act.)

*Layer two* is the harder one, and Feser doesn't dodge it: God isn't merely a knower; he is the *cause* of the present and the future, and knows it by causing it. Doesn't that make our acts his? Feser's reply is the crime novel. A character plots a murder for money and does it; we hold him responsible even though the author wrote it. We would change our verdict only if we learned another character had *hypnotized* him. What's the difference? The hypnotist is a cause of the same kind as the murderer, inside the story, pushing him to do what he otherwise wouldn't. The author is a cause of a completely different order — the source of the whole story, including the character's free choice.

The usual confusion is to picture God as the hypnotist: a very powerful agent alongside us, overriding our wills. Feser's diagnosis is that such objections speak of God univocally, as if his causing were the same kind of thing as one creature's causing another. Keep in mind the limits: characters are fictional and God is not in time as authors are. The analogy shows the two claims needn't conflict; it doesn't pretend to show *how* God does it.

checks.q: A student says: “Since God sees all of history at once, the future must already exist.” Which reply is Feser's?
options: That would follow only if God's knowledge were observational; he knows by causing, and timeless knowledge of a temporal world doesn't make the world timeless
God doesn't know the future at all
The future exists but isn't real
Physics has proved the future already exists
checks.explanation: The motionless hunter who knows he fired doesn't make the bullet motionless. Option B contradicts omniscience.

checks.q: In the crime-novel analogy, what would show that the murderer did NOT act freely?
options: The author wrote the scene
The author planned it from the first chapter
The author knew how the book would end
Another character hypnotized him
checks.explanation: Only a cause inside the story interfering with the character (the hypnotist) undermines his freedom; the author's authorship doesn't.

checks.q: Whose paper is the source of the foreknowledge objection Feser cites?
options: Patrick Grim
Nelson Pike
William Rowe
Norman Kretzmann
checks.explanation: Pike's 1965 paper ‘Divine Omniscience and Voluntary Action.’ Grim objected to omniscience itself (chapter 3); Rowe and Kretzmann concern divine freedom.

summary.heading: Omniscience IV: God's knowledge and simplicity — the prism and the dough (pp. 215–216)
summary.body:
Analogy matters in another way. Concepts and propositions cannot exist in God exactly as they do in us, where they are many distinct thoughts, because simplicity allows no such distinctions in God. One might try imagining a single thought whose content is one giant conjunction of all true propositions, but even that has component parts.

Feser offers a better, if imperfect, picture. **White light** passed through a prism yields beams of distinct colors; the colors were already in the white light, but in a unified way. A **lump of dough** can yield cookies of many shapes when cutters are applied; the shapes were in the uncut dough virtually. God is pure actuality, while each kind of creature is a particular way actuality can be limited by potentiality. Creation is like passing white light through the prism or applying cutters to the dough: it draws out limited ways of being actual (being a stone, a tree, a dog) from unlimited actuality, as green is color-limited-to-green. (The analogy is only suggestive: creatures are not made *out of* God, as cookies are made out of dough, since God is not a material with potentials.)

And just as perfect knowledge of white light would include knowledge of every color derivable from it, perfect knowledge of pure actuality includes knowledge of every limited way of being actual that could be derived from it. That is how God knows every kind of finite thing that is or could be: by perfectly knowing himself. If the analogy strains, that is to be expected when reason pushes this far beyond its ordinary home.
summary.plain: Because God has no parts, he can't have a pile of separate thoughts the way we do. Feser's picture: white light contains every color before a prism splits it up, and a lump of dough contains every cookie shape before the cutters are used. God is like the ‘white light’ of all being, and by knowing himself perfectly he knows every kind of thing that could come from him.
summary.takeaway: God's knowledge is one undivided act: by knowing himself as unlimited actuality, he knows every limited way of being actual, as perfect knowledge of white light would include every color.
summary.deepDive:
The difficulty is real: Feser has said concepts and propositions are ‘in’ God's intellect, but God is simple (step 21). How can many ideas exist in something with no parts?

Feser first rules out a tempting fix: bundle every truth into one enormous conjunction (“the cat is on the mat and unicorns don't exist and…”) and say God thinks that single thought. But a conjunction is made of conjuncts, so it still has parts.

The better picture begins with how Feser thinks of creatures. God is pure actuality. Every creature is actuality *limited* by potentiality in some particular way: a stone is actual-as-a-stone, a dog actual-as-a-dog. Each kind is like one color drawn from white light, or one shape cut from dough. Creation is like the prism or the cutter: it draws limited modes of being out of unlimited being.

Now the epistemic point. If you knew white light perfectly, you would thereby know every color that could be drawn from it — not by making a list, but by knowing the light. So, perfectly knowing oneself as unlimited actuality includes knowing every limited way of being actual that could be derived from it. The many-ness is on the side of the creatures; in God it is one act of self-knowledge.

This also explains how God knows *possible* things, like unicorns, that never exist — which matters later for his freedom (step 32). And notice the link to proportionate causality's ‘virtually’ and ‘eminently’ (step 11): the dough contains the shapes virtually; God contains the perfections of creatures eminently.

Feser flags the analogy's limit, and it's important: creatures are *not made out of God* the way cookies are made out of dough. Dough is a material with potentials; God has no potentials. Missing this caveat pushes the picture toward pantheism, which Feser rejects (step 43).

The usual confusion is to imagine God's mind as a filing cabinet of separate idea-cards. Feser admits every picture is imperfect — and adds that this is exactly what we should expect when reason pushes so far beyond its everyday home.

checks.q: Why doesn't one enormous conjunctive proposition capture God's knowledge?
options: It would be false
It would take God too long to think
It would still have component parts, which divine simplicity rules out
Propositions don't exist in any mind
checks.explanation: A conjunction is composed of conjuncts. Feser treats this as a first approximation that still fails because of simplicity.

checks.q: Which misreading of the dough analogy does Feser explicitly block?
options: That God knows only actual things
That creatures are made out of God as cookies are made out of dough
That God changes when he creates
That the colors in white light are unreal
checks.explanation: God is not a material with potentials. Without this caveat, the analogy would suggest pantheism.

summary.heading: Perfect goodness I: what goodness and badness are (pp. 216–219)
summary.body:
To show God is perfectly good, Feser first argues that goodness is objective, not mere preference. A **Euclidean triangle** has an essence (closed plane figure, three straight sides) with necessary properties we discover, such as angles summing to 180 degrees. A triangle hastily scrawled on the cracked seat of a moving bus fails to live up to that essence; one drawn carefully with a ruler comes closer. We naturally call the second a good triangle and the first a bad one, and the judgment follows from facts about triangles, not from any fondness for straight lines. Likewise a **tree** by nature sinks roots, draws in water and nutrients, and photosynthesizes; a damaged or diseased tree that cannot do these things is to that extent a bad tree, and this too is grounded in what a tree is.

This is the sense of “good” in “a good specimen”: success or failure in meeting the standard built into a thing's kind. It applies to everything, since everything is of some kind. **Moral** goodness is a special case: it arises with creatures who can *freely choose* to act in ways that promote or frustrate the realization of the potentials they need to flourish. Humans, as rational animals, are such creatures.

Notice that goodness always consists in being actual in some way the nature calls for (sides actually straight, roots actually sunk), while badness consists in failing to be actual in such a way. Badness is therefore a **privation**: the absence of something a fully realized specimen of the kind would have. Lacking a fourth side is no privation in a triangle, but a wavy side is; lacking wings is no privation in a tree, but weak roots are. So goodness and badness are not metaphysical equals. Goodness is primary, the presence of a feature; badness is derivative, the absence of good — a kind of unrealized potentiality, the way blindness is simply the lack of sight.
summary.plain: When we call something a good knife or a bad triangle, we're not just saying we like it — we're saying how well it lives up to what that kind of thing is supposed to be. So being good means being fully what you're meant to be, and being bad always means missing something you should have, the way blindness is missing sight. That makes badness a kind of gap, not an extra ingredient.
summary.takeaway: ‘Good’ in its basic sense means a thing's realizing what its nature calls for, so goodness is a kind of actuality and badness a privation — a lack of what should be there.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is that ‘good’ can be a matter of fact. We're used to thinking good-and-bad talk is opinion. Feser's examples show a sense of ‘good’ where that can't be right.

Take the phrase ‘good triangle.’ A triangle is a closed three-sided figure with straight sides. The one drawn with a ruler is a better triangle than the one scrawled on a bouncing bus seat — not because anyone prefers rulers, but because it more fully has the features triangles are supposed to have. Or take a heart (a course example): a heart that pumps blood strongly is a good heart and one that fibrillates is a bad one, regardless of anyone's tastes. In each case ‘good’ is measured against the thing's nature. This is the ‘good specimen’ sense (step 22).

Notice something about all the examples: goodness is always the *presence* of something the nature calls for (straight sides, strong roots, steady pumping), and badness always its *absence*. That's the privation account (step 23). A privation is not just any absence. A triangle lacking a fourth side isn't defective, since triangles shouldn't have four sides; a triangle with a wavy side is. A stone that can't see isn't blind; a dog that can't see is.

Why does this matter for God? Because it links goodness to actuality: to be good is to be actual in the ways your nature calls for. That link is what will let Feser conclude that pure actuality is perfect goodness (step 26).

Where does *moral* goodness fit? It's a special case, not a different subject. Rational creatures can freely choose to act in ways that help or frustrate the flourishing their nature calls for; that's where praise and blame come in. A bad triangle isn't blameworthy; a person who chooses cruelty is. Feser notes that a full ethics is beyond the book.

The usual confusion: people hear ‘badness is an absence’ and think it means evil isn't real or doesn't hurt. But absences can be devastating — the absence of oxygen suffocates. The next section takes up that objection directly.

checks.q: Which of these is a privation?
options: A dog that cannot see
A stone that cannot see
A triangle that has exactly three sides
A tree that has no wings
checks.explanation: A privation is the lack of something a thing's nature calls for. Dogs should see; stones shouldn't; trees needn't fly.

checks.q: Why, according to Feser, are goodness and badness not ‘on a metaphysical par’?
options: Because bad things are more common than good ones
Because goodness is subjective and badness objective
Because they are exactly equal opposites
Because goodness consists in the presence of a feature, badness only in its absence
checks.explanation: Goodness is primary, badness derivative — as blindness is simply the lack of sight.

terms: Privation (and the privation theory of evil)

summary.heading: Perfect goodness II: four objections to the privation account (pp. 219–221)
summary.body:
Many contemporary philosophers reject the privation account, but Feser argues their reasons fail.

**It denies the reality of evil.** No: saying blindness is the absence of sight does not deny that people are really blind; it explains what blindness is. Likewise, calling evil an absence of due good gives an account of evil's reality, not a denial of it.

**Pain is bad yet positive.** First, pain is not bad without qualification: it signals danger and damage, so an organism that felt no pain when touching something that would burn it would be worse off. Second, pain is not always even experienced as bad — the ache after a hard workout can feel satisfying. What is bad is what pain is associated with: the bodily damage it signals, or the lost peace of mind it causes. The condition called **pain asymbolia**, in which brain damage leaves people feeling pain without its unpleasantness, supports the point.

**Murder involves a positive intention** (Todd Calder): the murderer really has the intention to kill unjustly, plus positive beliefs and desires. Feser, following David Alexander, replies that the privation theory never claimed a bad act contains no positive features — only that its *badness* consists in a privation. The murderer's desire for money may itself be good; what is bad is the absence of an intention to pursue money only in ways that respect the rights of the innocent.

**Sadism is a positive delight in harm.** Sadistic desire is desire that is *misdirected*, aimed at an end contrary to the concern for others that social animals need in order to flourish. It is a psychological deformity, as blindness is a physiological one. Fully defending this requires ethics, but sadism is no more resistant to a privation analysis than any other badness.
summary.plain: Critics say some bad things aren't mere ‘gaps’: pain feels very real, and a murderer really does want something. Feser's answer is that there's usually something positive going on — a sensation, a desire — but what makes it *bad* is still something missing, like the missing respect for other people's lives. Even a sadist's desire is a real desire aimed the wrong way.
summary.takeaway: Each objection to the privation theory confuses the positive things that accompany something bad with the badness itself, which is always a lack of what ought to be there.
summary.deepDive:
It helps to see that all four replies share one structure. The objector points to something positive — a sensation, an intention, a desire — and says, “See, badness is a presence.” Feser grants the positive element and then locates the *badness* in a lack: missing health, missing respect, missing right order. The privation theory never claimed bad situations contain nothing positive; it claims their badness consists in a privation (step 24).

A worked example from medicine (a course illustration): a cancerous tumor is full of vigorous positive activity — cells dividing rapidly. What makes it bad isn't the dividing as such (cells dividing is how you heal a cut) but the missing regulation that would keep division in its proper order. The positive stuff is real; the badness is the disorder.

Apply that to Feser's cases:

- **Reality of evil.** Blindness is an absence of sight and is utterly real. Explaining what something is doesn't explain it away.
- **Pain.** Pain isn't bad without qualification: it warns of damage (not feeling a burn would be worse), and post-workout soreness can even feel satisfying. The badness is the damage it signals or the disturbed peace it causes. Pain asymbolia — pain felt without unpleasantness after certain brain damage — shows the sensation and its badness can come apart.
- **Murderous intention** (Calder). The murderer's desire for money may itself be fine. What's missing is an intention to pursue money only in ways that respect innocent people's rights (Feser following Alexander).
- **Sadism.** The sadist's desire is real, but it is misdirected — aimed against the concern for others that social animals need to flourish. It's a deformity of desire, as blindness is a deformity of the eye.

Feser is candid that the sadism analysis would need a full ethics to defend completely; his claim is only that sadism is no harder for the privation theory than any other badness.

The usual confusion is to think the theory says bad things are ‘made of nothing.’ It says instead that bad things are real things lacking something they should have. This is the premise that lets the next section keep evil out of God (step 28).

checks.q: What general strategy do Feser's four replies share?
options: Denying that bad things really exist
Granting that positive features are present but locating the badness in what is missing
Arguing that all pain is secretly good
Claiming that moral evil is merely subjective
checks.explanation: In each case — pain, murderous intent, sadism — the positive element is conceded and the badness traced to a privation.

checks.q: Which condition does Feser cite to show that pain can occur without its unpleasantness?
options: Phantom limb pain
Congenital analgesia
Pain asymbolia
Synesthesia
checks.explanation: In pain asymbolia pain is felt but isn't unpleasant, which separates the sensation from its badness. Congenital analgesia is the absence of pain altogether.

terms: Privation (and the privation theory of evil)

summary.heading: Perfect goodness III: God is all good, yet evil is not in him (pp. 221–223)
summary.body:
With the privation account in place, the conclusion is quick. If goodness corresponds to actuality and badness to unrealized potentiality, then God, who is **pure actuality** with no potentiality, is purely good with no badness at all (the forward route). And by proportionate causality, whatever good is or could be in the world must somehow be in God, so the source of all possible goodness is all-good (the backward route).

**Doesn't proportionate causality then put evil in God too?** No. Evil is not a positive reality but an absence. A world with evil in it is not made by making two kinds of thing, good things and bad things; it is made by making good things while refraining from making certain other goods. If I draw two sides of a triangle and stop partway through the third, the badness of the figure is not something extra I added — it is what I left out. Proportionate causality says the positive features of an effect must be in its cause; since evil is not a positive feature, it need not be in God.

**Isn't God's failure to create all the good he could a defect in him?** No more than my leaving the triangle unfinished shows a defect in me — I might have left it incomplete precisely to make a philosophical point in a lecture, and the understanding produced outweighs the trivial badness of the figure. Taken alone the triangle is bad, but the whole situation is good, and good in a way impossible without that element of badness. Similarly, some goods of creation require that certain local badness be permitted: **courage** cannot exist unless people face real danger of harm and do right anyway. Just as God cannot make a round square, he cannot make a world with courage but no real danger. (A footnote: the blessed in heaven keep the courage they acquired on earth, as an old veteran keeps the courage he won in battle.) The full treatment of the problem of evil comes in chapter 7.
summary.plain: If being good means being fully real in the way you should be, then God — who is completely real with nothing missing — is completely good. And God doesn't ‘contain’ evil, because evil isn't a thing he makes; it's a good that isn't there. Some good things, like courage, can't exist unless some bad things, like danger, are allowed.
summary.takeaway: God is perfectly good because he is pure actuality and the source of all good, and evil — being an absence rather than a thing — need not be in him.
summary.deepDive:
Once goodness is tied to actuality, the positive result comes quickly (steps 25–27): what is pure act, lacking nothing, is purely good; and by proportionate causality, the source of all good must itself be all-good.

The harder question is the one Feser raises against himself: if effects must be in their causes, and there is evil in the world, isn't evil in God? The answer turns on the principle's exact scope. Proportionate causality says the *positive* features of an effect must be in its total cause (step 11). Evil isn't a positive feature (step 23). So the principle simply doesn't apply to it.

Feser's picture: I draw two sides of a triangle and stop halfway through the third. The defect isn't something I added; it's what I left out. So too, God doesn't make two kinds of things, good ones and bad ones; he makes good things and refrains from making certain other goods (step 28).

A thought experiment to test this (course illustration): a sculptor leaves parts of a marble block rough to contrast with the polished face. Taken alone, the rough patch is ‘unfinished.’ Taken as part of the whole, it's part of the work's excellence. Feser's own version is the lecturer who leaves a triangle incomplete to make a philosophical point: the flaw is trivial, and the whole situation, including the students' understanding, is better than it could have been otherwise.

The courage example makes the point sharper. Courage is facing real danger and doing right anyway. A world with courage but no real danger is as impossible as a round square — so not even God can create it. That some goods logically require permitting some badness is why permitting badness is compatible with perfect goodness. (Feser adds, in a footnote, that the blessed in heaven keep the courage won on earth, as an old soldier keeps courage won in battle.)

Two cautions. First, this section doesn't solve the problem of evil; it establishes that God is not evil and evil is not ‘in’ him. Feser defers the full problem to chapter 7. Second, the usual confusion is to hear ‘God permits evil’ as ‘God makes evil and inserts it.’ On this account, there is nothing to insert — only goods not given.

checks.q: Which earlier result blocks the inference “there's evil in the world, so by proportionate causality evil is in God”?
options: Step 9: contradictions aren't powers
Step 15: God has an intellect
Step 33: God's will is free
Step 23: badness is a privation, not a positive feature
checks.explanation: Proportionate causality concerns the positive features of effects; because evil is a privation (step 23), the principle doesn't require it to be in God.

checks.q: How does Feser explain that the blessed in heaven still have courage, though they face no danger?
options: They acquired it while on earth and keep it, as an old veteran keeps courage won in battle
Heaven contains hidden dangers
Courage is not really a virtue
They lose it on entering heaven
checks.explanation: The footnote answers an obvious objection to the courage example: virtue acquired in danger is retained.

terms: Privation (and the privation theory of evil)

summary.heading: Will: from natural inclination to the divine will (pp. 223–224)
summary.body:
Every nature inclines toward its characteristic activities. A tree tends, wholly unconsciously, to sink roots and photosynthesize unless prevented. A dog seeks food, water, and mates *consciously*: animals have what the tradition calls **sensory appetite**. Rational creatures pursue ends consciously and also conceptualize them, inclining toward what they intellectually grasp as worth pursuing and away from what they grasp as not: this is **rational appetite, or will**.

Since God has something analogous to intellect, he must have something analogous to will, for two reasons. First, as plants and animals tend nonrationally toward realizing their natures and humans tend rationally, God must tend (rationally) toward his own nature — though he need do nothing to achieve it, being always already fully actual. He is more like something that has completed its striving than like something that never strove. Following Barry Miller, Feser calls this a **limit case** of rational appetite. A limit case differs from a mere upper limit: the speed of light is a limit that differs from lower speeds only in degree, but zero km/s is not a slowest speed — it is not a speed at all — yet the ordering of speeds points toward it. The divine will is the limit case toward which the appetites of plants, animals, and humans point. Second, God grasps all the things that could exist and causes some while not causing others, so there must be in him something analogous to willing the one and not the other.

It is worth seeing how the three grades build on each other. Each level keeps what the one below has and adds something: animals, like plants, have natural tendencies, but they also *feel* their way toward their goals; humans, like animals, feel desire, but they can also *think about* what is worth wanting and choose accordingly. The will, then, is not a mysterious extra faculty bolted onto the mind; it is simply the form inclination takes in a being that understands. That is why, having shown that God has something like an intellect, Feser can conclude he has something like a will — while insisting, as always, that the likeness is analogical.
summary.plain: Everything ‘leans’ toward what's good for it: a tree toward sunlight without knowing it, a dog toward food because it feels hungry, a person toward what she judges worth having. Since God has something like a mind and chooses which of all possible things to make real, he has something like a will. He doesn't strive or long for anything, though — he's already complete.
summary.takeaway: Because God has intellect and chooses which possible things to make actual, there is in him something analogous to will — the ‘limit case’ of the inclinations found in plants, animals, and humans.
summary.deepDive:
Two ideas carry this section: that will is a kind of *appetite* (inclination toward the good), and that God's will is a *limit case* of appetite.

First, appetite. We tend to think of ‘will’ as sheer decision-power. The Aristotelian tradition sees it differently: every nature tends toward its fulfillment. A tree tends unconsciously toward sinking roots (natural inclination); a dog consciously seeks food (sensory appetite); a human pursues what her intellect grasps as worth pursuing (rational appetite, or will). Will is inclination guided by understanding (step 29).

Second, the limit case, which is the subtle part. God doesn't *strive* toward his nature — he is already fully actual. So in what sense does he ‘incline’? Feser says he is more like something that has *completed* its striving than something that never strove at all. To make this precise he borrows Barry Miller's distinction. A *limit* differs only in degree from the series it tops: the speed of light is the fastest speed, still a speed. A *limit case* differs absolutely yet is what the series points toward: zero kilometres per second isn't the slowest speed — it isn't a speed at all — but the ordering of speeds points to it.

Try another example (course illustration): sounds of steadily decreasing loudness point toward silence, which is not the quietest sound but the absence of sound — yet you understand silence *through* the series. The divine will is like that relative to appetites: not a bigger craving, but the point toward which the progression from plant to animal to human tends, where inclination is pure rest in the good (step 30).

Feser's second reason is simpler: God grasps every possible thing and makes some actual but not others. That selection is analogous to willing some and not others.

The usual confusion: people picture God's will as a very strong desire, or as impulses and moods. That's precisely what the limit-case idea excludes. It also sets up the next question — whether this will is free.

checks.q: What distinguishes rational appetite (will) from sensory appetite?
options: Only rational appetite is conscious
Sensory appetite belongs to plants
Rational appetite follows what the intellect conceptually grasps as worth pursuing
Rational appetite has no object at all
checks.explanation: Animals pursue goals consciously too (so A is wrong); what's distinctive of will is that it follows intellectual apprehension of the good.

checks.q: Which of these is most like a ‘limit case’ in Barry Miller's sense?
options: The tallest mountain on Earth
Silence, relative to a series of ever-quieter sounds — not a sound at all, yet what the series points toward
The loudest possible sound
The average height of all mountains
checks.explanation: A limit case differs absolutely from the series (silence is no sound) while being pointed to by it, like zero speed. The tallest mountain is a mere limit.

summary.heading: The freedom of God's will — and two objections (pp. 224–226)
summary.body:
God's will is **free**. Nothing *external* can compel him, since everything else depends on him for its existence and activity at every instant. Nothing *internal* compels him either. All possibilities are grounded in the divine intellect: the concept of a lion and the concept of a unicorn are both there. Nothing in the concept of a lion requires that lions exist, nothing in the concept of a unicorn requires that unicorns not exist, and nothing in any other concept settles it. Before creation, a world with unicorns was as possible as one with lions, and God could have made either. Free of both external and internal compulsion, his will is free.

**Objection from simplicity** (Kretzmann, Richards): to act freely is to have potentials to do this or that and to actualize one of them; but a simple, purely actual God has no potentials; so either he is not free or he is not simple. (Kretzmann keeps strong simplicity and weakens freedom; Richards does the reverse.) Feser replies that this is another **fallacy of accident**. When *we* choose, we actualize potentials (moving a limb this way rather than that), but it does not follow that free choice *as such* requires actualizing potentials — just as the fact that creatures change when they act does not show that acting as such requires change. Granted, it is hard to picture a will that is free yet has no potentialities, and Brian Davies suggests reading “God's will is free” chiefly as negative theology: God is not compelled by anything outside or inside him. But difficulty is exactly what we should expect at the furthest remove from everyday experience; we know on independent grounds that God is simple and free; and our own freedom is famously mysterious too.
summary.plain: Nothing outside God can force him to do anything, since everything else depends on him; and nothing in his own ideas forces him to create one thing rather than another — lions and unicorns were equally possible. So God chooses freely. Critics say choosing requires being able to change, but that's only how choosing works for us, not what choosing essentially is.
summary.takeaway: God's will is free because nothing outside or inside him compels it, and the objection that freedom requires potentiality is a fallacy of accident.
summary.deepDive:
The argument for freedom has two halves (steps 31–33). *Nothing external* compels God, because nothing external is independent of him. *Nothing internal* compels him either — and this half is subtler.

Why isn't God's nature, or his knowledge, a kind of inner compulsion to create? Consider what's in his intellect: the concept of a lion and the concept of a unicorn. Nothing in the concept of a lion demands that lions exist. This connects to chapter 4's point that in creatures essence is distinct from existence: you can grasp *what* a thing is without that settling *whether* it is. So no idea in God carries a built-in necessity of being realized; before creation either world was equally possible.

Now the hard objection (Kretzmann, Richards). Freedom means having alternatives — potentials to go this way or that — and actualizing one. A purely actual God has no potentials. So either he isn't free, or he isn't truly simple. Kretzmann keeps strict simplicity and settles for a weaker freedom; Richards keeps robust freedom and settles for weaker simplicity.

Feser refuses the trade-off by identifying a fallacy of accident (step 34). *Our* free choices do involve actualizing potentials — moving a hand this way rather than that. But that is how freedom shows up in changeable, bodily beings; it isn't what freedom *is*. Compare Part A's point that our acting involves changing, though acting as such needn't. What freedom essentially is, is not being compelled.

A course note that may help: the ‘alternatives’ in divine freedom are alternative *effects*, not alternative states of God. Had God created unicorns instead, the difference would be in the world and in its relation to God (a Cambridge relation), not a different condition inside God.

Feser is candid that this is hard to picture. With Brian Davies, he suggests we understand divine freedom mainly negatively — God is not compelled. And he adds two sensible points: difficulty is exactly what we should expect this far from ordinary experience, and our *own* freedom is famously mysterious, yet we don't deny it.

The usual confusion: taking ‘free’ to mean ‘arbitrary’ or ‘could have been in a different mood.’ Freedom here means lack of compulsion, fully compatible with wisdom and goodness.

checks.q: Why is there nothing internal to God compelling him to create lions rather than unicorns?
options: Because lions are better than unicorns
Because God has no concept of lions
Because God is compelled by something external instead
Because no concept in the divine intellect includes the necessity that its instances exist
checks.explanation: Concepts of possible creatures don't contain existence; so God's knowledge of them doesn't force him to realize any (step 32).

checks.q: How do Kretzmann and Richards respond differently to the alleged conflict between simplicity and freedom?
options: Kretzmann keeps strong simplicity and weakens freedom; Richards keeps strong freedom and weakens simplicity
Kretzmann denies that God exists; Richards is an occasionalist
Both accept Feser's fallacy-of-accident reply
Both deny that God has a will
checks.explanation: Feser's footnote describes exactly this trade-off. His own view rejects the trade-off by denying that freedom as such requires potentiality.

summary.heading: Must God create the best possible world? (pp. 226–228)
summary.body:
A different challenge comes from **Leibniz**, revived by **William Rowe**: an omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God must create the best possible world, since otherwise he couldn't (against omnipotence), didn't know which was best (against omniscience), or didn't want to (against goodness). But if he could not have done otherwise, he was not free.

Feser identifies two hidden assumptions, both false. **(a) That one is always obliged to bring about the best one can.** Suppose a world with trees is better than one with only stones and water. Is God obliged to make it? Who would be wronged if he didn't? Not God, who is already perfectly good and fully actual and needs nothing, so he need not create at all. Not the trees, since what does not exist cannot be harmed or wronged. (If he created trees without water or sunshine, he might harm them, but only because they would then exist.)

**(b) That there is a best possible world.** If a world with trees is better than one without, a forest is better than one tree and many forests better than one — but there is no upper limit, since for any world with *x* forests there is a possible world with *x* + 1. So there is no best possible world, and God can no more be obliged to make one than to make a round square (Aquinas makes the same point).

**Rowe's rejoinder:** then for any world God makes, a being who made a better one would be more perfect, so there could be no most perfect being — and hence, if God must be perfect, no God. Feser replies that this assumes God's perfection depends on what he *does*. It follows instead from what he *is*: his pure actuality. A flawless **diamond** is a perfect diamond whether it cuts thin glass, thick glass, or no glass at all; by *agere sequitur esse* it has the *capacity* to cut many kinds of glass, but it need not exercise that capacity in any particular way. Likewise a perfect being has the power to create any possible world without having to create any given one, or any at all.
summary.plain: Some philosophers say a perfectly good God would have to make the best world possible, which would mean he had no real choice. Feser says nobody is wronged if God doesn't create something — things that don't exist can't be wronged — and anyway there's no ‘best possible world,’ just as there's no biggest number. God's perfection comes from what he is, not from what he makes.
summary.takeaway: God isn't obliged to create the best possible world, because no one is wronged by not being created and there is no best world — and his perfection flows from what he is, not from what he makes.
summary.deepDive:
The Leibniz–Rowe argument looks airtight at first: if God could, knew how, and wanted to make the best world, he would; so he must; so he isn't free. Feser's strategy is to expose two assumptions hiding inside it (step 34).

**Assumption (a): one must always bring about the best one can.** Ask the question moral obligation always raises: *to whom* would God owe it? Obligations are owed to someone who would be wronged. God himself can't be harmed by not creating; he is already perfectly good and lacks nothing. And trees that never exist can't be harmed either, because there is no one there to be harmed. Feser adds a careful qualification: if God created trees but withheld the water and sunlight they need, that *would* harm them — but only because they would then exist. Notice also that Feser frames the tree example hypothetically (“suppose a world with trees is better”); nothing hangs on the ranking.

**Assumption (b): there is a best possible world.** Here the structure is like a familiar mathematical fact (course comparison): for any number, there's a larger one, so there's no largest number. Feser's version: if trees make a world better, a forest is better than a tree, and a world with x forests is always outdone by one with x + 1. An unbounded series has no top member. So ‘the best possible world’ is like ‘the largest number’ — it names nothing, and God can no more be obliged to make it than to make a round square. (Aquinas made the same point.)

**Rowe's rejoinder** is clever: if every world could be bettered, then a being who made a better one would be more perfect than God, so there could be no most perfect being at all. Feser's answer relocates perfection. God's perfection follows from *what he is* — pure actuality — not from *what he produces*. A flawless diamond is perfect whether it cuts thick glass, thin glass, or nothing; by action-follows-being it has the *capacity* to cut many kinds, but its perfection doesn't wait on exercising it.

The usual confusion is to think Feser is saying the world is mediocre or that God chose carelessly. Neither follows. The point is only that ‘better world’ talk measures the product, not the maker, and that there is no ceiling the product must reach.

checks.q: “For any number there is a larger one, so there's no largest number.” This parallels which Feser argument?
options: The paradox of the stone
The privation account of badness
The argument that there is no best possible world
The argument against occasionalism
checks.explanation: For any world with x forests, one with x + 1 would be better, so there's no maximum — the same structure as the numbers.

checks.q: Who, according to Feser, would be wronged if God did not create trees?
options: The trees
No one: God needs nothing, and nonexistent trees can't be wronged
God himself
The angels
checks.explanation: What does not exist cannot be harmed or wronged; harm would arise only if God created trees and withheld what they need.

summary.heading: Love (pp. 228–229)
summary.body:
**Objection:** love requires being affected by the beloved — the parent anxious over a child's distress, the lover who cannot stop thinking of the beloved. Being affected is being changed. So an immutable God cannot love.

**Reply:** another **fallacy of accident**. Our love is usually accompanied by such emotional changes, but what is *essential* to love is that the lover **wills the good of the beloved**. That is why we call love shallow when it consists only of feelings that wax and wane with the beloved's presence, and serious when the lover keeps willing the other's good even when not feeling affectionate. It is why there is such a thing as “tough love,” where one does for the beloved's good what one's feelings resist, and love of enemies, where one does good to someone one dislikes; the willing is enough to make these acts loving despite the feelings. Love is essentially a matter of the will, which is active, rather than the emotions, which are passive.

Now God has will, directed toward creating the world. To be good is to be actual in some way, and to create is to actualize — and so to bring about all the goodness that follows from that actuality. To create trees is to will that trees exist and thereby to will what is good for trees: roots drawing in water, photosynthesis, and so on. So God's creating things entails that he **loves** them (Aquinas; Michael Dodds).

Notice how neatly this ties the chapter's threads together. Goodness was defined as actuality in line with a thing's nature; creating is actualizing; so creating just is conferring goodness. God's love is therefore not a response to some goodness already present in us, as human love often is — it is the very source of whatever goodness we have. And because love is located in the will rather than in fluctuating feeling, nothing about it requires God to change, grow warmer or cooler, or be moved by his creatures. The objection assumed that the most loving being would be the most emotionally affected one; Feser's answer is that the most loving being is the one who wills the most good, and God wills every good there is.
summary.plain: People often think love means feelings — worry, longing, being moved. But what makes love real is wanting and doing what's good for someone, even when the feelings aren't there; that's why ‘tough love’ is still love. God, by keeping us in existence and giving us everything good we have, is willing our good all the time. So an unchanging God can truly love.
summary.takeaway: Love is essentially willing the good of the beloved, so an unchanging God who wills the existence and flourishing of every creature genuinely loves them.
summary.deepDive:
The objection feels powerful because human love is so bound up with emotion. Feser's reply is another fallacy of accident (steps 35–37): emotional change usually *accompanies* our love, but it isn't what love *is*.

A thought experiment helps (course illustration). Picture a parent at 3 a.m. with a feverish child. She feels no warm glow — only exhaustion and irritation — yet she gets up, fetches medicine, and sits by the bed. Is that love? Obviously yes; arguably it's love at its most real. Now picture someone flooded with tender feelings for a friend who never lifts a finger when the friend needs help. We call that shallow. The difference lies in the will. That's why Feser appeals to ‘tough love’ (doing what the beloved needs even when feeling resists) and love of enemies (willing good to someone you dislike): in both, the will suffices to make the act loving despite the emotions.

Feser's contrast is between the will, which is *active*, and emotions, which are *passive* — things that happen to us. Since God has will (step 30) and no passivity, love can be predicated of him in its essential core.

The second half of the argument (step 36) is easy to miss. Why think God wills *our good*, rather than merely our existence? Because goodness just is actuality in line with a nature (step 23). To will that trees exist is thereby to will that they have roots drawing water and leaves photosynthesizing — the goods that make up a flourishing tree. Creating is conferring goodness.

A nuance worth stating: Feser doesn't claim human emotions in love are bad or unimportant. They are fitting for bodily creatures. His claim is only that they aren't *essential* to love, so their absence in God doesn't make his love less. Indeed (a course note in line with Aquinas, whom Feser cites), our love responds to goodness it finds, while God's love causes the goodness that is there.

The usual confusion is to equate ‘immutable’ with ‘indifferent.’ Indifference is a lack of will for another's good; God's immutability is the steady fullness of that will.

checks.q: Why does Feser point to ‘tough love’ and love of enemies?
options: They show love's essence is willing the other's good, which can persist against one's feelings
They show love is always painful
They show God is severe
They show love is essentially an emotion
checks.explanation: In both cases the will to do good makes the act loving despite contrary feelings, which isolates the will as love's core.

checks.q: What is the logical flaw Feser finds in the objection that an immutable God cannot love?
options: It confuses privation with negation
It is circular
It commits a fallacy of accident
It appeals to authority
checks.explanation: It treats a usual accompaniment of human love (being emotionally affected) as essential to love as such.

summary.heading: Incomprehensibility: known truly, never comprehended fully (pp. 229–232)
summary.body:
**In a loose sense we can comprehend God**, and the whole book shows it: understanding sound arguments for his existence and attributes just is understanding something of him. Much of this knowledge is negative (apophatic) — God is not composite, changeable, material, or in time or space — but negative knowledge is real knowledge. And positive attributes are predicated **analogically**, which is not metaphorical but literal, and which is used in fields other than theology.

The **analogy of attribution** gives a first grip on attributes like power: when we say both God and the sun have power (the sun to melt ice), God is the *primary analogate*, pure underived power, and the sun a *secondary analogate* whose power depends on God at every instant. Goodness and other attributes can be treated similarly. The **analogy of proper proportionality** adds more. As the eye is to a tree, so the intellect is to the Pythagorean theorem, which is why we speak of “seeing” in both cases. Similarly, a tree is to its goodness as a virtuous human is to his, and as an angel such as Saint Michael is to his — though the tree's goodness develops gradually and unconsciously, the human's gradually through choices made sometimes against disordered bodily desire, the angel's through choice but neither over time nor against bodily desire. (Whether angels exist doesn't matter to the point.) God is to his goodness as these are to theirs, though his is more radically different still: unlike a good angel who could have chosen evil, God cannot fail to be good, being pure actuality. His goodness is the **limit case** of goodness, and knowledge and will can be understood the same way.

So the position is rationalist, not fideist, and not purely negative. But **in the strictest sense we cannot comprehend God**, and simplicity guarantees this. We understand material systems deeply by learning their components and how they fit together; we understand even immaterial things by genus and specific difference. Neither method applies to what is utterly noncomposite. God is hard to understand *precisely because* he is simple — paradoxical only if we confuse “simple” (partless) with “easy.” As we strip creaturely limitations from goodness, knowledge, and power, the positive content of our predications thins out, though not to nothing.

This is not obscurantism. Physics tells us of entities with both wave and particle properties and of curved space itself, and rightly replies to skeptics that strange language is to be expected so far from everyday experience. Natural theology goes deeper still, to the deepest level of reality, and it is the arguments themselves that tell us our grasp of it must be feeble.
summary.plain: We can really know things about God — both what he isn't (he isn't physical, isn't changing) and, in a stretched but still literal sense, what he is (powerful, good). But we can never understand him completely, because we understand things by taking them apart, and God has no parts. That's not a cop-out; physics also has to use strange ideas when it studies things far from everyday life.
summary.takeaway: We know God truly — negatively and by literal analogy — but cannot comprehend him fully, because a simple being has no parts or genus-and-difference structure for the mind to analyze.
summary.deepDive:
This section walks a tightrope between two errors: saying we know nothing about God, and saying we have him figured out.

**Why we know something.** Negative knowledge is real knowledge (step 38). A course comparison: if a detective knows the culprit is *not* left-handed, *not* over six feet, and *not* in town Tuesday, he knows a good deal, even without a name. Likewise ‘not composite, not changing, not material, not in time’ tells us a lot. And positive predicates apply by analogy, which Feser insists is *literal*, not metaphorical. Two kinds:

- *Attribution*: God is the primary analogate of ‘power’ — pure, underived power — and the sun, which melts ice, is a secondary analogate whose power is borrowed at every instant.
- *Proper proportionality*: a tree is to its goodness as a virtuous person is to his, as an angel is to his, as God is to his. The goodness differs enormously: gradual and unconscious in the tree; gradual and chosen, sometimes against disordered desire, in the person; chosen but timeless and free of bodily desire in the angel. God's differs more still, since he *cannot* fail to be good: his goodness is the limit case.

**Why we can't comprehend him.** Strict comprehension works by analysis (steps 40–41): we understand an engine by its parts and their arrangement, a species by its genus and specific difference. God has neither. Hence the paradox-that-isn't: God is hard to understand *because* he is simple — ‘simple’ meaning partless, not easy. And as we strip creaturely limitations from ‘good,’ ‘wise,’ ‘powerful,’ the positive content thins out, though not to nothing.

**Why this isn't obscurantism.** The strangeness is a *result* of the arguments, not a patch applied when they fail. Physics offers the comparison: wave-particle duality and curved space are hard to picture because physics has traveled far from everyday experience, where our words were formed. Natural theology travels further, to the deepest level of reality.
