The usual confusion runs both ways: some hear ‘incomprehensible’ as ‘unknowable’ (so why argue?), others hear ‘analogy’ as ‘just a metaphor’ (so nothing is really said). Both miss Feser's middle position. Part A of the chapter supplied the theory of analogy; this section cashes it out.

checks.q: Why does Feser say God is hard to understand precisely because he is simple?
options: Because ‘simple’ is only a metaphor
Because God is actually highly complex
Because simplicity implies that God is ignorant
Because understanding normally proceeds by analysis into parts or genus and difference, which a noncomposite being lacks
checks.explanation: ‘Simple’ means ‘without parts,’ and our usual route to full understanding is analysis — which has nothing to work on in God.

checks.q: Which examples from physics does Feser use to show that strangeness is expected at reality's frontiers?
options: Entropy and black holes
Wave-particle duality and curved space
The Big Bang and dark matter
Quarks and strings
checks.explanation: Things with both wave and particle properties, and space itself being curved, are Feser's (and Part A's) examples.

checks.q: On Feser's view, the statement “God is good” is:
options: A metaphor, like “George is a lion”
Equivocal, like “bat” for the animal and the stick
Literal but analogical, God's goodness being the limit case
Univocal, like “dog” said of Fido and Rover
checks.explanation: Analogical predication is literal and intermediate between univocal and equivocal; God is to his goodness as creatures are to theirs, in the limit case.

summary.heading: Conservation: creation at every moment, no existential inertia, no pantheism (pp. 232–234)
summary.body:
The Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, Thomistic, and rationalist proofs all show that nothing distinct from God could continue to exist for an instant unless God sustained it. This is the doctrine of **divine conservation**: without divine causation the world would be instantly annihilated. Creation is not a one-time event in the distant past but something happening at every moment.

These arguments also answer the rival thesis of **“existential inertia”** (Beaudoin, Adler, Rundle): that some things, once they exist, tend to persist on their own until something destroys them, and so need no conserver. Its defenders never explain what about a material or contingent thing could give it this remarkable feature; it is merely suggested as if it were as plausible as conservation. Worse, no contingent thing *could* have it, since all such things are composite — mixtures of act and potency and of essence and existence — and anything composite in these ways needs a sustaining cause. Floating the idea does not answer those arguments; it ignores them. (A footnote dispatches the related suggestion that the *world* might be the necessary being: nothing composite, potential, or with essence distinct from existence can be necessary; and even a derived necessity would presuppose God, as Aquinas's Third Way argues.)

Dependent at every moment, created things are nonetheless **distinct from God**: they are composite, he is simple; they are act-plus-potency, he is pure act; their essence differs from their existence, his does not; they are contingent, he is necessary. This rules out **pantheism** (God identical with the world) and also **panentheism** (God not identical with the world but present in it so as to be changed by it), since God is immutable.
summary.plain: God didn't just start the world long ago and walk away; he's keeping it in existence right now, every instant, the way a song exists only while someone is singing it. Some philosophers suggest things might just keep existing on their own, but they never explain how, and anything made of parts needs something holding it in being. Still, depending on God doesn't make the world part of God — the world and God are genuinely different.
summary.takeaway: Creation is not a past event but God's present causing of everything's existence; nothing contingent can coast on ‘existential inertia,’ and this dependence doesn't blur the difference between God and the world.
summary.deepDive:
The key to this section is understanding *why* the proofs give us conservation and not merely a first moment (step 42).

Recall the distinction from chapter 1 between two kinds of causal series. In a *per accidens* series — grandfather, father, son — earlier members can vanish and later ones carry on. In a *per se* series — hand moves stick moves stone — each member acts only because it's being acted on *right now*; remove the hand and everything stops at once. The proofs are about per se dependence. A thing whose essence doesn't include existence, or which is a mix of act and potency, doesn't just need a cause to *start* existing; it needs one for existing *now*. That's why Feser says creation is happening at every moment.

A course illustration: the light in a room. Flip off the switch and the light doesn't drift on for a while by inertia; it's gone. The world is related to God more like the light to its source than like a house to its long-dead builder.

**Existential inertia** is the attempt to deny this: maybe things, once existing, just persist until destroyed. Feser's two replies are worth separating. (1) *No explanation is ever offered*: what feature of a contingent thing would give it this power? It's simply floated as a possibility. (2) *It can't be true*, given the composition arguments: whatever is composite of act and potency or essence and existence needs a sustaining cause. Proposing inertia doesn't refute those arguments; it ignores them. Don't confuse this with Newtonian inertia, which describes a body's *motion* on the assumption that the body exists.

Finally, dependence isn't identity (step 43). Creatures are composite, potential, contingent, with essence distinct from existence; God is simple, pure act, necessary, subsistent existence. The very features that make creatures need God make them *not* God — ruling out pantheism. And since God is immutable, panentheism (God changed by the world) is excluded too.

The usual confusion: picturing conservation as God occasionally shoring up a world that tends to fall apart, like a maintenance man. Conservation isn't repair; it's the ongoing giving of existence itself.

checks.q: Why do the proofs establish divine conservation rather than merely a first moment of creation?
options: Because they are arguments about the Big Bang
Because they show composite, contingent things need a cause of their existence at every instant, not just at a beginning
Because they assume the universe had a beginning
Because they are arguments from miracles
checks.explanation: The proofs concern per se, here-and-now dependence, which is why creation is happening at every moment.

checks.q: Why doesn't total dependence on God make the world part of God (pantheism)?
options: Because God is located inside the world
Because the world is an illusion
Because pantheism is condemned by tradition
Because creatures are composite, potential, and contingent, while God is simple, pure act, and necessary — so they depend on him yet are distinct
checks.explanation: The same features that make creatures need a cause distinguish them from their cause (step 43).

summary.heading: Concurrence: between occasionalism and mere conservationism (pp. 234–238)
summary.body:
Combine two theses — creatures depend on God for existence, yet are distinct from him — with *agere sequitur esse*, and the result is the doctrine of **divine concurrence**, best understood against two rivals. **Occasionalism** says no creature causes anything; only God does. When ice cubes in iced tea melt in the sun, God melts them on the occasion of the sun's being out; when the cue ball strikes the eight ball, God sends the eight ball into the pocket. **Mere conservationism** says God keeps things in being but they exercise their causal powers independently of him: God keeps the sun in existence, but the sun melts the ice on its own.

**Against occasionalism.** (1) Since action follows being, a thing that could truly do nothing would not truly exist, so occasionalism implies God alone exists. But you know you exist even if you doubt tables and chairs, and you are not God: you move from thought to thought (so you change), you are uncertain (so you are not omniscient), you can't stop having experiences you judge unreal (so you are not omnipotent). A footnote adds that this also sinks pantheism-by-illusion: whatever *has* the illusion of a changing, many-sided world undergoes successive, distinct, erroneous experiences, so it is changeable, composite, contingent, and ignorant — not God. (2) Occasionalism is self-undermining. We reached God as First Cause only by reasoning from real things that change, are composite, and so on, and require a cause. Saying only God exists abandons the very grounds of the ascent, like a man who carefully climbs a ladder and then zaps it out from under himself with a ray gun. (Nor can the occasionalist retreat to the Augustinian proof, which does not start from causality and so does not give him God as the source of all causal power.)

**Against mere conservationism.** (1) By the same principle, if something could act independently of God, it could exist independently of him — yielding essentially **deism**, a God whose creatures carry on without him. But nothing composite can exist an instant without conservation. (2) It too blasts away the ladder, since the proofs began from the fact that things cannot exist on their own even for an instant.

**Concurrentism** holds that **secondary causes are real**. They are genuine *causes* because they make a real contribution: the effect would differ if a different secondary cause were involved. They are *secondary* because without God's concurrence they would be inert. In **Alfred Freddoso's** example, when you draw a square with blue chalk, you are responsible for there being a square at all, the chalk for its being blue — red chalk or a pencil would change the effect, but without your hand there is no effect. Or consider the **moon**, whose appearance depends on its own surface, but which gives no light without the sun. Does this undermine human freedom? No: in **David Oderberg's** example, a father guides his small son's hand to write an A. The boy can resist or cooperate, and his choice makes a real difference, but the A will not appear without the father's guidance. God's concurrence with our free acts is like that.
summary.plain: Does the sun really melt ice, or does God do it? Feser says both, at different levels: the sun is a real cause, and its particular features really matter, but it can act only because God is giving it being and power at every moment — like chalk that really makes a square blue but only moves if your hand moves it. Saying only God acts makes creatures unreal; saying creatures act on their own makes God unnecessary. Neither works.
summary.takeaway: Created things are real but secondary causes: they genuinely contribute to their effects, yet act only as God concurs — the middle way between occasionalism and mere conservationism.
summary.deepDive:
The central idea here is that God and creatures are *not dividing up the same job*. That's what both rival views get wrong (steps 44–46).

A tempting picture (a course warning) is a split: God does 90 percent of the causing and the creature does 10, or God supplies the push and the creature the rest. On that picture, whatever God does, the creature doesn't, and vice versa. Occasionalism takes the logic to one extreme (God does it all, creatures nothing); mere conservationism to the other (creatures do all the acting, God only keeps them in existence). Concurrentism rejects the split itself.

Freddoso's chalk shows how. When you draw a blue square, you are why there is a square *at all*; the chalk is why it is *blue*. These are different contributions, not shares of one. Swap in red chalk or a pencil and the effect changes, so the chalk is a *true* cause. Take away your hand and nothing happens, so it is a *secondary* cause. The moon is the same: its look depends on its own surface, but without the sun it gives no light.

Notice the elegant symmetry in Feser's refutations — both use *agere sequitur esse*:

- If creatures could do *nothing*, they would *be* nothing; so occasionalism leaves only God existing. But you exist and are clearly not God (you change, you doubt, you can't stop your own experiences).
- If creatures could act *independently*, they could *exist* independently; so mere conservationism becomes deism. But no composite thing can exist independently for an instant.

And both views are self-defeating: the proofs climbed from real things that change and can't sustain themselves. Deny either fact and you blast away the ladder you climbed.

Freedom (steps 47–48) follows the same pattern. In Oderberg's example the father guides his son's hand to write an A; the boy can resist or cooperate, and his choice really shapes the result, but no A appears without the father. Keep the caveat: the father is still a force alongside the child, which God is not. The analogy shows compatibility, not mechanism.

The usual confusion is to hear ‘God concurs in everything’ as occasionalism. It's the opposite: concurrence is precisely what lets creatures be real causes.

checks.q: A pool player's cue ball sinks the eight ball. On concurrentism, what caused the eight ball's motion?
options: Both: the cue ball as a real secondary cause, and God as first cause giving it being and power
Only God, on the occasion of the collision
Only the cue ball, independently of God
Neither; causation is an illusion
checks.explanation: B is occasionalism, C is mere conservationism. Concurrentism affirms both causes, operating at different levels.

checks.q: Why does mere conservationism slide into deism, according to Feser?
options: Because it denies God exists
Because it denies creatures exist
Because what could act independently of God could exist independently of him
Because it affirms miracles
checks.explanation: By agere sequitur esse, independence in acting implies independence in being — the deist picture of a world that could run without God.

checks.q: Whose example is the father guiding his son's hand to write an A?
options: Alfred Freddoso
Herbert McCabe
Anselm Ramelow
David Oderberg
checks.explanation: Oderberg's example concerns freedom; Freddoso's is the blue chalk.

summary.heading: Miracles I: why “violation of a law of nature” is the wrong definition (pp. 238–241)
summary.body:
Whether any particular miracle, such as the Resurrection, occurred is beyond natural theology, but what a miracle would be and whether one could occur are questions the book's metaphysics can answer.

Since **Hume**, a miracle has often been defined as a *violation of a law of nature*: a regular correlation between A-type causes and B-type effects fails in some instance. Skeptics then argue that evidence of such a “violation” would really be evidence that the supposed law was not a law, so miracles are incoherent.

On the **Aristotelian-Thomistic** view, a law of nature describes the tendencies or dispositions a thing has by virtue of its nature. That water freezes at 32°F just is water's natural disposition to freeze at that temperature — and the example is oversimplified, since liquid water can in unusual circumstances exist below that temperature, which only confirms that laws concern dispositions, which can be blocked or can manifest only under certain conditions. Anselm Ramelow puts it that for Aquinas laws describe what happens *normally*, according to things' natures, and exceptions are compatible with them. So one problem with the Humean definition is that it assumes too crude a picture: a disposition that is blocked or untriggered is not a violated law, and so is evidence neither of a miracle nor of a failed law.

A second problem: as Oderberg puts it, “The laws of nature are the laws of natures.” So laws are not contingent in the Humean way. For the Humean, water could be just what it is yet turn into chocolate mousse at 32°F; fire could freeze water; an acorn could grow into a dog; a dog could fly by wagging its tail, if only the laws were different. For the Aristotelian this makes no sense: different laws would mean different natures and so different things. Whatever reliably turned into mousse at 32°F would not be water. Laws of nature are therefore **metaphysically necessary** — given that the things whose natures they express exist. (There could have been a world without water, fire, acorns, or dogs, only look-alikes; in that limited sense the actual laws are contingent.) But if laws are necessary in this way, *violations are impossible*: if the triggers are present and nothing blocks the disposition, the manifestation follows.
summary.plain: Many people define a miracle as God ‘breaking the laws of nature.’ Feser says that's the wrong picture: a law of nature is just a description of how a kind of thing tends to behave because of what it is, so it can't be ‘broken’ — if water reliably turned into pudding at freezing temperature, it simply wouldn't be water. That leaves the question of what a miracle really is, which the next part answers.
summary.takeaway: Because laws of nature are the laws of the natures of things, they cannot be violated — so Hume's definition of a miracle as a ‘violation’ misunderstands both laws and miracles.
summary.deepDive:
Two ideas carry this section: laws as dispositions, and the necessity of laws given that the things exist (steps 49–50).

**Dispositions.** A course example: salt has a disposition to dissolve in water. That disposition is really there in the salt shaker even though nothing is dissolving; it needs a trigger (water). And it can be blocked: in water already saturated with salt, more salt won't dissolve. Neither fact refutes the ‘law’ that salt dissolves in water. Feser makes the same point with water freezing at 32°F: in unusual conditions water stays liquid below that temperature, which only shows that laws describe tendencies that can be blocked or untriggered. So a failure to manifest isn't a violation — and isn't evidence *either* of a miracle *or* of a false law.

That matters because Hume's skeptical argument depends on the crude picture. If laws are just exceptionless regularities, then any exception, including a purported miracle, proves the ‘law’ wasn't a law. On the dispositional picture, the argument has nothing to grip.

**Necessity.** The Humean thinks the *very same* water could have obeyed different laws — turning to chocolate mousse at 32°F — just as an acorn could have grown into a dog, if the laws had been otherwise. The Aristotelian says this makes no sense: laws flow from natures, so different laws mean different natures and therefore different things. Anything that reliably turned to mousse at 32°F wouldn't be water.

The qualification is crucial and often missed: Feser does *not* say the world or its laws had to exist. There might have been no water, fire, or acorns at all — only look-alikes. In that sense the actual laws are contingent. What's necessary is conditional: *given* that water exists, it behaves as water does. And given that, a genuine violation — all the triggers present, nothing blocking, yet the manifestation fails — is impossible.

The usual confusion is to think this makes miracles impossible. It makes *violations* impossible. That's exactly why Feser needs a better account of miracles, which comes next.

checks.q: Why doesn't liquid water below 32°F refute the law that water freezes at 32°F?
options: Because the law is actually false
Because such water is a miracle
Because laws describe dispositions, which can be blocked or lack their triggers
Because thermometers are unreliable
checks.explanation: A disposition can be present without manifesting; its failure to manifest isn't a violation of the law.

checks.q: In what sense are the actual laws of nature contingent, on Feser's view?
options: There might have been no water, fire, acorns, or dogs at all — only look-alikes
The very same water could have behaved differently
God could alter water's nature while it stayed water
Laws are just statistical averages
checks.explanation: What's contingent is whether such things exist; given that they do, their laws are metaphysically necessary. B and C are the Humean view Feser rejects.

summary.heading: Miracles II: supernatural, not an intervention (pp. 241–244)
summary.body:
What then is a miracle? Following Ramelow's summary of the Thomistic view: what defines a miracle is not merely being an exception to the natural course (defects are exceptions too) but **elevating a thing to a power its nature cannot account for**. Defects are *sub*-natural; miracles are *super*-natural — not contrary to nature but beyond it. Because a miracle's cause lies outside the natural order altogether, it can only be God. It must not be confused with merely **preternatural** effects that a finite spirit such as an angel might produce, since angels are still creatures with natures, part of the natural order broadly construed, existing and acting only as God conserves them and concurs with them.

So miracles are nothing like **magic** or advanced technology. God is not an especially powerful cause alongside natural and preternatural causes; he is outside that whole order, the precondition of there being any causal power at all — “first” in the sense of fundamental, not merely earliest. It is therefore a mistake to think ordinary events happen on their own while God causes miracles. The world is not an **airplane on autopilot** with God occasionally correcting course; he causes the ordinary as much as the miraculous, and in fact the ordinary course of things, not miracles, is the most direct evidence of God as First Cause. Brian Davies notes that on classical theism such events cannot literally be “interventions,” since they and what preceded them are equally God's work. Herbert McCabe adds that God cannot interfere in the universe, not for lack of power but “because, so to speak, he has too much”: to interfere you must be an alternative to, or alongside, what you interfere with, and the cause of everything is alongside nothing.

“Violation” and “intervention” both wrongly suggest God must *force* things, as a machinist tinkers with a machine. Better analogies: the world is **music** and God the musician; the ordinary course is his playing from the score, a miracle is a jazz-style improvisation — every note, written or improvised, is his, yet the improvisation adds something new. Or the world is a **movie** and a miracle belongs to the “director's cut”; or a **story** and a miracle is material added in a second edition. In each case the original was complete and good as far as it went, so a miracle is not essentially a repair of a defect but a raising of something already good to a higher level. (A footnote cites C. S. Lewis: when God creates a miraculous cell in a virgin's body, nature at once takes it over and pregnancy proceeds by all the normal laws.)
summary.plain: A real miracle, Feser says, is God lifting something beyond what its nature could ever do on its own — not something even a very powerful creature could pull off. And God doesn't ‘break in’ to do it, because he's already the one making everything happen all the time, like a jazz musician who improvises on a tune he's already playing. The ordinary running of the world is actually the best evidence for God.
summary.takeaway: A miracle is God elevating a thing beyond what any created nature can do — and it is no ‘intervention,’ because God, as the source of all causal power, is not a cause alongside the others.
summary.deepDive:
The pivotal idea is *not a cause among causes* (step 52), and it's worth slowing down on.

Picture two ways God might relate to the world (a course contrast). On the *interventionist* picture, the world is a machine that runs by itself and God is an outside mechanic who occasionally reaches in. On Feser's picture, God is already giving every part of the world its existence and power at every moment (conservation and concurrence). On the first picture, a miracle is an interruption. On the second, the idea of ‘interruption’ doesn't apply: you can't interfere in what you yourself are doing. That's the force of McCabe's and Davies's point that God can't intervene — not because he's too weak, but because he isn't standing alongside the world as one agent next to another.

So what *is* a miracle? Following Ramelow, an effect that raises a thing to a power its nature can't account for (step 51). Three categories keep this clear:

- *Subnatural*: falling below a nature — a defect, like a diseased tree.
- *Preternatural*: extraordinary, but within the power of some creature, such as an angel, if angels exist. Still part of the natural order broadly construed.
- *Supernatural*: beyond every created nature, with a cause outside the natural order. Only God.

This is also why miracles are nothing like magic or advanced technology, which are just more causes within nature, possibly hidden ones.

Feser's analogies make the positive picture vivid. A jazz musician improvising doesn't force the music anywhere; every note, written or improvised, is his, yet the improvisation adds something the score didn't contain. A director's cut adds scenes; a second edition adds chapters. In each case the original was complete and good, so the addition *raises* rather than *repairs*. (Feser's footnote cites C. S. Lewis: a miraculous conception is immediately taken up by nature's ordinary laws.)

A striking corollary: the ordinary course of nature, not miracles, is the most direct evidence of God, since the proofs show that anything's existing and acting requires the First Cause. The usual confusion — a ‘god of the gaps’ who shows up only in the unexplained — gets things backward.

checks.q: Why does Feser say the ordinary course of nature is better evidence for God than miracles?
options: Because miracles are rare
Because miracles are all fraudulent
Because nature is beautiful
Because the proofs show that the ordinary existence and activity of things already requires God as First Cause
checks.explanation: The book's arguments start from ordinary change, composition, and existence; miracles are not needed to show God is at work.

checks.q: Which analogy best fits Feser's view of a miracle?
options: A mechanic fixing a broken car
A jazz musician improvising on a tune he is himself playing
A pilot taking over from autopilot
A hacker breaking into a secure system
checks.explanation: The other three picture an outsider interfering with a system that runs without him — exactly the picture Feser rejects.

summary.heading: Miracles III: subtraction miracles, suspension, and the bridge to revelation (pp. 244–246)
summary.body:
Feser supplements Ramelow: a miracle need not *add* to nature; it could *subtract*. A resurrection or the multiplication of loaves and fishes adds something, but in the story of **Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego** in the fiery furnace, what matters is what does *not* happen: they are not burned. Doesn't that violate the law that fire burns? No. Following Oderberg, a miracle is a **suspension** of a law, not a **breach**. By analogy with human law, a breach would be like a government leaving a law on the books but not enforcing it; a suspension is like temporarily revoking the law, so that what would have been a violation no longer is.

In terms of the analogies: the Resurrection is like a musician adding to the score; the furnace is like the musician omitting notes, a director cutting a key scene, or a novelist dropping a planned passage. Since a thing can act at any instant only as God conserves it and concurs with it, a subtractive miracle involves not special divine action but God's **refraining** from conserving or concurring with some or all of the factors (the fire, its preconditions such as oxygen), so the normal effect does not follow. It is not God making fire act against its nature — that would be a violation — but God not bringing certain things about in the first place. (Whether these particular miracles happened is not being argued; they illustrate kinds of possible miracle.)

Since God can add to or subtract from the natural order, **miracles are possible**. Why would he work one? For instance, to confirm a revelation of truths we could not reach by philosophy or science. How would we know a prophet was sent by God and not making things up? If he worked miracles, since only God can — a divine **“seal of approval.”** Miracles are thus the **bridge between natural and revealed theology**. They provide a rational basis for faith, which is not believing without or against evidence, but (for Aquinas and others) believing something *because God has revealed it* — and that God has revealed it needs evidence, which only a miracle could supply. Faith is grounded in reason, not opposed to it.

Natural theology cannot by itself establish any particular religion, but it screens claims. A religion that denies one ultimate divine cause, identifies God with the world, makes God impersonal, material, or finite in power or knowledge, is thereby shown false. And a religion claiming revelation without the backing of a miracle in the strict sense gives us no reason to take that claim seriously.
summary.plain: Some miracles add something, like a person raised from the dead; others take something away, like the story of three men thrown into a furnace who weren't burned. In the second kind, God doesn't force fire to act against its nature — he simply stops giving it the power to burn, which he has to give at every moment anyway. Why would God do miracles? One reason is to show that a messenger really speaks for him, which makes faith reasonable rather than blind.
summary.takeaway: Miracles can subtract as well as add — by God withholding his conserving and concurring action, a suspension rather than a breach — and their purpose is to certify revelation, bridging natural and revealed theology.
summary.deepDive:
The subtle move here is how a *subtractive* miracle avoids being a violation (step 53).

Start from what concurrence already taught: a fire burns at any instant only because God is conserving it and concurring with its activity at that instant. Normally that concurrence is given, and fire does what fire does. Now suppose God simply doesn't give it — withholds his conserving or concurring action from the fire, or from its preconditions such as oxygen. Then the burning doesn't happen. Nothing has been *forced* to act against its nature. Something just hasn't been brought about.

Contrast the impossible alternative: God keeps conserving the fire and all its conditions, concurs with all of it, and yet somehow makes the whole collection act contrary to its nature. *That* would be a violation — which, since laws express natures (step 50), can't happen.

Oderberg's human-law analogy sharpens this. A *breach* is like a government leaving a law on the books but not enforcing it. A *suspension* is like temporarily revoking the law, so that what would have been a violation isn't one. The musician analogy works too: an additive miracle is an improvised flourish; a subtractive one is leaving out notes from the score.

Feser is careful to add disclaimers: whether the Resurrection or the fiery furnace actually happened is beyond natural theology; they're illustrations of kinds of possible miracle.

**The purpose** (steps 55–56). Suppose a prophet teaches something no philosophy or science could establish. How could we know he isn't making it up? If he works a miracle — which only God can do — that functions as God's endorsement. This explains Feser's claim about faith: not believing without evidence, but believing something *because God revealed it*, where *that* God revealed it needs evidence. Faith rests on reason.

A practical corollary (course note): natural theology works as a filter. It can't prove any particular religion, but it rules out religions that make God many, material, finite, impersonal, or identical with the world — and it tells us to ignore claims of revelation that come without genuine miracles.

The usual confusion is to think Feser has smuggled in his religion. He explicitly stops short: the argument shows miracles are possible and what they'd be for, not that any occurred.

checks.q: Why does Feser say a subtractive miracle, like the fiery furnace, involves ‘not God acting in a special way’?
options: Because it consists in God refraining from conserving or concurring with some of the relevant factors
Because God never acts in the world at all
Because the fire acted against its own nature
Because an angel performed it
checks.explanation: Since things act only with God's ongoing concurrence, withholding it means the normal effect simply doesn't arise — a suspension, not a breach.

checks.q: Why would a miracle count as evidence that a teaching is revealed by God?
options: Because miracles are rare events
Because prophets are generally honest
Because only God can cause a strict miracle, so it works as a divine endorsement
Because a miracle proves any claim whatsoever
checks.explanation: Only a strictly supernatural effect must come from God, so it can certify that a message has a divine source.

summary.heading: Appendix: Is God male? (pp. 246–248)
summary.body:
God is immaterial and incorporeal, so he is not an animal, not a human being, and therefore **not literally a man or a woman: he is sexless**. Yet Feser, like the tradition, uses masculine language, and argues that there are good philosophical reasons for it, against critics who call it sexist and adopt the clumsy “he/she/it.”

First, God has intellect and will, which define **personality**, so the impersonal “it” is inappropriate. Second, why “he” rather than “she”? Because God's relation to the world is much more like a **paternal** than a maternal relationship, biologically considered. In procreation the father's role is active (he impregnates) and the mother's passive (she is impregnated); the father's body is unchanged while the mother's changes radically; the mother becomes more dependent on the father for provision, while the father does not depend physically on mate or child (which is why, sadly, he can walk away); and the child is physically continuous with the mother but not the father, who remains more distant throughout gestation.

The parallels: God is active in creating, the world passive in being created; God is unchangeable, the world constantly changing; the world depends on God at every instant, God not at all on the world; God is utterly distinct from the world, neither identical to it (pantheism) nor continuous with it (panentheism). So paternal, masculine language is the most natural and least misleading, while maternal imagery would suggest a God who changes with, or is continuous with, the world — at odds with immutability, immateriality, eternity, and pure actuality.
summary.plain: God has no body, so he's neither male nor female. Feser still defends calling God ‘he’: God is a person (he knows and wills), so ‘it’ is wrong, and his relation to the world — acting on it, not being changed by it, not depending on it — is more like a father's role than a mother's in bringing a child into being. Feser thinks mother-imagery would suggest a God who is part of the world or changed by it.
summary.takeaway: God is sexless, but ‘he’ is the least misleading pronoun: God is personal (not ‘it’), and his active, independent, distinct relation to the world resembles fatherhood more than motherhood.
summary.deepDive:
It's important to get the exact shape of Feser's claim, because it's easy to mishear. He does *not* say God is male; he says explicitly that God, being immaterial and not an animal, is sexless (step 57). His question is which language is *least misleading*, given everything the book has argued.

The argument has two stages. First, why a personal pronoun at all? Because God has intellect and will, which are what personhood consists in. ‘It’ would suggest an impersonal force — a view Feser says natural theology refutes.

Second, why masculine rather than feminine? Feser draws on a biological asymmetry, used analogically (step 58). In procreation the father's role is active and the mother's receptive; the father's body is unchanged by conception while the mother's changes radically; the father is not physically dependent on mother or child (which is why, sadly, he *can* leave); and the child is physically continuous with the mother, not the father. Map these onto God: he is active in creating; he is unchanged by it; he doesn't depend on the world; and he is utterly distinct from it, not continuous with it.

A comparison may help (course illustration). Many ancient myths picture the world being *born from* a divine mother or *emanating from* a divine body — the world as a piece or product of the divine substance. That is exactly the picture classical theism denies: the world isn't made out of God, and God isn't changed by making it. Feser's worry is that maternal imagery, with its connotations of continuity and change, drifts toward pantheism or panentheism (step 59).

Nuances worth stating when you teach this: the argument concerns an analogy about roles in generation, not the worth of men and women; and it presupposes the classical attributes defended earlier (immutability, distinctness). Someone who rejects the analogy needn't reject those attributes, but Feser's point is that they need *some* way of speaking that doesn't suggest a changing, world-continuous God.

The usual confusion is to treat the appendix as a claim about gender. It's really a final application of the chapter's main theme: God's radical distinctness from, and independence of, the world.

checks.q: What does Feser say about God's sex?
options: God is male
God is sexless
God is female
God is both male and female
checks.explanation: Since God is immaterial and not an animal, he isn't literally a man or a woman. The pronoun question is about least misleading language.

checks.q: Why, according to Feser, would maternal imagery for God mislead?
options: It would be disrespectful
It has no basis in any tradition
Mothers are less important than fathers
It suggests a God changed by, or continuous with, the world — as in panentheism or pantheism
checks.explanation: The mother is changed by and physically continuous with the child; applied to God, that suggests the views the book rejects.

argument.name: Deriving the personal attributes of God and his relation to the world
argument.overview:
Feser gives no single numbered proof in this half of chapter 6. Instead he runs a series of short derivations, each starting from what the five proofs already secured — that God is **purely actual, absolutely simple, subsistent existence itself, absolutely necessary, and unique**, and that everything else is composite, contingent, and dependent on him at every instant — and then applying three background principles from Part A: the **principle of proportionate causality** (PPC: whatever is in an effect is in its total cause formally, virtually, or eminently), **agere sequitur esse** (action follows being), and the **analogy of being**.

The reconstruction below lays those derivations out as one continuous line of reasoning. A recurring pattern is worth watching for: most attributes are reached by **two routes**, *backward* from the world as effect (via PPC or dependence) and *forward* from God's nature as pure act (via agere sequitur esse). Each stage also contains a **defensive step**, where Feser shows that the standard objection trades on a fallacy of accident or on treating God as a cause alongside other causes.

- Stages 1–4 derive **power, intellect and knowledge, goodness, will, freedom, and love**.
- Stage 5 explains why these results give real but incomplete knowledge (**incomprehensibility**).
- Stages 6–7 turn to **God's relation to the world**: conservation, concurrence, and miracles.
- Stage 8 is the short coda on **why God is called “he.”**

Step wording is a paraphrase and reconstruction, not Feser's own numbered formulation.

stages.title: Stage 1 — Omnipotence
stages.gist: Because everything depends on God for existence and therefore for action, and because subsistent existence can act in the fullest way, God has all power; ‘powers’ to do the contradictory are not powers at all.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Intellect and omniscience
stages.gist: By proportionate causality every feature of every possible thing is in God, and since not as instances nor in a Platonic realm, as concepts and propositions in an intellect; God meets every condition of knowledge and knows all by knowing himself as cause, in a unified, simple act.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Perfect goodness
stages.gist: Goodness is actuality in line with a thing's nature and badness a privation; so pure actuality is pure goodness, all good in creatures comes from God, and evil — being an absence — need not be in God.

stages.title: Stage 4 — Will, freedom, and love
stages.gist: An intellect that selects among possibles has will; nothing inside or outside God compels it, so it is free; no best world or obligation to create binds it; and willing the good of creatures just is love.

stages.title: Stage 5 — Incomprehensibility
stages.gist: Negative knowledge and literal analogy give real knowledge of God, but simplicity means he cannot be analyzed into parts, so full comprehension is impossible — as the arguments themselves predict.

stages.title: Stage 6 — Conservation and concurrence
stages.gist: God sustains all things at every instant yet is distinct from them; with action-follows-being this excludes both occasionalism and mere conservationism, leaving real secondary causes that act only with God's concurrence.

stages.title: Stage 7 — Miracles
stages.gist: Laws of nature express natures and cannot be violated, but God, who is not a cause among causes, can elevate nature beyond its powers or suspend an effect by withholding concurrence; such miracles can certify revelation.

stages.title: Stage 8 — Coda: speaking of God as ‘he’
stages.gist: God is sexless but personal, and his active, independent, distinct relation to the world resembles fatherhood more than motherhood.

steps.text: Everything other than God that exists or could exist is composite, a mixture of actuality and potentiality, has an essence distinct from its existence, and is contingent.
steps.why: Established by the five proofs and by the derivations of unity and simplicity in Part A: only the purely actual, simple, necessary being lacks these features, and there can be only one such being.
steps.example: A tree has parts (roots, trunk, leaves), unrealized potentials (to grow taller), and an essence that doesn't include existence (you can understand ‘tree’ without knowing any trees exist) — so it is contingent.
steps.challenge: Maybe some fundamental physical entity is simple and necessary, so not everything besides God is composite.
steps.answer: Part A argues that even the most fundamental particles have distinct attributes and come into and go out of existence, so they are not simple in the relevant sense; and anything truly purely actual and simple would just be God, since there can be only one such being.

steps.text: Anything of that kind can exist even for an instant only if it is being caused to exist by the one purely actual, simple, necessary being who is subsistent existence itself.
steps.why: This is the conclusion of the Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, Thomistic, and rationalist proofs, all of which concern per se (here-and-now) causation, not a first push in the past.
steps.example: Just as a stone moved by a stick moves only while a hand moves the stick, a tree exists at this moment only because something that is existence itself is sustaining it now.
steps.challenge: Why can't the chain of sustaining causes go on forever, with no first member?
steps.answer: In a per se series, the intermediate members have no causal power of their own to pass on; without a first member that has existence in itself, there would be nothing to explain the existence of any member (chapter 1's argument against an infinite per se regress).

steps.text: So everything other than God depends on God at every instant for its very existence.
steps.why: Follows directly from 1 and 2.
steps.example: Like a song that exists only while it is being sung, the world exists only while God is causing it to exist.

steps.text: Action follows being (agere sequitur esse): what a thing can do cannot exceed what it is, and existing is presupposed by acting.
steps.why: Defended in Part A as the formal-cause counterpart of proportionate causality, grounded in the principle of sufficient reason; acting that outran being would be unexplained.
steps.example: A stone can't digest food and eyes see while ears hear, because what a thing does flows from what it is; nothing acts without first existing.
steps.challenge: Puppets move, though moving isn't in a wooden puppet's nature — so activity can outrun being.
steps.answer: Part A answers this: the puppet moves only because the puppeteer moves it. What the principle rules out is a thing's doing, on its own, what goes beyond its nature.

steps.text: So everything other than God depends on God at every instant for its power to act as well as for its existence.
steps.why: From 3 and 4: if a thing has no independent capacity to exist, it cannot intelligibly have an independent capacity to act.
steps.example: The sun's power to melt ice is no more its own independent possession than its existence is; both are received from God at every instant.
steps.challenge: Couldn't God give things existence and then let them exercise their powers independently?
steps.answer: That is mere conservationism. By agere sequitur esse, a thing that could act independently could exist independently, which contradicts step 3 (see step 45).

steps.text: Therefore nothing lies outside God's power and all power derives from him; that is, God is omnipotent (backward route).
steps.why: To be the source of all power, with nothing beyond its reach, is what ‘all-powerful’ means.
steps.example: Every power in the universe — gravity's pull, a magnet's attraction, your lifting a cup — is ultimately borrowed from God, and nothing has any power that isn't.
steps.challenge: If all power derives from God, do creatures have any real power at all?
steps.answer: Yes. Derived power is still real power, as the moon really lights the night by the sun's light; Feser defends real secondary causation against occasionalism (steps 44–46).

steps.text: God exists in the fullest possible way, and to have power is to be able to actualize potential.
steps.why: God is subsistent existence and pure act (from the proofs); to do or make just is to actualize some potential.
steps.example: To bake a cake is to actualize the flour's and eggs' potential to become a cake; power is the capacity to bring about such actualizations.
steps.challenge: How can something with no potentials of its own have the power to actualize potentials in others?
steps.answer: Having power means being able to actualize *other things'* potentials, which requires actuality, not potentiality; the fullest actuality gives the fullest ability (Part A also shows acting needn't involve change in the agent).

steps.text: So there is no actualizable potential God cannot actualize — omnipotence again (forward route).
steps.why: From 4 and 7: what exists in the fullest way acts in the fullest way, and nothing could possibly block such a being.
steps.example: Try to name something that could stop God from making a stone rise or a new star exist: every candidate obstacle itself depends on God for its existence.
steps.challenge: Couldn't God's own goodness or wisdom limit which potentials he actualizes?
steps.answer: That concerns what God wills, not what he can do. Omnipotence is about power; God freely chooses which possibilities to realize (step 33).

steps.text: Omnipotence does not include making round squares, a stone God cannot lift, or a sinning perfectly good being, because there are no such capacities to lack.
steps.why: Self-contradictory descriptions pick out nothing; since a stone's rising is always something that can occur, God can always cause it, so ‘a stone too heavy for God’ is as incoherent as a round square.
steps.example: ‘Make a stone too heavy for God to lift’ is like ‘draw a square circle’: the words describe nothing, so failing to do it is not failing at anything.
steps.challenge: Then logic is a law above God that restricts him.
steps.answer: No: there is no capacity for self-contradiction that God lacks. Contradictions aren't difficult tasks but non-tasks; Frankfurt notes that even if God could do them, the stone paradox would still fail.

steps.text: Every thing, feature, and state of affairs that exists or could exist depends on God's causal activity at every moment.
steps.why: From 3 and 5.
steps.example: Not just the cat and the mat but the cat's being on the mat at this moment depends on God's causal activity.

steps.text: Whatever is in an effect must be in its total cause in some way — formally, virtually, or eminently (proportionate causality).
steps.why: Defended in Part A: an aspect of the effect that came from nothing in the cause would violate the principle of causality and the principle of sufficient reason.
steps.example: If I give you $20, the money must be in the total cause somehow: in my wallet (formally), my bank account (virtually), or my access to a printing press (eminently).
steps.challenge: Effects often have new properties their causes lack — sponginess in a cake that wasn't in the eggs, or new species in evolution.
steps.answer: Part A replies that PPC concerns the *total* cause, not just the materials, and allows virtual or eminent containment; baking conditions and chemistry, or mutation plus environment, contain the new features in that sense.

steps.text: So every feature of every actual or possible thing — colors, shapes, chemical structures, powers of plants, animals, humans, angels — must be in God in some way.
steps.why: From 10 and 11.
steps.example: The shape of a snowflake, the chemistry of chlorophyll, and a dog's ability to run must each be in God in some way, since he causes them.

steps.text: These features cannot be in God as instances, the way they are in creatures.
steps.why: God is immaterial; and more deeply, if God merely instantiated redness or roundness, his own instance would need explaining like any other, so he would not be the ultimate cause of red and round things.
steps.example: Explaining why countless books share a text by pointing to one more copy explains nothing; likewise God's being one more red thing wouldn't explain redness.
steps.challenge: Maybe God could contain these features in some non-mental way we can't imagine.
steps.answer: The universals must exist somewhere other than their instances, and chapter 3 showed the only options are an intellect or a Platonic realm; since the latter fails, a mind is the only remaining mode.

steps.text: Universals are real, and apart from concrete instances they can exist only as concepts in an intellect or in a Platonic ‘third realm’; there is no such realm.
steps.why: Established in chapter 3 (the Augustinian proof), which rejected nominalism, conceptualism, and Platonism.
steps.example: Triangularity is real and shared by every triangle, including triangles no one has ever drawn — so it isn't just a word or a human idea.
steps.challenge: Nominalists deny universals are anything more than names for resemblances.
steps.answer: Feser relies on chapter 3's case against nominalism and conceptualism (for instance, that they presuppose the very universals they deny); a critic must answer those arguments, not just restate nominalism.

steps.text: So the forms of all things exist in God as concepts in an intellect: God has intellect.
steps.why: From 12, 13, and 14 by elimination.
steps.example: The concept ‘catness’ exists in God's intellect as the source of all actual and possible cats.
steps.challenge: This anthropomorphizes God by giving him a human-style mind.
steps.answer: Feser insists that ‘intellect’ applies to God analogically: not as a series of distinct thoughts but as one simple act of self-knowledge (steps 20–21).

steps.text: Likewise every state of affairs that obtains or could obtain exists in God as a proposition, including thoughts that given propositions are true or false.
steps.why: God causes not just the cat and the mat but the cat's being on the mat; a proposition is the intellectual correlate of a state of affairs as a concept is of a universal.
steps.example: God's intellect contains the proposition that the cat is on the mat and the thought that it is false that unicorns exist.
steps.challenge: Propositions are distinct items, so this multiplies parts in God.
steps.answer: Feser grants they can't be in God as distinct thoughts, as they are in us; the prism-and-dough analogy explains how one undivided knowledge includes them all (step 21).

steps.text: To know p is (a) to think p true, (b) with p actually true, (c) as the result of a reliable process — understood analogically when applied to God.
steps.why: The standard philosophical account of knowledge, applied with the analogy of being from Part A.
steps.example: You know it's raining if you believe it, it is raining, and you believe it because you looked outside (a reliable process), not because of a lucky guess.
steps.challenge: Gettier-style cases show this definition of knowledge is inadequate.
steps.answer: Feser applies the conditions only analogically; whatever refinement of the analysis one prefers, the relevant point stands, since making p true is the least luck-dependent way of believing it.

steps.text: God meets all three conditions for each such proposition, so God has knowledge.
steps.why: (a) the thought is in his intellect (16); (b) it is true because he makes it so (10); (c) no process is more reliable than being the one who makes p true — as an author knows a character is in the story because he put him there.
steps.example: An author knows her detective is in the story because she wrote him in; God knows the cat is on the mat because he makes it so.
steps.challenge: The ‘reliable process’ condition implies a process in time, which the timeless God can't have.
steps.answer: Feser says something *analogous* to each condition holds of God: what corresponds to reliability is that the truth of p depends on God's causing it.

steps.text: God also knows himself fully, so he knows every proposition about himself and everything else: he is omniscient.
steps.why: An author cannot know less of his own creative act than of the story; unlike a human author with an opaque body, God is simple, so nothing in him is hidden from his intellect. (The forward route was chapter 3's argument from an infinite intellect.)
steps.example: An author can't be ignorant of her own decision to write a story; God, being simple, has no hidden parts, like a human author's digestive system, outside his knowing.
steps.challenge: Patrick Grim argues that the very idea of knowing all truths is incoherent.
steps.answer: Feser answered Grim in chapter 3; here he adds that omniscience follows independently from God's being cause of all truths and knowing himself fully.

steps.text: God knows the world not by observing it but by knowing himself as its cause, in a single timeless act.
steps.why: He is eternal (need not wait for events), incorporeal (no senses), and immutable (cannot learn). This blocks the inference to four-dimensionalism and shows his knowledge no more compels our acts than an author's writing compels a character — he is author, not hypnotist.
steps.example: A motionless hunter knows in an instant that he fired a bullet, without the bullet being motionless or everywhere along its path at once.
steps.challenge: If God causes and knows all our acts, we can't be free.
steps.answer: God relates to us as an author to a character, not as a hypnotist to a victim; a cause of the whole order doesn't compete with free causes within it.

steps.text: Given simplicity, God's knowledge is not a collection of distinct thoughts but a unified knowledge of himself as pure actuality, which contains every limited way of being actual.
steps.why: As knowing white light perfectly would include knowing every color a prism could draw from it, or knowing the dough every cookie shape, knowing unlimited actuality includes knowing every finite kind.
steps.example: Knowing white light perfectly would include knowing every color a prism could draw from it; knowing pure actuality includes knowing every limited way of being.
steps.challenge: This analogy suggests creatures are pieces of God, as cookies are pieces of dough.
steps.answer: Feser explicitly rejects that reading: God is not a material with potentials, so creatures are not made out of him.

steps.text: A thing is good, as a specimen of its kind, to the extent that it actualizes the potentials its nature directs it toward; moral goodness is the special case of free rational agents.
steps.why: Shown by the triangle (bus-seat scrawl vs. ruled drawing) and the tree (healthy vs. diseased roots): these judgments follow from natures, not preferences.
steps.example: A triangle drawn carefully with a ruler is a better triangle than one scrawled on a bouncing bus seat, whatever anyone's preferences.
steps.challenge: Moral goodness is different in kind from the ‘goodness’ of triangles.
steps.answer: Feser treats moral goodness as a special case of the same notion, arising when free rational beings choose to promote or frustrate their own flourishing; the full ethics lies beyond the book.

steps.text: So goodness is a kind of actuality, and badness is a privation — the absence of an actuality a thing's nature calls for.
steps.why: A wavy side is a privation in a triangle, a missing fourth side is not; weak roots are a privation in a tree, missing wings are not. Goodness is primary; badness, like blindness, is a lack.
steps.example: Blindness in a dog is a privation; a stone's inability to see is not, because stones aren't supposed to see.
steps.challenge: Then evil isn't real.
steps.answer: Blindness is an absence and is perfectly real; explaining what evil consists in isn't denying it.

steps.text: The privation account withstands its main objections.
steps.why: It explains rather than denies evil's reality; pain is bad only by association (it can be useful or satisfying; cf. pain asymbolia); a murderer's positive desires may be good in themselves, the badness lying in what his intention lacks; sadism is desire misdirected, a psychological deformity.
steps.example: A murderer's desire for money may itself be fine; what's bad is his missing intention to pursue money only in ways that respect the innocent.
steps.challenge: Pain is plainly a positive presence, not an absence.
steps.answer: Pain isn't bad without qualification (it warns; post-workout pain satisfies); its badness is the damage or disturbance it signals, and pain asymbolia shows the sensation and its unpleasantness can come apart.

steps.text: God is pure actuality with no unrealized potential.
steps.why: From the Aristotelian proof and Part A.
steps.example: Unlike a sapling that can still grow, God has no ‘not-yet’ in him.

steps.text: So God is purely good, with no badness of any kind (forward route).
steps.why: From 23 and 25.
steps.example: If a good tree is one whose potentials are realized, pure actuality, with nothing unrealized, is goodness without any shortfall.
steps.challenge: This is just a play on words: ‘fully actual’ isn't the same as ‘morally good.’
steps.answer: The inference uses the specimen sense of good, which the privation analysis ties to actuality; God's goodness is then the limit case, not a creaturely moral virtue (step 38).

steps.text: And since all good in the world must be in its cause, God is the source of all possible good and in that sense all-good (backward route).
steps.why: From 11 applied to goodness.
steps.example: Whatever is good in a sunrise, a friendship, or a healthy body must be in God somehow, since he causes it.
steps.challenge: By the same reasoning, whatever is bad must be in God too.
steps.answer: Proportionate causality concerns positive features; badness is a privation, not a positive feature (step 28).

steps.text: Proportionate causality does not put evil in God, and permitting evil is compatible with his goodness.
steps.why: Evil is an absence, not a positive feature, so making a world with evil is making goods while refraining from others (the unfinished triangle); some goods, such as courage, are impossible without real danger, just as round squares are impossible.
steps.example: A lecturer who deliberately leaves a triangle's third side unfinished to make a point adds no badness; he leaves something out, and the whole lesson is better for it.
steps.challenge: An all-good God should have filled every gap.
steps.answer: Some goods logically require permitted badness — courage requires real danger — and a world with courage but no danger is as impossible as a round square; the full problem of evil is treated in chapter 7.

steps.text: Every nature inclines toward its fulfillment: unconsciously in plants, with sensory appetite in animals, with rational appetite (will) in intellectual beings.
steps.why: The tree, the dog, and the human being illustrate the three grades of appetite.
steps.example: A tree grows toward light without awareness; a dog seeks food because it feels hunger; a person pursues a career she judges worthwhile.

steps.text: Since God has intellect, there is in him something analogous to will: the limit case of rational appetite, by which he wills some possibles to exist and not others.
steps.why: He ‘rests’ in his fully realized nature rather than striving (like zero km/s as the limit case of speed); and he grasps all possibles yet causes only some, which is analogous to willing.
steps.example: As zero speed isn't the slowest speed but no speed, yet the ordering of speeds points to it, God's will is the limit case of appetite: rest in the good rather than striving.
steps.challenge: A will that neither strives nor desires isn't a will at all.
steps.answer: Feser says God is more like something that has completed its striving than something that never strove; and since God selects among possibles, there must be something analogous to willing.

steps.text: Nothing external can compel God's will.
steps.why: Everything other than God depends on him for existence and action at every instant (3, 5).
steps.example: No force, law, or rival power exists independently of God, so nothing could pressure him to create.

steps.text: Nothing internal compels it either.
steps.why: No concept in the divine intellect (lion, unicorn) contains any necessity that its instances exist or not; before creation either world was equally possible.
steps.example: The concepts of a lion and a unicorn are both in the divine intellect, yet nothing in either requires that its kind exist.
steps.challenge: God's goodness might internally necessitate creating something.
steps.answer: God is already perfectly good and lacks nothing, so creating adds nothing he needs; and the Leibniz–Rowe version of the objection fails because there is no best world to be necessitated toward (step 34).

steps.text: So God's will is free.
steps.why: From 31 and 32: freedom from all external and internal compulsion.
steps.example: God could have created a world with unicorns instead of lions, or no world at all.
steps.challenge: Freedom requires potentials, and a purely actual God has none.
steps.answer: That is a fallacy of accident: our free choices involve actualizing potentials, but freedom as such is just the absence of compulsion (step 34).

steps.text: Neither simplicity nor perfect goodness removes this freedom.
steps.why: Freedom as such does not require actualizing potentials (to assume so is a fallacy of accident); no one is wronged if God does not create; there is no best possible world (always x + 1 forests); and God's perfection follows from what he is, not what he makes (the diamond that need not cut any glass).
steps.example: A flawless diamond is perfect whether it cuts thin glass, thick glass, or none; God's perfection doesn't depend on which world, if any, he makes.
steps.challenge: If every world can be bettered, a being who made a better one than God would be more perfect (Rowe).
steps.answer: God's perfection follows from what he is — pure actuality — not from what he produces, so no product could make a maker more perfect.

steps.text: What is essential to love is willing the good of the beloved, not being emotionally affected.
steps.why: Hence shallow love is mere fluctuating feeling, while serious love, tough love, and love of enemies persist in willing the good against feeling; will is active, emotion passive.
steps.example: A parent up at 3 a.m. with a sick child, feeling only exhaustion, still loves; so do tough love and love of enemies.
steps.challenge: Love without feeling is cold and not really love.
steps.answer: We call love made only of fluctuating feelings shallow; the will to the other's good is what makes love serious, so feelings are an accompaniment, not the essence.

steps.text: To create is to actualize, and so to will that a thing exist together with the goods that flow from its nature.
steps.why: Goodness is actuality (23); willing trees exist is willing their roots, nourishment, and photosynthesis.
steps.example: To will that trees exist is to will that they have roots drawing in water and leaves photosynthesizing — the goods of a flourishing tree.

steps.text: So God loves what he creates, and does so without any change in him.
steps.why: From 30, 35, and 36; the objection that love requires changeability is a fallacy of accident.
steps.example: God's love doesn't respond to goodness already in us; by willing our existence and flourishing, it is the source of whatever good we have.
steps.challenge: A love that is never moved by our suffering is indifference.
steps.answer: Indifference is the absence of will for another's good; God wills every good we have at every instant, and being unmoved means lacking nothing, not caring less.

steps.text: Negative (apophatic) knowledge of God is real knowledge, and positive attributes are predicated of him literally by analogy of attribution and of proper proportionality.
steps.why: God is the primary analogate of power (the sun's power is derived); a tree, a human, an angel, and God are each to their own goodness in proportionally similar ways, God's being the limit case.
steps.example: God is the primary analogate of ‘power’ and the sun a secondary analogate; a tree, a person, an angel, and God are each related to their own goodness in proportionally similar ways.
steps.challenge: Analogy is just a polite name for metaphor.
steps.answer: Part A distinguishes proper proportionality, where the property is literally in each analogate, from improper (metaphorical) proportionality like ‘George is a lion.’

steps.text: So in a loose sense we genuinely comprehend God; the position is neither fideist nor purely negative.
steps.why: From 38 and the fact that we understand the book's arguments.
steps.example: Understanding and accepting the arguments of chapters 1–6 already is understanding something of God.

steps.text: Comprehension in the strict sense works by analyzing a thing into its parts, or into genus and specific difference.
steps.why: This is how we come to understand material systems and even immaterial natures.
steps.example: We understand a car engine by learning its parts and how they fit, and ‘human’ by genus (animal) and difference (rational).

steps.text: Since God is absolutely simple, he cannot be comprehended in the strict sense; the mystery is predicted by the arguments themselves, not a retreat into obscurantism.
steps.why: From 40 and simplicity; compare physics, which must speak strangely (wave-particles, curved space) far from everyday experience.
steps.example: As physics must speak strangely of wave-particles and curved space, natural theology must speak strangely of a being with no parts at all.
steps.challenge: Appealing to mystery is a way of dodging objections.
steps.answer: The mystery is a conclusion derived from simplicity, not a patch applied when arguments fail; the arguments themselves tell us our grasp must be feeble.

steps.text: God conserves every created thing in being at every instant; creation is ongoing, and nothing contingent has ‘existential inertia.’
steps.why: From 2 and 3; anything composite of act and potency or of essence and existence needs a sustaining cause, and the inertia thesis never explains how a contingent thing could lack that need.
steps.example: The world is like a song that exists only while sung, not a painting that survives its painter.
steps.challenge: Things might have existential inertia, persisting on their own until destroyed.
steps.answer: Its defenders never explain what would give a contingent thing that power, and nothing composite of act and potency or essence and existence could have it.

steps.text: Yet created things are really distinct from God, so pantheism and panentheism are false.
steps.why: They are composite, potential, essence-distinct-from-existence, and contingent; he is simple, pure act, subsistent existence, necessary, and immutable (so not changed by the world).
steps.example: A tree depends on God for its existence, yet a tree is composite and changing while God is simple and immutable — so the tree is not God.
steps.challenge: Maybe change and multiplicity are illusions, so the world really is the one God.
steps.answer: Whoever has the illusion has successive, differing, mistaken experiences, so it is changeable, composite, and ignorant — not God.

steps.text: Occasionalism (only God causes) is false.
steps.why: By action-follows-being, what does nothing is nothing, so only God would exist; but you exist and are not God (you change, doubt, and lack power). And it destroys the premises about real, changing, composite things that led us to God — pulling away the ladder.
steps.example: Occasionalism says God, not the sun, melts the ice in your iced tea, and God, not the cue ball, sinks the eight ball.
steps.challenge: Giving God all the causation magnifies his glory.
steps.answer: It actually makes creatures unreal (what does nothing is nothing) and saws off the ladder of the proofs, which began from real changing things; a God who makes real causes is greater than a puppet-master.

steps.text: Mere conservationism (creatures act independently once sustained) is false.
steps.why: By action-follows-being, whatever could act independently could exist independently — essentially deism; but nothing composite can exist without conservation, and this view too undermines the proofs' starting point.
steps.example: On mere conservationism, God keeps the sun around but the sun melts ice entirely on its own.
steps.challenge: Concurrence makes creaturely causes redundant, so mere conservationism is more reasonable.
steps.answer: God and creatures contribute at different levels, as your hand accounts for there being a square and the chalk for its blueness — neither is redundant.

steps.text: Concurrentism is true: created things are genuine but secondary causes, making a real contribution to their effects while able to act only as God concurs with them.
steps.why: The only position left once both extremes fail; illustrated by the blue chalk (you make the square, the chalk its blueness) and the moon (its look is its own, its light is the sun's).
steps.example: Draw a square with blue chalk: you account for there being a square at all, the chalk for its being blue.
steps.challenge: If God concurs in everything, the creature's contribution seems illusory.
steps.answer: The effect would be different with a different secondary cause (red chalk, a pencil), which shows the creature's contribution is real.

steps.text: Among these secondary causes are free human agents.
steps.why: Human beings are creatures conserved and concurred with like any other.
steps.example: A person deciding whether to tell the truth is a secondary cause whose act depends on God's concurrence like any other.

steps.text: God's concurrence does not destroy human freedom.
steps.why: Like a father guiding his son's hand to write an A: the boy's cooperation or resistance is a real contribution, but no letter appears without the father's guidance.
steps.example: A father guides his son's hand to write an A; the boy can resist or cooperate, but no A appears without the father's guidance.
steps.challenge: God concurs even with the choice to cooperate, so the analogy breaks down and freedom is lost.
steps.answer: The analogy is admittedly imperfect because the father is a force alongside the child; the underlying point is that God is not a rival cause on our level (author, not hypnotist), so his concurrence gives our choice its being rather than replacing it.

steps.text: Laws of nature describe the dispositions things have by virtue of their natures; dispositions can be blocked or lack their triggers.
steps.why: The Aristotelian account of laws (Ramelow, Oderberg): water's disposition to freeze at 32°F, which unusual conditions can prevent.
steps.example: Salt has a disposition to dissolve even in a dry shaker; water's disposition to freeze at 32°F can be blocked in unusual conditions.
steps.challenge: Laws are just observed regularities, not powers in things.
steps.answer: That is the Humean view; Feser adopts the Aristotelian account defended by Ramelow and Oderberg, on which laws express what things do because of their natures.

steps.text: So, given that the things exist, laws are metaphysically necessary and cannot be violated; the Humean definition of a miracle as a violation is mistaken.
steps.why: Different laws would mean different natures, hence different things (whatever turned to mousse at 32°F would not be water); if triggers are present and nothing blocks, the manifestation follows.
steps.example: Anything that reliably turned into chocolate mousse at 32°F simply wouldn't be water.
steps.challenge: Surely the laws of nature could have been different.
steps.answer: Different things with different laws could have existed instead, so the actual laws are contingent in that sense; but given that water exists, it could not obey different laws and still be water.

steps.text: A miracle is an effect that elevates a thing beyond what any created nature can account for: supernatural, as opposed to subnatural (defects) or preternatural (what angels might do).
steps.why: Ramelow's Thomistic definition.
steps.example: Raising a dead man is supernatural; an angel's extraordinary feat would be preternatural; a two-headed calf is subnatural.
steps.challenge: ‘Beyond any created nature’ is unknowable, since we might just be ignorant of hidden natural causes.
steps.answer: Whether a given event is a miracle is a further evidential question beyond natural theology; the definition identifies what would count, and some effects (like a resurrection) are clearly beyond the natural factors present.

steps.text: Only God can work miracles, and in doing so he does not ‘intervene,’ since he is not a cause alongside the others but the source of all causal power, already causing the ordinary course.
steps.why: From 5, 46, and 51; McCabe: God cannot interfere, not for lack of power, but because he is alongside nothing.
steps.example: A novelist doesn't ‘interfere’ in her novel when she adds a chapter; she is writing all of it.
steps.challenge: Any miracle is a divine intervention into nature.
steps.answer: To intervene you must stand alongside what you intervene in; God causes the ordinary course as much as the miraculous and is alongside nothing (McCabe, Davies).

steps.text: A miracle may add to nature (resurrection, loaves) or subtract from it (the fiery furnace) — the latter by God refraining from conserving or concurring with some factors, which is a suspension rather than a breach of the law.
steps.why: From 42, 46, and 50: withholding concurrence means the normal effect simply does not arise; nothing is forced to act against its nature.
steps.example: In the fiery furnace story, God withholds his concurrence from the fire, so the men aren't burned; like a musician leaving out notes from the score.
steps.challenge: This is just a violation of the law that fire burns, relabeled.
steps.answer: A violation would be God sustaining fire and all its conditions yet making them act against their natures; a suspension is God not bringing the burning about at all — like revoking a law rather than failing to enforce it (Oderberg).

steps.text: Therefore miracles are possible.
steps.why: From 52 and 53.
steps.example: Since God can add to or subtract from nature's course without violating anything, there is no incoherence in the idea of a miracle.

steps.text: If God willed to reveal truths reason cannot reach, a miracle worked by his messenger would be the fitting divine ‘seal’ on the message, since only God can work one.
steps.why: From 52: no creature can counterfeit a strictly supernatural effect.
steps.example: A prophet teaching doctrines no philosophy could reach would have his message certified if he raised the dead.
steps.challenge: An impostor might fake a miracle, or a powerful creature might produce one.
steps.answer: Faking is an evidential problem to assess case by case; and a merely preternatural effect is not a miracle in the strict sense, which by definition only God can cause.

steps.text: Miracles are the bridge from natural to revealed theology: they ground faith in reason, and natural theology tests any religion's claims about God.
steps.why: Faith is believing because God has revealed; that he has revealed needs miraculous evidence. Religions that make God many, identical with the world, impersonal, material, or finite — or that claim revelation without miracle — are thereby discredited.
steps.example: Natural theology rules out a religion whose god is finite or material, and gives no reason to accept a claimed revelation that lacks miraculous backing.
steps.challenge: Faith just is believing without evidence.
steps.answer: For Aquinas faith is believing because God revealed something, and that God revealed it requires evidence; so faith is grounded in reason.

steps.text: God is not an animal and so not literally male or female, but he has intellect and will, which define personhood.
steps.why: Immateriality (Part A) and stages 2 and 4.
steps.example: God has no body, so he isn't male; but he knows and wills, so he isn't an ‘it.’

steps.text: God's relation to the world — active, unchanged, independent, distinct — resembles a father's role in procreation more than a mother's.
steps.why: The father acts, is unchanged, is not physically dependent, and is not physically continuous with the child; the mother is changed and continuous with the child.
steps.example: A father is active, unchanged by conception, not physically dependent, and not physically continuous with the child; so God is active, unchanged by creating, independent, and distinct from the world.
steps.challenge: This analogy relies on outdated or sexist assumptions about parenthood.
