steps.answer: The analogy concerns a biological asymmetry in generation — who is changed, who is continuous with the child — not the worth or social roles of men and women.

steps.text: So personal, paternal (masculine) language is the least misleading way to speak of God; ‘it’ denies his personhood and maternal imagery suggests pantheism or panentheism.
steps.why: From 57 and 58.
steps.example: Speaking of God as a mother from whose body the world emerged would suggest the world is continuous with God, the pantheist picture.
steps.challenge: Feminine imagery could be used carefully without implying pantheism.
steps.answer: Feser's claim is comparative: given classical theism's stress on God's immutability and distinctness from the world, paternal language is the most natural and least misleading, because maternal imagery carries connotations of change and continuity.

keyTerms.definition: The attribute of having all power; a being with it is called omnipotent, or all-powerful. For Feser this means being the source of every power anything has, with no actualizable potential beyond one's ability to actualize.
keyTerms.example: God can cause any possible state of affairs, such as a stone's rising, but ‘making a round square’ names no possible state of affairs and so no power.
keyTerms.origin: Latin omnis (“all”) + potens (“powerful”); the classical account is Aquinas's (Summa Theologiae I.25).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being able to do anything that can be put into words — omnipotence covers every possible actualization, and contradictions name no possible actualization.

keyTerms.definition: Latin, ‘action follows being’: what a thing does reflects and cannot exceed what it is.
keyTerms.example: Because creatures cannot exist on their own, they cannot act on their own; because God is existence itself, he can act in every way.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, literally “acting follows being”; a Scholastic maxim used constantly by Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The principle of proportionate causality — PPC compares an effect with its efficient cause, while agere sequitur esse compares a thing's activity with its own nature (formal cause).

keyTerms.definition: Whatever is in an effect must be in its total cause in some way — formally, virtually, or eminently.
keyTerms.example: Every feature of every possible creature must be in God somehow — which, Feser argues, means as ideas in an intellect.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic principle (Aquinas); Descartes defended a variant that scholars call the “causal adequacy principle.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: The “heirloom” view of causation — PPC does not say the cause must pass on the very same feature, only that the feature be in the total cause formally, virtually, or eminently.

keyTerms.definition: Three ways an effect's feature can be in a cause: as the same form (formally), as a power to produce it (virtually), or in a higher way that contains the power to produce it (eminently).
keyTerms.example: A $20 bill in my wallet (formally), $20 in my bank account (virtually), a Federal Reserve printing press (eminently).
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic Latin formaliter, virtualiter, eminenter.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Each other — ‘virtually’ means having the resources or power to produce the feature, while ‘eminently’ means possessing it in a higher, more fundamental way (the power to make $20 bills, not just to transfer them).

keyTerms.definition: The puzzle: can God make a stone too heavy for him to lift? Either way, something seems beyond him.
keyTerms.example: Dissolved because ‘a stone too heavy for God to lift’ is self-contradictory, like a round square.
keyTerms.origin: A traditional puzzle about omnipotence; Feser cites George Mavrodes (1963) and Harry Frankfurt (1964).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A genuine limitation of power — the ‘task’ in the paradox is self-contradictory, so failing to perform it is not failing to do anything.

keyTerms.definition: The attribute of knowing all truths; a being with it is called omniscient, or all-knowing. For Feser this means knowing every proposition about oneself and about everything that is or could be.
keyTerms.example: God knows the cat is on the mat because he knows himself as causing the cat to be on the mat.
keyTerms.origin: Latin omnis (“all”) + scientia (“knowledge”).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Foreknowledge — God does not know the future ahead of time, since he is not in time; he knows all things in one timeless act.

keyTerms.definition: S knows p when S thinks p is true, p is true, and S's thinking so comes from a reliable process.
keyTerms.example: God meets each condition analogically; making p true is the most reliable way of ‘finding out’ that p.
keyTerms.origin: Descends from the ‘justified true belief’ analysis going back to Plato's Theaetetus; Feser uses a reliable-process version of the third condition.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere true belief — a lucky guess can be true, but it isn't knowledge without the reliable-process condition.

keyTerms.definition: Knowing something by knowing oneself as its cause, rather than by perceiving it.
keyTerms.example: An author knows his characters by knowing his own intentions, not by watching them.
keyTerms.origin: Aquinas's teaching that God's knowledge is the cause of things rather than caused by them (scientia Dei causa rerum).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Observational (perceptual) knowledge — observation depends on the thing known; causal knowledge is something the known depends on.

keyTerms.definition: The view that past, present, and future all exist and time is a spacelike fourth dimension.
keyTerms.example: Feser denies that timeless divine knowledge implies it — just as a motionless hunter's instant knowledge doesn't make the bullet motionless.
keyTerms.origin: Contemporary metaphysics of time; also called eternalism or the ‘block universe’ view. Feser cites Katherin Rogers's discussion.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Divine eternity — God's being outside time is a claim about God, not a claim that past, present, and future all exist together.

keyTerms.definition: Feser's contrast between a cause outside the story (compatible with characters' freedom) and a cause inside the story that interferes with others (incompatible with their freedom).
keyTerms.example: The crime novel's murderer acts freely though the author wrote him; not so if another character hypnotized him.
keyTerms.origin: Feser's own illustration, developed in the omniscience section.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Causal determinism by an outside force — the hypnotist is such a force; the author is not a force within the story at all.

keyTerms.definition: The degree to which a thing actualizes the potentials its nature or essence directs it toward.
keyTerms.example: A carefully ruled triangle is a good triangle; a tree with deep roots is a good tree.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian-Thomistic ‘natural goodness’ tradition; Feser also cites Philippa Foot's Natural Goodness.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Good’ as ‘pleasant’ or ‘preferred’ — a good specimen is measured by its nature, whether or not anyone likes it.

keyTerms.term: Privation (and the privation theory of evil)
keyTerms.definition: The absence of something a thing ought to have given its nature, as opposed to a mere absence; the classical theory holds that all badness, evil included, is a privation of due good rather than a positive reality.
keyTerms.example: Blindness in a dog is a privation, while a tree's lacking wings is not; the badness of a murder lies in the missing intention to seek gain only by just means.
keyTerms.origin: Latin privatio, “a depriving”; the theory is classical (Platonic, Aristotelian, Augustinian, Scholastic).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere negation (negatio) — the absence of something a thing's nature does not call for, which is no defect at all.

keyTerms.definition: A condition caused by certain brain damage in which pain is felt without its usual unpleasantness.
keyTerms.example: Cited as evidence that what is bad is not pain itself but what accompanies it.
keyTerms.origin: Greek a- (“without”) + symbolon (“sign, token”); a clinical neurological term.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Congenital insensitivity to pain — in that condition no pain is felt; in asymbolia pain is felt but without its unpleasantness.

keyTerms.definition: Conscious inclination toward ends apprehended by the senses, found in animals.
keyTerms.example: A dog seeking food and water.
keyTerms.origin: Latin appetitus, “a striving toward”; Aristotelian-Scholastic psychology.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Will — sensory appetite follows what the senses present; will follows what the intellect judges worth pursuing.

keyTerms.definition: Inclination toward what the intellect grasps as worth pursuing (and away from what it grasps as not).
keyTerms.example: A human choosing a career because he judges it worthwhile; analogously, God willing some possibles to exist.
keyTerms.origin: Latin voluntas; the Aristotelian-Thomistic account of the will as appetite that follows intellect.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Emotion or feeling — emotions are passions of sensory appetite, while will is an active inclination following reason.

keyTerms.definition: (From Barry Miller) Something toward which a series points but which differs absolutely, not merely in degree, from the members of the series.
keyTerms.example: Zero km/s is not the slowest speed but no speed; the divine will and divine goodness are limit cases of creaturely appetite and goodness.
keyTerms.origin: From Barry Miller, A Most Unlikely God (1996).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A limit simpliciter — a mere limit (like the speed of light) differs only in degree from what it limits, whereas a limit case differs absolutely.

keyTerms.definition: Inferring that what usually accompanies something in our experience is essential to it.
keyTerms.example: ‘Our love involves emotional change, so love as such requires change.’
keyTerms.origin: Named in Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations (Latin fallacia accidentis).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Hasty generalization — close cousins, but the fallacy of accident specifically treats a merely accompanying feature as belonging to a thing's essence.

keyTerms.definition: A hypothetical world than which no better could exist; Leibniz held God must create it.
keyTerms.example: Feser denies there is one: for any world with x forests there is a possible world with x + 1.
keyTerms.origin: Leibniz, Theodicy (1710); revived against divine freedom by William Rowe.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A very good world — Feser denies there is a maximum of possible goodness, not that the actual world is good.

keyTerms.definition: Knowledge of God by denying creaturely limitations of him: not composite, not changing, not material, not temporal.
keyTerms.example: Feser counts it real knowledge, though not the whole story.
keyTerms.origin: Greek apophasis, “denial”; also via negativa; associated with Pseudo-Dionysius and Maimonides.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Agnosticism — negative theology yields real knowledge of what God is not, whereas agnosticism claims no knowledge.

keyTerms.definition: A term applies intrinsically to a primary analogate and to secondary analogates by their relation to it.
keyTerms.example: God is the primary analogate of ‘power’; the sun has power only as derived from him.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic analogia attributionis; the classification is associated with Cajetan.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Analogy of proper proportionality — in attribution the property is intrinsic only to the primary analogate; in proper proportionality it is intrinsic to each analogate.

keyTerms.definition: A term applies intrinsically and literally to several things because each stands in a proportionally similar relation.
keyTerms.example: A tree is to its goodness as a human to his, an angel to his, and God to his.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic analogia proportionalitatis propriae; Cajetan's classification.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphor (improper proportionality) — ‘George is a lion’ has the form of lion only figuratively in George, whereas life or goodness is literally present in each analogate.

keyTerms.definition: The impossibility of fully grasping God's nature; God is incomprehensible (in the strict sense) because simplicity leaves no parts, or genus-and-difference structure, for the mind to analyze. It does not mean he is unknowable.
keyTerms.example: We know truly that God is good, but cannot grasp what his goodness is in itself.
keyTerms.origin: Latin incomprehensibilis, “not able to be grasped completely”; Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I.12.7.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Unknowability — God can be known truly (by argument and analogy) though never comprehended exhaustively.

keyTerms.definition: The doctrine that God keeps every creature in existence at every instant; without him it would be instantly annihilated.
keyTerms.example: Creation is not a past event but happening now.
keyTerms.origin: Latin conservare, “to keep, preserve”; standard Scholastic doctrine.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Creation as a one-time past event — conservation says the world depends on God now, at every moment.

keyTerms.definition: The claim that some things, once existing, persist on their own until destroyed, needing no conserving cause.
keyTerms.example: Feser: never explained, and impossible for anything composite of act and potency or essence and existence.
keyTerms.origin: Contemporary label; Feser discusses John Beaudoin, Mortimer Adler, and Bede Rundle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Physical (Newtonian) inertia — that concerns a thing's state of motion given that it exists, not what keeps it existing.

keyTerms.definition: The view that only God causes anything; creatures are merely occasions on which he acts.
keyTerms.example: God, not the sun, melts the ice; God, not the cue ball, moves the eight ball.
keyTerms.origin: Latin occasio, “occasion”; associated with al-Ghazali and Nicolas Malebranche.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Concurrentism — both say God is involved in every event, but concurrentism insists creatures are also genuine causes.

keyTerms.definition: The view that God keeps things in being but they exercise causal power independently of him.
keyTerms.example: God sustains the sun, but the sun melts the ice on its own — a view Feser says collapses into deism.
keyTerms.origin: Term from Alfred Freddoso's classification of views of divine causality (associated historically with Durandus).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Concurrentism — both affirm conservation, but mere conservationism makes creatures' activity independent of God.

keyTerms.definition: The view that creatures are real but secondary causes that can act only as God, the primary cause, concurs with their action.
keyTerms.example: You and the blue chalk jointly cause a blue square — you the square, the chalk the blueness.
keyTerms.origin: Latin concurrere, “to run together”; the view of Aquinas and most Scholastics, analyzed by Freddoso.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Occasionalism — occasionalism makes God the only cause; concurrentism makes him the first cause of every real secondary cause.

keyTerms.definition: A genuine cause that makes a real contribution to its effect but whose causal power is derived from and dependent on the first cause.
keyTerms.example: The moon lights the night sky with its own look, but only by the sun's light.
keyTerms.origin: Latin causa secunda.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An unimportant or minor cause — ‘secondary’ means derived and dependent, not insignificant; the chalk really determines the square's color.

keyTerms.definition: Supernatural: beyond the power of any created nature (only God); preternatural: extraordinary but within the power of created natures such as angels; subnatural: falling short of a nature, a defect.
keyTerms.example: A resurrection is supernatural; an angel's feat would be preternatural; a two-headed calf is subnatural.
keyTerms.origin: Latin super (“above”), praeter (“beyond, besides”), sub (“below”) + natura; Feser follows Anselm Ramelow.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Magic or advanced technology — these are just more (possibly hidden) natural or preternatural causes, not supernatural ones.

keyTerms.definition: Oderberg's distinction: a breach leaves the law in force but unenforced; a suspension temporarily removes the law.
keyTerms.example: The fiery furnace: God withholds his concurrence from the fire, so the burning simply does not arise.
keyTerms.origin: David Oderberg, Real Essentialism, drawing an analogy with human positive law.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Each other — a breach leaves the law in force but disobeyed; a suspension removes what the law's operation presupposes.

keyTerms.definition: Being fully actual with no potentiality at all; a being that is purely actual has nothing in it waiting to be realized. The Aristotelian proof concludes to such a being, and most attributes in this module are derived from it.
keyTerms.example: Because God is pure act, there is no unrealized potential in him that could count as badness, so he is perfectly good.
keyTerms.origin: Latin actus purus; Aristotle's unmoved mover as developed by Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being very active or busy — pure actuality is fullness of being, not constant motion; in fact it rules out change.

keyTerms.definition: That whose essence just is existence, rather than something that has existence added to its essence. The conclusion of the Thomistic proof.
keyTerms.example: The forward route to omnipotence: what exists in the fullest possible way can act in the fullest possible way.
keyTerms.origin: Latin ipsum esse subsistens, “existence itself, subsisting”; Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The sum total of existing things — subsistent existence is not the universe or ‘existence in general’ but the one being whose essence is to exist.

keyTerms.definition: The doctrine that God has no parts of any kind; he is simple, or noncomposite: no physical parts, and no metaphysical ones (no essence-existence, act-potency, or substance-attribute composition). His intellect, will, power, and existence are identical.
keyTerms.example: Because God is simple, he cannot be comprehended by analysis into parts, and his knowledge cannot be a collection of separate thoughts.
keyTerms.origin: Classical theism (Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas); the Neo-Platonic proof's conclusion.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being easy to understand — ‘simple’ here means ‘not composed,’ which is exactly why God is hard to understand.

keyTerms.definition: Changelessness; an immutable being undergoes no real change. God is immutable because change is the actualization of potential and he has no potential to actualize.
keyTerms.example: The objections that an immutable God cannot love or choose freely are answered by showing that love and freedom do not essentially require change.
keyTerms.origin: Latin immutabilis, “unchangeable”; derived in Part A of the chapter.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inertness or inactivity — immutability is the fullness of act, not the stillness of a stone.

keyTerms.definition: A merely relational ‘change’ in which a description of a thing changes because something else changed, while the thing itself undergoes no real change.
keyTerms.example: Socrates becomes shorter than Plato when Plato grows; God becomes ‘Creator’ with no real change in him, only in the world.
keyTerms.origin: Coined by Peter Geach after Cambridge philosophers Russell and McTaggart; discussed in Part A.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Real change — a real change involves a thing's own potential being actualized.

keyTerms.definition: A pattern or form that many individual things can share, such as redness, triangularity, or catness. Realism holds that universals are real and not mere words or concepts.
keyTerms.example: The ‘catness’ in every cat must exist in God's intellect as the concept catness, given proportionate causality.
keyTerms.origin: Latin universalis, “pertaining to all”; defended in chapter 3 (the Augustinian proof).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A particular instance — this cat's color is an instance of the universal black, not the universal itself.

keyTerms.definition: Nominalism holds that only particulars exist and universals are just names; conceptualism holds that universals exist only as concepts in human minds. Both were rejected in chapter 3.
keyTerms.example: If nominalism were true, Feser's argument that universal forms must exist in God as concepts would lose a premise.
keyTerms.origin: Latin nomen, “name”; conceptus, “concept”; medieval debates (Ockham, Abelard).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Each other — nominalism denies universals any reality; conceptualism grants them reality, but only in finite minds.

keyTerms.definition: The view that universals, numbers, and propositions exist in a realm of their own, independent of both concrete things and any mind.
keyTerms.example: Because chapter 3 argued there is no Platonic third realm, the only place left for the forms of possible things is a divine intellect.
keyTerms.origin: From Plato's theory of Forms; ‘third realm’ is Frege's phrase.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Neo-Platonism — Plotinus's system places the Forms in the divine Intellect, which is close to Feser's Augustinian position rather than to Platonic realism.

keyTerms.definition: A state of affairs is a way things are or could be in the world; a proposition is its counterpart as the content of a thought, capable of being true or false.
keyTerms.example: The cat's being on the mat is a state of affairs; that the cat is on the mat is a proposition in God's intellect.
keyTerms.origin: Standard terms of analytic philosophy.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A sentence — sentences are strings of words in a language; a proposition is what a sentence expresses and could be thought without any language.

keyTerms.definition: The intellect Feser attributes to God, in which the forms of all possible things exist as concepts and all possible states of affairs as propositions — though not as distinct thoughts, given simplicity.
keyTerms.example: Both the concept lion and the concept unicorn exist in the divine intellect, though God willed only lions to exist.
keyTerms.origin: Augustine's doctrine of divine ideas, developed by Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A human-style mind with successive thoughts — God's intellect is one timeless, undivided act of self-knowledge.

keyTerms.definition: The special case of goodness arising in free rational creatures, who can deliberately choose to act in ways that promote or frustrate the realization of the potentials they need to flourish.
keyTerms.example: A well-drawn triangle is good but not morally praiseworthy; a person who chooses honesty is morally good.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian-Thomistic natural law ethics (Feser refers to his book Aquinas, chapter 5).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Natural (specimen) goodness — every thing can be a good or bad specimen; only free agents can be morally good or bad.

keyTerms.definition: The view that God is identical with the world.
keyTerms.example: Feser rejects it because the world is composite, potential, and contingent while God is simple, purely actual, and necessary — and the ‘world is an illusion’ version fails because whatever has the illusion is not God.
keyTerms.origin: Greek pan (“all”) + theos (“god”).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Panentheism — panentheism says God is not identical to the world but includes it and is affected by it.

keyTerms.definition: The view that God is not identical to the world but is present in it in such a way that he is changed by it; the world is ‘in’ God.
keyTerms.example: Process theology is a leading form; Feser rejects it because God, being pure act and simple, is immutable.
keyTerms.origin: Greek pan (“all”) + en (“in”) + theos (“god”); coined by K. C. F. Krause.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Divine omnipresence — classical theism says God is present to everything as its cause, without being changed by it.

keyTerms.definition: The view of God as a creator who does not sustain or act in the world after making it, so that creatures carry on without him.
keyTerms.example: Feser argues that mere conservationism amounts to deism in all but name, since whatever could act independently of God could also exist independently of him.
keyTerms.origin: Latin deus, “god”; associated with 17th–18th-century English and French thinkers.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere conservationism — the conservationist affirms God sustains creatures' existence, but Feser argues this is unstable and slides into deism.

keyTerms.definition: Three uses of a term: univocal (same sense each time), equivocal (unrelated senses), analogical (related but not identical senses).
keyTerms.example: ‘Dog’ for Fido and Rover is univocal; ‘bat’ for the mammal and the stick is equivocal; ‘good’ for wine and for a man is analogical.
keyTerms.origin: Latin univocus (“one-voiced”), aequivocus (“equal-voiced,” i.e., same word for different things), Greek analogia (“proportion”); Aristotle and the Scholastics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Literal vs. metaphorical — analogical predication is literal; metaphor is only one (improper) kind of analogy.

keyTerms.definition: In an analogy of attribution, the primary analogate is what the term applies to intrinsically; secondary analogates receive the term because of their relation to it.
keyTerms.example: God is the primary analogate of ‘power’; the sun, whose power to melt ice is derived from God, is a secondary analogate.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic logic of analogy.
keyTerms.confuseWith: More and less important examples — ‘primary’ means the source of the term's application, not merely the best example.

keyTerms.definition: A definition places a thing in a broader kind (genus) and names what distinguishes it within that kind (specific difference).
keyTerms.example: Human = animal (genus) + rational (difference). Because God has no such composition, he cannot be defined or fully comprehended this way.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle's Topics and Porphyry's Isagoge; Latin genus and differentia specifica.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Species — the species is the whole defined kind (human), made up of genus plus difference.

keyTerms.definition: A description of the tendencies or dispositions a kind of thing has by virtue of its nature; such dispositions can be blocked or fail to be triggered without the law being violated.
keyTerms.example: Water's disposition to freeze at 32°F, which unusual conditions can prevent (liquid water below freezing).
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian-Thomistic essentialism; Feser cites Anselm Ramelow and David Oderberg.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Humean regularity view — for Hume, laws are exceptionless regularities that could have been different for the very same things.

keyTerms.definition: The view, from Hume, that laws of nature are contingent regularities: the very same things could have obeyed entirely different laws.
keyTerms.example: On it, water might have turned to chocolate mousse at 32°F or an acorn grown into a dog, if only the laws were different.
keyTerms.origin: David Hume and his followers.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Aristotelian view — for which different laws would mean different natures and so different things.

keyTerms.definition: Feser's claim that, given that certain kinds of things exist, the laws expressing their natures could not be otherwise; only whether such things exist at all is contingent.
keyTerms.example: Anything that reliably grew into a dog just wouldn't be an acorn.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian essentialism (Oderberg, Real Essentialism).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Absolute necessity of the world — the actual laws need not have obtained, since there might have been no water or acorns at all.

keyTerms.definition: An effect that elevates a thing to a power its nature cannot account for (or, in the subtractive case, suspends a natural effect), having God as its cause from outside the natural order.
keyTerms.example: A resurrection (additive) or the three young men unburned in the fiery furnace (subtractive).
keyTerms.origin: Latin miraculum, “object of wonder”; Aquinas as summarized by Anselm Ramelow.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A violation of a law of nature (Hume's definition), which Feser argues is impossible.

keyTerms.definition: Natural theology reasons to God from premises available to anyone (philosophy, observation); revealed theology rests on what God has revealed.
keyTerms.example: The five proofs are natural theology; doctrines accepted on a prophet's miraculously attested word would be revealed theology. Miracles are the bridge.
keyTerms.origin: Traditional Scholastic distinction (Aquinas, Summa Contra Gentiles I).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Reason vs. faith as enemies — for Aquinas, revealed theology is reasonable because the fact of revelation is supported by evidence.

keyTerms.definition: Believing something because God has revealed it — where the claim that God has revealed it must itself be supported by evidence.
keyTerms.example: Accepting a teaching because a prophet who worked miracles, which only God can do, proclaimed it.
keyTerms.origin: Aquinas and the classical theological tradition.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Blind faith (belief without or against evidence), which Feser calls a very common misconception.

keyTerms.definition: The view that religious belief rests on faith alone and cannot or need not be supported by reason.
keyTerms.example: Feser describes his position as rationalist rather than fideist, since it holds that God's existence and attributes can be demonstrated.
keyTerms.origin: Latin fides, “faith.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Apophatic theology — negative theology says our knowledge of God is limited; fideism says reason can't reach God at all.

keyTerms.definition: The traditional conception of God as purely actual, simple, immutable, eternal, necessary, omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good, the creator and sustainer of all things and distinct from them.
keyTerms.example: Feser argues maternal imagery for God would conflict with classical theism by suggesting change or continuity with the world.
keyTerms.origin: The common view of Augustine, Anselm, Maimonides, Avicenna, and Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Theistic personalism — the view of God as a very great person alongside others, with changing states, which classical theists reject.

keyTerms.term: Principle of sufficient reason (PSR) and principle of causality (PC)
keyTerms.definition: PSR: there is an explanation for why anything exists and has the attributes it has. PC: any potential that is actualized is actualized by something already actual.
keyTerms.example: PPC and agere sequitur esse both follow from PSR and PC: a feature of an effect with no source in its cause would be unexplained and an actualization with no actualizer.
keyTerms.origin: PSR is associated with Leibniz; PC is Aristotelian-Scholastic. Both defended in earlier chapters.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Each other — PC concerns actualizations of potential; PSR concerns intelligibility or explanation in general.

keyTerms.definition: Actuality is the way a thing actually is; potentiality is a way it can be but isn't yet. A thing actual in some respect is ‘in act’; one with an unrealized capacity is ‘in potency.’ Change is the actualization of a potential.
keyTerms.example: A tree actually has leaves and potentially has deeper roots; when the roots grow, a potential is actualized. A good tree is one whose natural potentials are actualized.
keyTerms.origin: Latin actus and potentia, rendering Aristotle's energeia and dunamis.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Logical possibility — a potential is a real capacity in an existing thing, not merely something that involves no contradiction.

keyTerms.definition: A thing's essence is what it is; its existence is that it is. In every creature the two are really distinct, so its existence must be caused; in God essence just is existence.
keyTerms.example: You can grasp what a unicorn is (its essence) without knowing whether any unicorn exists — which is why the concept of a unicorn doesn't compel God to create unicorns.
keyTerms.origin: Aquinas, De Ente et Essentia; the basis of the Thomistic proof (chapter 4).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Essence and accident — accidents (like color or size) are features a thing can gain or lose; existence is not a feature among others but the act by which the thing is.

keyTerms.definition: Made up of parts of some kind — physical parts, or metaphysical ‘parts’ such as act and potency or essence and existence. Whatever is composite needs a cause of the combination of its parts. Its opposite is simple or noncomposite.
keyTerms.example: A tree is composite (roots, trunk, leaves; and also act and potency), which is why it cannot have existential inertia; God, being noncomposite, needs no cause.
keyTerms.origin: Latin componere, “to put together”; the Neo-Platonic proof (chapter 2) turns on it.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Complicated — even a thing with few physical parts is composite if its essence is distinct from its existence.

keyTerms.definition: Able to exist or not exist; not existing by the necessity of its own nature. Every composite thing is contingent.
keyTerms.example: Trees, dogs, and you are contingent: the world might have lacked all of them. Laws of nature are contingent only in the sense that the things they govern need not have existed.
keyTerms.origin: Latin contingere, “to happen, to befall.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Random — a contingent thing may be caused in a thoroughly orderly way; ‘contingent’ means only that it doesn't have to exist.

keyTerms.definition: A being that cannot fail to exist, because its existence is not received from anything; absolutely necessary being is what the rationalist proof concludes to. Contrasted with contingent being.
keyTerms.example: Feser's footnote: the world can't be the necessary being, since whatever is composite, potential, or has essence distinct from existence cannot be necessary.
keyTerms.origin: Latin necessarius; Avicenna, Aquinas's Third Way, Leibniz.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Derived necessity — something might be necessary in a secondary way (Aquinas's Third Way) yet still owe its necessity to God.

keyTerms.definition: Existence without beginning, end, or succession — not an endless stretch of time but being outside time altogether. God is eternal in this sense, and so knows and causes in a single timeless act.
keyTerms.example: Because God is eternal, he doesn't wait for tomorrow to know what will happen; he knows it by knowing himself as timelessly causing a temporal world.
keyTerms.origin: Latin aeternitas; Boethius's classic definition, the whole and perfect possession of unending life all at once.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Everlastingness — lasting through all time, which still involves succession; God's eternity involves none.

keyTerms.definition: Immaterial: not made of matter at all. Incorporeal: not having a body. God is both, which is why features like color and shape can't be in him as they are in bodies.
keyTerms.example: God can't be red or round, and he has no perceptual organs, so he doesn't know the world by sensing it.
keyTerms.origin: Latin in- (“not”) + materia (“matter”) / corpus (“body”).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Imaginary or unreal — being immaterial is a way of being real, not a failure to be real.

keyTerms.definition: The attribute of being one and only one: there is, and in principle can be, only one purely actual, simple, necessary being. Derived in Part A of the chapter.
keyTerms.example: Omnipotence relies on unity: since there cannot be more than one ultimate cause, everything else depends on that one cause for existence and power.
keyTerms.origin: Latin unitas; classical monotheism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Simplicity — unity says there is only one God; simplicity says that one God has no parts.

keyTerms.definition: The cause from which all other causes derive their causal power; ‘first’ in the sense of most fundamental, not merely earliest in time.
keyTerms.example: When the sun melts ice, God is the first cause and the sun a secondary cause; without the first, the secondary would be inert.
keyTerms.origin: Latin causa prima; Aristotle and Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The first event in a temporal sequence (like the Big Bang) — Feser's First Cause is first in a here-and-now hierarchy of dependence.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which each member causes only because it is here and now being caused to cause by a prior member, so the whole depends at every moment on a first member. Contrasted with a per accidens (linear) series extended in time, where earlier members can vanish.
keyTerms.example: A stone moved by a stick moved by a hand is per se; a grandfather begetting a father who later begets a son is per accidens. The proofs concern per se series, which is why they yield conservation and concurrence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin per se (“through itself, essentially”) vs. per accidens (“incidentally”); developed in chapter 1.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A temporal chain going back to a beginning — a per se series can be simultaneous and says nothing about whether the universe had a beginning.

keyTerms.definition: An efficient cause brings about a thing's existence or a change in it; a formal cause is a thing's nature, what makes it the kind of thing it is. PPC concerns efficient causes; agere sequitur esse concerns formal causes.
keyTerms.example: The baker is the efficient cause of the cake; being a rational animal is the formal cause (nature) of a human being, from which language use flows.
keyTerms.origin: Two of Aristotle's four causes (with material and final causes).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Each other — the efficient cause is an agent distinct from the effect; the formal cause is intrinsic to the thing itself.

keyTerms.definition: What a thing is — the kind of thing it is — from which its characteristic attributes, tendencies, and activities flow. ‘Nature’ emphasizes the essence as a source of activity.
keyTerms.example: It is the tree's nature to sink roots and photosynthesize; it is water's nature to freeze at 32°F. Goodness and laws of nature are both defined by reference to natures.
keyTerms.origin: Latin natura (from nasci, “to be born”), rendering Aristotle's phusis; ‘essence’ is Latin essentia.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Nature’ as the whole physical world — Feser often means the nature of a particular kind of thing.

keyTerms.definition: A real feature by which a thing of a certain nature tends to manifest some quality or behavior under certain conditions; it can be present even when blocked or not triggered.
keyTerms.example: Salt's disposition to dissolve is there even in a dry shaker; water's disposition to freeze at 32°F can be blocked in unusual conditions.
keyTerms.origin: Latin dispositio, “arrangement”; central to the Aristotelian account of laws (Ramelow, Oderberg).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A regularity — a regularity is a pattern of observed events; a disposition is the power in the thing that explains the pattern and can exist without manifesting.

keyTerms.definition: God's attribute of being wholly good with no privation or badness of any kind; he is all-good both as pure actuality and as the source of all goodness in creatures. Sometimes called omnibenevolence.
keyTerms.example: Because God is perfectly good, he cannot sin — no more a limit on omnipotence than being unable to make a round square.
keyTerms.origin: Classical theism; Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I.6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Moral virtue — God's goodness is not the achievement of a striving moral agent but the limit case of goodness, unable to fail.

keyTerms.definition: Completeness or full actuality; a perfect being lacks nothing it could have. For Feser, God's perfection follows from what he is (pure actuality), not from what he makes.
keyTerms.example: A flawless diamond is perfect whether it cuts thick glass, thin glass, or none — the reply to Rowe's claim that without a best world there's no most perfect being.
keyTerms.origin: Latin perfectus, “completed, thoroughly made.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Maximal output — a perfect maker needn't produce a maximal product, especially where no maximum exists.

keyTerms.definition: The power of grasping concepts, forming propositions, and reasoning — distinct from sensation and imagination. Feser argues there is in God something analogous to intellect, where the forms of all possible things exist as concepts.
keyTerms.example: We use intellect when we ‘see’ that the Pythagorean theorem is true; God's intellect contains the concept catness and the proposition that the cat is on the mat.
keyTerms.origin: Latin intellectus, from intellegere, “to understand.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: The brain — for Aristotelians intellect is an immaterial power; a brain is its bodily condition in humans, and God has none.

keyTerms.definition: The will's not being compelled by anything external or internal to choose as it does. Humans have it; God has it in the fullest sense, since nothing outside him exists independently and nothing in his ideas necessitates creation.
keyTerms.example: God could have created a world with unicorns rather than lions; a novel's murderer freely chooses his crime even though the author wrote it.
keyTerms.origin: Latin liberum arbitrium; debated from Augustine and Aquinas to Pike, Kretzmann, and Rowe.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Randomness or arbitrariness — a free choice is uncompelled, not uncaused or unreasoned.

keyTerms.definition: Knowledge of the future before it happens. Feser answers the objection that divine foreknowledge destroys freedom, but strictly God has no ‘fore’-knowledge: he knows all times in one timeless act.
keyTerms.example: Knowing by a promise or a crystal ball that you'll sit in the next room tomorrow wouldn't make your sitting unfree.
keyTerms.origin: Old English prefix fore- (“before”); the classic objection is Nelson Pike's (1965).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Eternal knowledge — God's knowledge is not earlier than events, since he is not in time.

keyTerms.definition: In its essence, love is the lover's willing the good of the beloved — an act of the active will, not primarily a passive emotion. On this account an immutable God can love.
keyTerms.example: A parent who gets up at 3 a.m. for a sick child while feeling only exhaustion still loves; tough love and love of enemies are love for the same reason.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle's account of love as willing good to another, taken up by Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I.20).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Affection or emotional attachment — these usually accompany human love but are not its essence (the fallacy of accident).

keyTerms.definition: A being with intellect and will. Because God has (analogues of) intellect and will, he is personal, which is why Feser rejects the impersonal pronoun ‘it’ for God.
keyTerms.example: A religion that says the divine is an impersonal force is, on Feser's view, refuted by natural theology.
keyTerms.origin: Latin persona; Boethius's definition, an individual substance of a rational nature.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A human being or a body — being personal does not require a body, sex, or change.

keyTerms.definition: God's causing things to exist — not only at a beginning but at every moment (conservation). God's being Creator is a Cambridge property: the real change is in creatures, not in God.
keyTerms.example: Creation is like a song that exists only while being sung, not a painting that outlasts its painter.
keyTerms.origin: Latin creatio; the classical doctrine of creation out of nothing.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Making from pre-existing material — creatures are not made out of God or anything else; God isn't a material with potentials (the limit of the dough analogy).

keyTerms.definition: The view that judgments of good and bad merely express personal preferences or feelings rather than stating facts.
keyTerms.example: Feser's reply: calling a ruled triangle a better triangle than one scrawled on a bus seat isn't a preference for straight lines; it follows from what a triangle is.
keyTerms.origin: Modern moral philosophy (emotivism, expressivism).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Disagreement about values — people's disagreeing doesn't show there is no fact of the matter.

keyTerms.definition: Deliberately making a subject obscure, or appealing to mystery to avoid rational scrutiny.
keyTerms.example: Feser denies that his claim of divine incomprehensibility is obscurantist: the arguments themselves predict it, as physics predicts strangeness at its frontiers.
keyTerms.origin: From ‘obscurant,’ Latin obscurare, “to darken.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Acknowledging genuine limits of knowledge — which is what a conclusion derived from simplicity does.

keyTerms.definition: A hypothetical rational but incorporeal creature, intermediate between humans and God. Feser uses angels as examples while noting their actual existence is irrelevant to his points.
keyTerms.example: An angel's goodness comes from choice but not over time or against bodily desires; an angel's extraordinary feat would be preternatural, not a miracle.
keyTerms.origin: Greek angelos, “messenger.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: God — angels would be creatures with natures, conserved and concurred with like anything else.

keyTerms.definition: Truths communicated by God that could not be reached by philosophical or scientific reasoning; accepting them on God's authority is faith.
keyTerms.example: A prophet teaching a doctrine reason can't reach would need miracles to show his message really comes from God.
keyTerms.origin: Latin revelatio, “unveiling.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Natural theology — which reaches truths about God by reason alone.

keyTerms.definition: Feser's position that God's existence and attributes can be demonstrated by reason (in contrast with fideism), yielding real positive knowledge (in contrast with purely negative theology).
keyTerms.example: Feser describes the book's position as rationalist rather than fideist, while still holding that God is strictly incomprehensible.
keyTerms.origin: Feser's usage; related to, but not the same as, the ‘rationalist proof’ of chapter 5.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Rationalism in the Descartes–Leibniz sense (knowledge from pure reason without experience) — most of Feser's proofs start from experience.

keyTerms.definition: An individual thing that has, or ‘instantiates,’ a universal form. Many instances can share one universal.
keyTerms.example: Each red apple instantiates redness. If God merely instantiated redness, his redness would be one more instance needing explanation.
keyTerms.origin: Latin instantia; standard metaphysical vocabulary.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The universal itself — the redness of this apple is an instance, not redness as such.

keyTerms.definition: The tendency of a thing, by its nature, toward its characteristic activities and ends, even without any awareness. The lowest grade of appetite, found in plants and even inanimate things.
keyTerms.example: A tree inclines toward sinking roots and photosynthesizing and will do so unless disease or damage prevents it.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian-Thomistic teleology (natural appetite).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Sensory appetite — natural inclination involves no consciousness; sensory appetite does.

keyTerms.definition: Feser's recurring point that God is not one more cause alongside created causes, competing with them, but the source of there being any causes at all. It underlies his replies on freedom, concurrence, and miracles.
keyTerms.example: The author isn't a character in the novel, so he doesn't interfere with his characters as a hypnotist would; God can't ‘intervene’ in what he is already doing.
keyTerms.origin: Classical theism; Feser cites Herbert McCabe and Brian Davies.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Distance or absence — being ‘outside’ the order of causes means being intimately present to all of them as their source, not being far away.

keyTerms.definition: A figurative use of a term, grounded in a real likeness but in which the form named is not literally present in one of the things. Metaphor is one kind of analogy, but not all analogy is metaphor.
keyTerms.example: ‘George is a lion’ is metaphorical; ‘God is good’ is analogical but literal.
keyTerms.origin: Greek metaphora, “a carrying over”; Scholastic analogia proportionalitatis impropriae.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Analogy of proper proportionality — there the property (life, goodness) is literally in each analogate.

distinctions.name: Occasionalism vs. mere conservationism (and the concurrentist middle)

left.label: Occasionalism
left.desc: Only God causes anything. Creatures are mere occasions: God melts the ice when the sun is out, and moves the eight ball when the cue ball touches it. The first cause is the only cause.

right.label: Mere conservationism
right.desc: God keeps creatures in existence, but once sustained they exercise their causal powers on their own. The sun melts the ice independently of God. In effect this is deism: creatures could carry on without him.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Both extremes fail by agere sequitur esse: what does nothing would not exist (so occasionalism leaves only God), and what could act independently could exist independently (so mere conservationism denies conservation). Both also destroy the starting points of the proofs. The truth is concurrentism: creatures are real but secondary causes, making a genuine contribution while acting only with God's concurrence. This is the key to seeing that God and creatures are not competitors for the same causal job.

distinctions.name: Observational knowledge vs. knowledge by being the cause

left.label: Observational (spectator) knowledge
left.desc: Knowing something by receiving information from it — perceiving, being told, waiting for it to happen. The knower depends on the known, changes by learning, and must be present to it in time.

right.label: Knowledge as cause (author's knowledge)
right.desc: Knowing something by knowing oneself as its cause, as an author knows his characters by knowing his own intentions. The known depends on the knower. This is how God knows the world: in one timeless act of self-knowledge.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Almost every puzzle about divine knowledge assumes the spectator model: that God must ‘see’ the future (so the future must already exist, as four-dimensionalism says), or that he learns what we will do. Once God's knowledge is understood as an author's knowledge, those puzzles lose their grip, and his knowledge no more crowds out our freedom than an author's writing crowds out a character's.

distinctions.name: Cause of the whole story vs. cause within the story

left.label: Hypnotist (cause alongside)
left.desc: A character within the story who interferes with other characters, making them do what they otherwise would not. Such causation competes with and overrides the agent's own choice.

right.label: Author (cause of the whole)
right.desc: The source of the entire story, including the characters and their free choices. He does not interfere with anyone because he is not one of them; his causality is of a completely different order.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This contrast answers the free-will objections, grounds the account of concurrence, and explains why God does not ‘intervene’ in miracles. Nearly every objection to classical theism in this module quietly models God as a hypnotist — a very powerful character — instead of as an author.

distinctions.name: Privation vs. mere absence

left.label: Mere absence (negation)
left.desc: Lacking something a thing's nature does not call for. A triangle lacking a fourth side, a tree lacking wings, a stone lacking sight: no defect at all.

right.label: Privation
right.desc: Lacking something a thing's nature does call for. A triangle with a wavy side, a tree with weak roots, a blind dog, a will lacking the intention to respect others' rights.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The privation theory does not say evil is ‘nothing at all’ or unreal; it says evil is a real lack of what ought to be there. That is what lets Feser say God is the source of all positive reality without being the source of evil, and why the objection that the theory denies evil's reality misses its target.

distinctions.name: What usually accompanies an activity vs. what is essential to it

left.label: Accidental accompaniment
left.desc: Features our acts of loving, choosing, or acting happen to involve because we are bodily, temporal, changeable creatures: feelings rising and falling, actualizing potentials, undergoing change.

right.label: Essence of the activity
right.desc: What makes the activity what it is: love is willing the good of the beloved; freedom is not being compelled from within or without; acting is producing an effect in another.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Confusing the two is the fallacy of accident, and it drives the objections that an immutable God cannot love, a simple God cannot choose freely, and an unchanging God cannot act. Once the essence is isolated, the attribute can be ascribed to God analogically without its creaturely baggage.

distinctions.name: Comprehending God loosely vs. comprehending him strictly

left.label: Loose comprehension (possible)
left.desc: Genuine understanding that God exists and what he is not (apophatic knowledge), plus literal analogical knowledge of his positive attributes (power, knowledge, goodness, will, love).

right.label: Strict comprehension (impossible)
right.desc: Understanding a thing fully by analyzing it into parts and their arrangement, or into genus and specific difference. God, being simple, has no such structure, so our positive concepts of him ‘thin out.’

distinctions.whyItMatters: It lets you hold both that natural theology yields real knowledge (against fideism and pure negative theology) and that God remains mysterious (against the charge that the theist claims to have God figured out). The mystery is not a dodge; the arguments predict it, as physics predicts strangeness at its frontiers.

distinctions.name: Violation (breach) of a law vs. suspension of a law

left.label: Violation / breach
left.desc: The law stays in force but is not obeyed: the conditions for fire burning are all present and sustained, yet the fire somehow acts against its own nature. Feser says this is metaphysically impossible, since laws express natures. Compare a government that keeps a law on the books but declines to enforce it.

right.label: Suspension
right.desc: The law temporarily does not apply because some of what it presupposes is withdrawn: God refrains from conserving or concurring with some factors, so the normal effect simply does not arise. Compare a government temporarily revoking a law.

distinctions.whyItMatters: It shows how miracles are possible even though laws of nature are metaphysically necessary. Additive miracles elevate nature beyond its powers; subtractive miracles (the fiery furnace) involve God not doing something rather than forcing something.

distinctions.name: Supernatural vs. preternatural

left.label: Preternatural
left.desc: Extraordinary effects within the power of some created nature, such as an angel, if angels exist. Still part of the natural order broadly construed, since such beings are creatures conserved and concurred with by God.

right.label: Supernatural
right.desc: Effects that elevate a thing to a power no created nature can account for, and whose cause lies outside the natural order altogether. Only God can produce them. (Contrast also the subnatural: defects that fall short of a nature.)

distinctions.whyItMatters: Only a strictly supernatural effect can serve as God's ‘seal’ on a revelation, because nothing but God could produce it. It also shows why miracles are nothing like magic or advanced technology, which are just more (hidden) natural causes.

illustrations.title: The author who conceives the whole story in a flash
illustrations.body:
Imagine an author who comes up with an entire novel in one instantaneous insight. At that instant he cannot be mistaken about whether a certain character is in the story or what happens to her, because she is there only because he put her there. He does not find out about his characters by watching them; he knows them by knowing his own creative intentions.

Feser uses this to explain three things: why God cannot be mistaken (he makes true what he knows), how God meets the ‘reliable process’ condition on knowledge (nothing is more reliable than being the one who makes p true), and why God's knowledge of the world is really his self-knowledge. A human author can forget, but only because he is temporal, changeable, dependent on a brain, and subject to outside forces — none of which applies to God.

illustrations.title: The crime novel: author vs. hypnotist
illustrations.body:
In a crime novel a character plots a murder for money, carries it out, is caught, and is justly punished. It would be silly to say he didn't act freely because the author wrote it that way. But if a later chapter revealed that another character had hypnotized him, we would say: ‘So it wasn't free after all.’

The difference is that the hypnotist is a character alongside the murderer, interfering with him, while the author is not in the story at all and interferes with no one; his causality is of a different order entirely. Use this whenever someone says that God's knowing or causing everything must crowd out human freedom: they are picturing God as the hypnotist.

illustrations.title: The prism and the lump of dough
illustrations.body:
White light contains all the colors of the spectrum in a unified way; a prism draws out distinct beams of green, red, and so on. A lump of dough virtually contains countless cookie shapes; cutters draw out a star, a circle, a heart. If you knew the white light perfectly, you would know every color it could yield; if you knew the dough perfectly, every shape it could yield.

God is unlimited actuality, and each kind of creature is a limited way of being actual — being actual *as a dog* rather than as a tree, as green is color limited to green. So by knowing himself perfectly, God knows every finite way of being that could be drawn from him, in one undivided act. Feser flags the limits: creatures are not made *out of* God as cookies are made of dough, since God is not a material with potentials.

illustrations.title: Triangles on a bus seat and in a lecture
illustrations.body:
A triangle scrawled on the cracked seat of a moving bus has gaps and wobbly sides; one drawn carefully with a ruler and art pen comes much closer to the essence of triangularity. Calling the second a good triangle and the first a bad one is not a matter of taste; it follows from what a triangle is. Badness here is just a shortfall: the straightness that is missing.

Now suppose a lecturer draws two sides and deliberately stops partway through the third, to make a philosophical point. The badness of the figure is not something extra he put there; it is what he left out. And his leaving it out is no defect in him, since the whole situation — lecture, audience, understanding — is good in a way it could not have been otherwise. That is Feser's model for how God can create a world containing evil without evil being in God.

illustrations.title: The diamond that need not cut any glass
illustrations.body:
A flawless diamond is a perfect diamond whether it cuts a sheet of glass an eighth of an inch thick, a quarter of an inch thick, or never cuts anything. Its perfection comes from what it is. Because action follows being, it has the capacity to cut many kinds of glass, but its perfection does not depend on which it cuts or whether it cuts at all.

Feser uses this against Rowe's claim that if there is no best possible world, there can be no most perfect being (since a being that made a better world would be more perfect). God's perfection flows from his pure actuality, not from his products, so whether he makes a world with x forests, x + 1, or none is irrelevant to it.

illustrations.title: The blue chalk and the moon
illustrations.body:
When you draw a square on a chalkboard with blue chalk (Alfred Freddoso's example), you and the chalk are joint causes. You are why there is a square at all; the chalk is why it is blue. Red chalk or a pencil would produce a different effect, so the chalk contributes something real. But with no hand pressing it, nothing happens at all.

Or take the moon: its appearance in the night sky depends on its own surface and material, so it contributes something real, yet it gives no light at all without the sun. That is concurrence: creatures are true causes (their natures make a difference to the effect) and secondary causes (their activity depends at every instant on the first cause).

illustrations.title: The father guiding his son's hand
illustrations.body:
A father teaches his young son to write the letter A by guiding his hand (David Oderberg's example). The child can resist and pull his hand the wrong way, or cooperate and let it be guided. Nothing in the father's guidance as such rules out either, so the child's choice makes a real contribution. Yet no letter A appears on the page without the father's guidance.

Feser offers this as a picture of how God's concurrence with our free acts leaves them genuinely ours. It is an analogy, not a mechanism — God does not push against us as one force against another.

illustrations.title: The jazz musician, the director's cut, and the second edition
illustrations.body:
Think of the world as music and God as the musician. The ordinary course of nature is his playing from the score; a miracle is like a jazz improvisation. He doesn't have to force the music anywhere, since every note, written or improvised, is his; yet the improvisation adds something the score did not contain. Or the world is a film: the natural order is the theatrical release and miracles belong to the director's cut. Or it is a novel, and miracles are new material in a second edition.

In each case the original was complete and good, so a miracle is not a repair job but a raising of something good to a higher level. Subtractive miracles fit too: the musician omits notes, the director cuts a scene. Contrast the misleading picture of an airplane on autopilot with a pilot occasionally grabbing the controls.

illustrations.title: Climbing the ladder and blasting it away
illustrations.body:
Someone slowly and carefully climbs a ladder, then pulls out a ray gun and blasts it out from under himself. He falls, and his careful climb was pointless.

Feser uses this image twice. Occasionalism does it by concluding that creatures do nothing (and so, by action-follows-being, are nothing), when the proofs began from real, changing, composite things that need a cause. Mere conservationism does it by concluding that creatures can act, and so exist, independently of God, when the proofs began from the fact that they cannot exist on their own even for an instant. Any account of God's relation to the world must keep the rungs we climbed on.

illustrations.title: The singer and the song
illustrations.body:
A painting, once finished, can survive its painter's death; a song, by contrast, exists only while someone is singing it. Stop singing and the song does not slowly fade by inertia — it simply is not there. Feser's doctrine of conservation says the world is related to God more like the song to the singer than like the painting to the painter.

The analogy also helps with concurrence and miracles. Every note is truly a note, with its own pitch and place in the melody (secondary causes are real), yet none sounds without the singer (they act only with God's concurrence). And the singer doesn't ‘intervene’ in his own song when he adds an ornament or holds a note longer; he is producing all of it. Limit: a singer is in time and can tire; God is neither.

objections.title: The paradox of the stone
objections.whoRaises: Classic puzzle; popular skeptics and introductory philosophy classes
objections.objection: Can God make a stone so heavy he cannot lift it? If he can, there is something he cannot do: lift it. If he cannot, there is something he cannot do: make it. Either way there is something God cannot do, so he is not omnipotent — and the very idea of omnipotence is incoherent.
objections.reply:
1. Omnipotence is the power to actualize any potential that can be actualized, to cause anything that could in principle exist or occur.
2. It is not a limitation to be unable to do what is self-contradictory, since there is no *capacity* to make a round square for anyone to lack; the phrase describes nothing.
3. A stone's rising is something that can occur, so God can always cause any stone to rise.
4. So ‘a stone too heavy for God to lift’ is self-contradictory — as empty as ‘round square.’ Failing to make it is not failing to do anything.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘an omnipotent being should be able to do even the contradictory,’ note Frankfurt's point (cited by Feser): then God could make the unliftable stone and also lift it, so the paradox still refutes nothing. But the better answer is that ‘doing the contradictory’ isn't a doing at all; asking for it is asking for a word-salad, not a feat.

objections.title: A God who cannot sin is not all-powerful
objections.whoRaises: Typical skeptic; some philosophers of religion
objections.objection: Humans can sin and God, being perfectly good, cannot. So there is at least one thing we can do that God cannot, and he is not omnipotent.
objections.reply:
1. Being perfectly good is shown later in the chapter to follow from pure actuality.
2. ‘Perfectly good yet sinning’ is self-contradictory, just like ‘round square.’
3. So God's not sinning is no more a limit on his power than his not making round squares.
4. Moreover sin, on the privation account, is a *defect* — a failure to realize what one should. The ability to sin is a liability of finite, fallible wills, not an additional power.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘but *I* can do something he can't,’ point out that the ‘something’ is a way of falling short. Being able to trip is not an athletic skill; being able to forget is not an extra kind of knowledge.

objections.title: Timeless knowledge implies a ‘block universe’
objections.whoRaises: Philosophers of time (discussed by Katherin Rogers and others)
objections.objection: If God knows past, present, and future all in a single timeless act, then past, present, and future must all somehow exist together for him to know them together. So classical theism commits us to four-dimensionalism: time is a spacelike dimension and nothing really comes into or passes out of being.
objections.reply:
1. That inference would follow if God's knowledge were observational: to observe everything at once, everything would have to be there at once.
2. But God does not know the world by observing it; he knows it by knowing himself as its cause.
3. What he knows timelessly is that he causes, timelessly, a world with a temporal history. It does not follow that the world he causes is itself timeless.
4. Compare a motionless hunter who knows in an instant that he fired a bullet: it doesn't follow that the bullet is motionless or present all along its path at once.
objections.pushback: If pressed on how a timeless act can have a temporal effect, point back to Part A: the change is in the effect, not the cause (a ‘Cambridge’ change in God). And stress that the time of the effect and the ‘time’ of the cause needn't match any more than the hunter's stillness must match the bullet's motion.

objections.title: Infallible foreknowledge rules out free will
objections.whoRaises: Nelson Pike and many popular skeptics
objections.objection: If God infallibly knows I will go to work tomorrow, then if I didn't go, God would have been wrong, which is impossible. So it is impossible that I not go, and I don't freely choose to go.
objections.reply:
1. Knowing that someone does something does not make them do it.
2. If I know, however certainly, that you are sitting in the next room, that is compatible with your freely deciding to sit there.
3. If I somehow knew with certainty (a promise, a crystal ball) that you would sit there tomorrow, why would that be any different? Knowledge of a free act in the future no more compels it than knowledge of a free act in the present.
4. And if it isn't incompatible when I am the knower, why would it be when God is?
objections.pushback: The skeptic may say the problem is infallibility: God *can't* be wrong. Reply that ‘if God knows I will do X, I will do X’ is necessarily true, but that is only because knowledge implies truth; it doesn't make ‘I will do X’ itself necessary. The necessity attaches to the conditional, not to my act. Then note Feser's deeper point: God's knowledge isn't foreknowledge at all, since he is not in time looking ahead.

objections.title: But God causes everything — so we aren't free
objections.whoRaises: Critics of classical theism; the follow-up to the foreknowledge objection
objections.objection: Unlike a human knower, God doesn't merely know the future; he causes it, and he knows it precisely by causing it. The same goes for the present. So all our actions, present and future, are caused by God, and none is freely chosen.
objections.reply:
1. Consider a crime novel in which a character plots and commits a murder for money. He acts freely and is justly punished, and it would be silly to deny this because the author wrote the story.
2. Contrast a plot twist in which another character hypnotized him: then we'd say the act wasn't free.
3. The difference: the hypnotist is a character alongside the others who interferes with them; the author is not in the story and interferes with no one.
4. God relates to us as the author, not as a hypnotist. His causal relation to the world is radically unlike the relations creatures have to each other.
5. The objection only seems strong when we speak of God's knowledge and causation univocally, as if he were one more agent in the world.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘the characters aren't really free — they're fictional,’ concede the analogy is imperfect: the point is logical. ‘X was caused by the author of the whole’ doesn't compete with ‘X was the character's free choice,’ whereas ‘X was caused by another character’ does. Then add concurrence (the father guiding the hand): God gives our choices their being and power; he doesn't substitute for them.

objections.title: Ideas in God contradict divine simplicity
objections.whoRaises: Critics of simplicity; careful students
objections.objection: Feser says concepts and propositions exist in God's intellect. But concepts and propositions are many and distinct, and a simple God can contain no multiplicity. So either God is not simple or he doesn't have ideas.
objections.reply:
1. Feser grants that concepts and propositions cannot exist in God as they do in us, as distinct thoughts; that is why language about them is analogical.
2. Even the idea of one vast conjunctive proposition fails, since it too would have parts.
3. Better: think of white light that contains all colors in a unified way before a prism separates them, or dough that virtually contains all cookie shapes.
4. God is unlimited actuality; each creature is a limited way of being actual. By knowing himself perfectly in one act, God knows all the limited ways of being that could be drawn from him. The multiplicity is on the side of creatures, not in God.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘that's just a metaphor,’ answer that the analogy is offered as suggestive, and that its imperfection is expected: we are describing the deepest level of reality with concepts formed from composite things. The argument for intellect in God doesn't depend on picturing it, only on the elimination argument from proportionate causality and the reality of universals.

objections.title: Good and bad are just subjective preferences
objections.whoRaises: Popular relativists; emotivists and expressivists
objections.objection: Calling something good or bad just expresses our likes and dislikes. So talk of God's ‘goodness’ is either projection or empty.
objections.reply:
1. Take a triangle: its essence (closed, three straight sides) has objective consequences, like angles summing to 180 degrees.
2. A triangle scrawled on a moving bus seat falls short of that essence; one drawn with a ruler comes closer. Calling the first bad and the second good simply reports how well each realizes the nature of a triangle.
3. Likewise a tree that sinks deep roots and photosynthesizes is a good tree; one damaged by disease is to that extent bad. This is grounded in what a tree is, not in anyone's preference.
4. So ‘good’ in the sense of ‘good specimen’ is objective, and moral goodness is the special case of creatures who freely promote or frustrate their own flourishing.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘that's not *moral* goodness,’ agree and explain that moral goodness is the same notion applied to rational creatures who can choose to act for or against their natural ends. Feser notes a full ethics is beyond this book; the point needed here is only that goodness tracks actuality in line with nature.

objections.title: The privation theory denies that evil is real
objections.whoRaises: Many contemporary philosophers; people moved by the horror of evil
objections.objection: If evil is ‘just the absence of good,’ then evil isn't real — which is an insult to victims of real horrors.
objections.reply:
1. Blindness is the absence of sight, yet nobody thinks saying so denies that blindness is real.
2. Explaining what blindness consists in (the failure of eyes or optic nerves to function) gives an account of its reality.
3. Likewise, saying evil is a privation of due good explains what evil's reality consists in; it does not explain it away.
objections.pushback: If they insist that absences can't hurt, point out that absences hurt all the time: the absence of oxygen suffocates, the absence of food starves, the absence of a railing on a cliff kills. A privation is a real lack of what should be there, and that can be devastating.

objections.title: Pain is a positive evil, not an absence
objections.whoRaises: Contemporary critics of the privation account (discussed by David Alexander)
objections.objection: Pain is bad, but it's not the absence of anything; it's the presence of something — a vivid sensation. So not all badness is privation.
objections.reply:
1. Pain is not bad without qualification: it signals damage and danger. An organism that felt no pain when touching something that would burn it would be worse off. Sometimes its *absence* is the bad thing.
2. Pain isn't always even experienced as bad: the ache after a hard workout can feel satisfying.
3. What is bad is what pain is associated with: the bodily damage it signals, or the loss of peace of mind it causes.
4. Pain asymbolia, in which brain damage leaves people feeling pain without its unpleasantness, supports separating the sensation from its badness.
objections.pushback: If they point to pointless agony, reply that its badness still lies in privations: the damaged tissue, the disrupted functioning, the lost tranquility. The sensation is a positive reality, but its *badness* is the harm and disorder it involves or signals.

objections.title: Murder involves a positive intention
objections.whoRaises: Todd Calder, ‘Is the Privation Theory of Evil Dead?’
objections.objection: The murderer doesn't just fail to respect a duty; he positively intends to kill an innocent person unjustly, and he has positive beliefs and desires. Those are presences, not absences, so moral evil can't be analyzed as privation.
objections.reply:
1. Following David Alexander: the privation theory never said that a bad act has no positive features, only that its *badness* consists in a privation.
2. The murderer does have beliefs and desires, and having a desire is really having something.
3. The desire may even be good in itself — for example, a desire for money.
4. What is bad is what is missing: an intention to pursue money only in ways that respect the rights of the innocent.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘but the *intention to kill* is itself positive,’ answer that an intention is a real act of will, and what makes it evil is its disorder: it lacks the conformity to right reason and justice that a good will has. The positive ‘stuff’ of the act is good qua being; the evil is the missing order.

objections.title: Sadism is a positive delight in harm
objections.whoRaises: Critics of the privation account
objections.objection: The sadist doesn't merely fail to respect others; he positively enjoys harming them. Sadistic desire is a presence, not an absence.
objections.reply:
1. Sadistic desire is desire that is misdirected: aimed at an end contrary to the concern for others that we, as social animals, need in order to flourish.
2. It is a psychological deformity or defect, just as blindness is a physiological one.
3. Fully defending this needs ethics, but it suffices to show that sadism is no more resistant to a privation analysis than any other badness.
objections.pushback: If they say the sadist's pleasure is intense and real, agree: pleasure is real, and the capacity to take pleasure is good. What is evil is that it attaches to the wrong object, the harm of another, reflecting a missing rightly ordered concern. A deformed limb is real tissue; its deformity is the lack of proper form.

objections.title: By proportionate causality, evil must be in God
objections.whoRaises: Natural objection to Feser's own principle
objections.objection: If whatever is in an effect must be in its cause, and there is evil in the world, then evil must be in God.
objections.reply:
1. Evil is not a positive reality but an absence of due good.
2. So making a world with evil in it is not making two kinds of thing, good ones and bad ones; it is making good things while refraining from making certain other goods.
3. If I draw two sides of a triangle and stop partway through the third, the badness isn't an extra thing I added but what I left out.
4. The principle says that positive features of an effect must be in its total cause. Evil isn't that sort of thing, so the principle doesn't put it in God.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘fine, but then God is responsible for what he left out,’ that is really the next objection — and ultimately the problem of evil (chapter 7). Here the claim is only metaphysical: God is not evil and evil is not in him.

objections.title: Not creating all possible good is a defect in God
objections.whoRaises: Typical skeptic; a preview of the problem of evil
objections.objection: Even if evil is a mere absence, God could have filled that absence. His failing to create all the good he could have created is a defect in him, so he isn't perfectly good.
objections.reply:
1. My leaving a triangle unfinished indicates no defect in me if I had a good reason — say, to make a philosophical point in a lecture.
2. The incomplete triangle is bad taken alone, but the whole situation (lecture, audience, understanding) is good, and good in a way impossible without that element of badness.
3. Similarly, some goods of creation are impossible without the permission of local badness. Courage requires facing real danger of harm and doing right anyway.
4. God can no more make a world with courage but no real danger than he can make a round square. So permitting some badness is consistent with perfect goodness.
