objections.pushback: If they ask about courage in heaven, where there is no danger, Feser's footnote answers: the blessed keep the courage they acquired on earth, as an old veteran keeps the courage he won in battle. For the general problem of evil, note that chapter 7 treats it at length.

objections.title: A simple, purely actual God cannot be free
objections.whoRaises: Norman Kretzmann; Jay Wesley Richards
objections.objection: To act freely is to have the potential to do this or that and to actualize one. A purely actual, simple God has no potentials. So either he isn't free (Kretzmann weakens freedom) or he isn't strictly simple (Richards weakens simplicity).
objections.reply:
1. When *we* choose, we do actualize potentials, such as moving a limb one way rather than another.
2. But inferring that free choice as such requires actualizing potentials is a fallacy of accident, like inferring that all acting requires change because our acting does.
3. What freedom essentially requires is that the agent not be compelled by anything outside or inside it, and that holds of God (nothing external exists independently; no possible creature's concept necessitates its existence).
4. Granted, it is hard to picture a will that is free yet has no potentialities. Brian Davies suggests treating divine freedom mainly as a negative claim: God is not compelled. But difficulty is expected when reasoning reaches this far beyond everyday experience, and our own freedom is famously mysterious too.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘then God could have done otherwise, so there's an unrealized alternative in him,’ answer that the alternatives are alternative effects, not alternative states of God. Different creations would mean different Cambridge relations to God, not a different God; the variation is on the side of the world.

objections.title: God must create the best possible world (so he isn't free)
objections.whoRaises: Leibniz; revived by William Rowe, Can God Be Free?
objections.objection: An omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God must create the best possible world; otherwise he couldn't, didn't know how, or didn't want to. But then he could not have done otherwise, so he is not free.
objections.reply:
The argument assumes (a) that one is always obliged to bring about the best one can, and (b) that there is a best possible world. Both are false.

1. Against (a): suppose a world with trees is better than one with only stones and water. Who is wronged if God doesn't make it? Not God, who is already perfectly good and needs nothing — so he need not create at all. Not the trees, since what does not exist cannot be harmed or wronged. (Creating trees without water would harm them, but only because they'd then exist.)
2. Against (b): if trees make a world better, a forest is better than a tree and two forests better than one — and for any world with x forests, there is a possible world with x + 1. So there is no best possible world (Aquinas makes the point).
3. God can no more be obliged to create a best world than to create a round square.
objections.pushback: If they propose that goodness comes in some other dimension that does have a maximum, ask what it would be — and note that the first reply (no one is wronged by not being created) still stands on its own.

objections.title: No best world means no most perfect being
objections.whoRaises: William Rowe
objections.objection: If there is no best world, then whatever world God makes, a being who made a better one would be more perfect than God — and so on forever. So there can be no most perfect being, and if God must be perfect, there is no God.
objections.reply:
1. The objection assumes God's perfection depends on what he does or makes.
2. It doesn't: it follows from what he is — pure actuality and all that entails. He has it whatever he creates, or if he creates nothing.
3. A perfect diamond is perfect whether it cuts thin glass, thick glass, or none; because action follows being, it has the capacity to cut many kinds, but need not exercise it in any particular way.
4. Likewise a perfect being has the power to create any possible world without having to create any given one. Which world God makes is irrelevant to whether he is the most perfect possible being.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘but surely making a better world shows more goodness,’ reply that it would show more goodness *in the product*, not more perfection in the maker. A maker who is already infinite act has nothing to gain; the ‘more’ is all on the side of creatures.

objections.title: An immutable God cannot love
objections.whoRaises: Open theists, process theologians, many ordinary believers
objections.objection: Love means being affected by the beloved: the parent's worry for a distressed child, the lover who can't stop thinking of the beloved. Being affected is being changed. So if God is immutable, he doesn't love us.
objections.reply:
1. This is a fallacy of accident: our love usually comes with such emotional changes, but that doesn't make them essential to love.
2. What is essential is that the lover wills the good of the beloved.
3. That's why love made only of feelings that wax and wane counts as shallow, while love that keeps willing the other's good when feelings flag counts as serious — and why ‘tough love’ and love of enemies are genuine love despite conflicting feelings.
4. Love is chiefly an act of will (active), not an emotion (passive).
5. God has will, and in creating he wills that things exist together with all the goods that flow from their natures (the tree's roots and photosynthesis). So he loves what he creates.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘a love that isn't moved by my suffering is cold,’ reply that the love that moves us to feeling is a finite love that needs to be stirred. God's love is not less than ours but more: it doesn't wait to be stirred because it is the very source of our existence and every good we have. Nothing is added to it by our pain because nothing is lacking in it.

objections.title: Analogy and mystery are obscurantism
objections.whoRaises: Skeptics; some analytic philosophers
objections.objection: When pressed, the classical theist retreats to ‘analogy’ and ‘mystery.’ That's an evasion: either your words mean what they normally mean or they are empty.
objections.reply:
1. We do comprehend God in a loose sense: we understand the arguments, we have real negative knowledge, and analogical predication is literal, not metaphorical, and is used outside theology too.
2. Analogy of attribution: God is the primary analogate of power; the sun's power to melt ice is derived. Proper proportionality: a tree, a human, an angel, and God are each to their own goodness in proportionally similar ways.
3. What we cannot do is comprehend God strictly, since strict comprehension analyzes things into parts or genus and difference, and God is simple. He is hard to understand precisely because he is simple (partless, not easy).
4. This isn't obscurantism but what we should expect. Physics, far from everyday experience, must speak of wave-particles and curved space, and no one calls that evasion. Natural theology reaches a deeper level still, and the arguments themselves predict our grasp will be feeble.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘physics has equations; you have nothing,’ answer that natural theology has deductive arguments whose conclusions include precisely the claim that God lacks composition. The limits of our concepts are a *result* of the reasoning, not a patch added when the reasoning fails.

objections.title: Existential inertia: things might just keep existing
objections.whoRaises: John Beaudoin, Mortimer Adler, Bede Rundle
objections.objection: Maybe things, once they exist, just tend to keep existing until something destroys them, the way a moving body keeps moving. Then they need no divine conserver, and the proofs fail.
objections.reply:
1. Defenders of existential inertia never explain what feature of a material or contingent thing could give it this remarkable power; they merely suggest it as if it were as plausible as conservation.
2. No contingent thing could have it. Every such thing is composite — a mixture of act and potency and of essence and existence — and anything composite in these ways needs a cause of its being here and now.
3. So proposing existential inertia doesn't answer the arguments of chapters 1, 2, 4, and 5; it ignores them.
objections.pushback: If they appeal to physical inertia, point out that Newtonian inertia concerns a thing's *state of motion*, given that it exists; it says nothing about what keeps the thing itself in being. The question is why a thing whose essence doesn't include existence has existence at this moment.

objections.title: Maybe the world itself is the necessary being
objections.whoRaises: Some atheists (addressed in a footnote)
objections.objection: Grant that there must be a necessary being. Why not the universe itself rather than God?
objections.reply:
1. Nothing that is a mixture of act and potency, or has an essence distinct from its existence, or is composite in any way can be absolutely necessary.
2. The world is all of these, so it cannot be the necessary being.
3. And as Aquinas's Third Way shows, even if something other than God had necessity of some kind, it would be a derived necessity presupposing God as its source.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘maybe the fundamental physical stuff is simple and necessary,’ ask whether it changes, has distinct parts or properties, or could be otherwise; anything that does is not the purely actual, simple being the proofs require, and anything that doesn't has the divine attributes, whatever it's called.

objections.title: Occasionalism: God is the only real cause
objections.whoRaises: Al-Ghazali, Malebranche and other occasionalists; also some who over-apply divine sovereignty
objections.objection: If God is the source of all causal power, why not say he is the *only* cause? The sun doesn't really melt the ice; God does, on the occasion of the sun's being out.
objections.reply:
1. Action follows being: whatever could truly do nothing would not truly exist. So occasionalism implies only God exists.
2. But you know at least one thing other than God exists — you. Even if you doubted tables and chairs, you would know you exist, and you are not God: you move from thought to thought (so you change), you are uncertain (so you are not omniscient), you cannot stop experiences you judge unreal (so you are not omnipotent).
3. Occasionalism is also self-undermining: we reached God as First Cause by reasoning from real things that change and are composite. Denying they really exist or act pulls away the ladder we climbed.
4. Nor can the occasionalist fall back on the Augustinian proof, since it does not begin from causality and so doesn't give him God as the source of all causal power.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘it magnifies God to give him all causation,’ answer that it actually diminishes him: a God who can only make puppets that do nothing is less than a God who can make real causes that share in his causality.

objections.title: Pantheism rescued: the world of change is an illusion
objections.whoRaises: Some pantheists (addressed in a footnote)
objections.objection: The obstacle to identifying God with the world is that the world is changing, many, and contingent. But if change and multiplicity are illusions, nothing prevents identifying reality with the one immutable, simple, necessary God.
objections.reply:
1. Someone or something would still have to *have* the illusion.
2. Having the illusion of a changing world means having one experience and then another, which is itself change; so the subject isn't immutable.
3. Having different experiences means having parts, so it isn't simple; whatever changes or has parts is contingent, so it isn't necessary.
4. Having an illusion involves error and ignorance, so it isn't omniscient. So whatever has the illusion isn't God.
objections.pushback: If they say the illusion has no subject, ask who is being deceived — an illusion without anyone deceived is not an illusion at all.

objections.title: Mere conservationism (deism-lite)
objections.whoRaises: Many modern theists and deists
objections.objection: God keeps things in existence, sure, but once they exist they use their powers on their own. The sun melts the ice by itself; God just keeps the sun around.
objections.reply:
1. Action follows being: if something could act independently of God, it could exist independently of him.
2. That yields essentially a deist God, whose creatures could carry on without him once created.
3. But nothing other than God can exist for even an instant without being conserved, since it is composite, a mix of act and potency, with essence distinct from existence.
4. And like occasionalism it is self-undermining: the proofs began precisely from the fact that things cannot exist on their own even for an instant.
objections.pushback: If they worry that concurrence makes creatures' causation redundant, use Freddoso's chalk: you are why there's a square at all, the chalk is why it's blue. The two causes are not doing the same job, so neither is redundant.

objections.title: Divine concurrence destroys human freedom
objections.whoRaises: Libertarian free-will theorists; typical skeptic
objections.objection: If God must concur with everything a creature does, including every human choice, then our choices are really his, and we are not free.
objections.reply:
1. Consider David Oderberg's example of a father guiding his young son's hand to write an A.
2. The child can resist and move his hand wrongly, or cooperate; nothing in the father's guidance as such rules out either. So the child's choice makes a real contribution.
3. Yet the A will not appear without the father's guidance.
4. God's concurrence with our free acts is analogous: it gives our acts their being and power without substituting for them. And as with the author and the hypnotist, God is not a rival cause on the same level as we are.
objections.pushback: If they say the analogy fails because God concurs even with the child's *choice* to cooperate, admit that the analogy is imperfect precisely there — every creaturely analogy puts God alongside us. The key logical point remains: a cause of the whole order is not a competing force within it, so ‘God causes it’ and ‘I freely do it’ are not in rivalry.

objections.title: Miracles are violations of natural law — and so incoherent
objections.whoRaises: David Hume and his followers
objections.objection: A miracle is a violation of a law of nature. But any evidence that a supposed law was violated is really evidence that it wasn't a law after all. So there can be no genuine miracle, and the concept is incoherent.
objections.reply:
1. On the Aristotelian view, a law of nature describes the dispositions things have by virtue of their natures (water's disposition to freeze at 32°F).
2. Dispositions can be blocked or can lack their triggers (liquid water can exist below 32°F in unusual conditions), and such failures to manifest are not violations; they are evidence neither of a miracle nor of a failed law. The Humean picture of laws is too crude.
3. Because the laws of nature are the laws of natures, they are not contingent in the Humean way: anything that reliably turned to chocolate mousse at 32°F just wouldn't be water. Given that the things exist, their laws are metaphysically necessary, and genuine violations are impossible.
4. So a miracle is not a violation at all; it is an effect that elevates nature beyond the power of any created nature (supernatural), or, in the subtractive case, a suspension of a law.
objections.pushback: If they ask how anything could count as a miracle if not by breaking a law, answer: an effect no created cause could produce — a dead man raised — given that all the natural factors present are known to be incapable of it. That's identifiable without any ‘violation.’ Whether such an event happened is a historical question beyond natural theology.

objections.title: A miracle is God tinkering with a defective machine
objections.whoRaises: Deists; skeptics; some theists who talk of ‘intervention’
objections.objection: If God performs miracles, he must be stepping in to fix or override his own creation — which implies either that it was defective or that he is an interfering outside force.
objections.reply:
1. God is not a cause alongside natural and preternatural causes; he is the precondition of there being any causal power at all. So ordinary events don't ‘happen on their own’ while God causes miracles; he causes both.
2. The world is not a plane on autopilot with a pilot occasionally grabbing the controls. The ordinary course of nature is in fact the most direct evidence of God as First Cause.
3. As McCabe argues, God cannot interfere — not from a shortage of power but, as it were, from an excess of it: to interfere you must be alongside what you interfere with, and the cause of everything is alongside nothing.
4. A miracle is like a jazz improvisation, a director's cut, or a second edition: it adds to something already complete and good, raising it higher, rather than correcting a defect.
objections.pushback: If they ask why God doesn't do it all the time, note that the value of a miracle as a sign depends on its standing out against the regular order — and that the regular order is itself God's continuous, constant work.

objections.title: The fiery furnace would be a violation
objections.whoRaises: Careful critics of Feser's own view
objections.objection: Feser says laws are metaphysically necessary and can't be violated. But in the story of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego the fire fails to burn them. Isn't that exactly a violation of the law that fire burns?
objections.reply:
1. Not every miracle adds to nature; some subtract. What matters in the furnace story is what does *not* happen.
2. Following Oderberg, a miracle is a suspension of a law, not a breach — like a government temporarily revoking a law, rather than leaving it on the books and not enforcing it.
3. Since a thing can act at any moment only as God conserves it and concurs with it, God can simply refrain from conserving or concurring with some or all of the relevant factors (the fire, its preconditions such as oxygen).
4. Then the normal effect doesn't follow. God isn't making fire act against its nature (which would be a violation); he is not bringing certain things about in the first place.
objections.pushback: If they ask whether this is a trick of wording, point to the analogy: a musician who omits notes from the score is not ‘violating’ the notes he plays; he is just not playing some. The difference between forcing something to act against its nature and not giving it the act at all is real.

objections.title: Faith is belief without evidence
objections.whoRaises: Richard Dawkins, popular New Atheism; also some fideists
objections.objection: Religious faith just means believing without evidence, or against it. So even if natural theology works, revealed religion is irrational.
objections.reply:
1. As understood by Aquinas and the tradition, faith is believing something *because God has revealed it*.
2. That God has in fact revealed it is something for which evidence must be given.
3. Only a miracle in the strict sense could supply that evidence, since only God can work one; it functions as a divine ‘seal of approval’ on a prophet's message.
4. So miracles are the bridge between natural and revealed theology, and faith is grounded in reason, not opposed to it.
objections.pushback: If they ask for proof that any miracle happened, grant that this is a historical question beyond natural theology — but note that natural theology already shows miracles possible and rules out many religions (those making God many, material, finite, impersonal, or identical with the world) and any religion claiming revelation without miraculous credentials.

objections.title: Calling God ‘he’ is sexist
objections.whoRaises: Some contemporary theologians and writers
objections.objection: God has no sex, so masculine language for God is arbitrary and sexist. We should say ‘he/she/it’ or use feminine language equally.
objections.reply:
1. Agreed: God is immaterial, not an animal, so not literally male or female; he is sexless.
2. But he has intellect and will, which define personhood, so the impersonal ‘it’ is wrong.
3. And his relation to the world is more like a father's role in procreation than a mother's: the father is active, unchanged by conception, not physically dependent on mate or child, and not physically continuous with the child; the mother is changed and continuous with the child.
4. God likewise is active in creating, unchanging, independent of the world, and utterly distinct from it. Maternal imagery would suggest a God changed by or continuous with the world — panentheism or pantheism.
objections.pushback: If they say this relies on a dated view of parenthood, clarify that the point is not about social roles or worth but about a biological asymmetry of dependence and continuity used analogically; and ask which pronoun would better convey a personal being who is utterly independent of and distinct from what he makes.

objections.title: The Euthyphro dilemma (course addition)
objections.whoRaises: Plato's Euthyphro, pressed by modern skeptics
objections.objection: Is something good because God wills it, or does God will it because it is good? If the first, goodness is arbitrary; if the second, goodness is a standard above God.
objections.reply:
1. The chapter's account of goodness escapes both horns. Goodness is actuality in line with a thing's nature, not an arbitrary decree.
2. Nor is it a standard external to God: God is pure actuality, so he is goodness itself, the limit case of goodness, and the natures of creatures are ways of participating in his actuality, known in his intellect.
3. So God wills the good because he is the good, and what is good for creatures follows from their natures, which reflect the divine intellect. Neither arbitrariness nor an external standard results.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘then God couldn't have made torture good,’ agree: given what human beings are, their good cannot be otherwise, and God's will is not a force that can override his own intellect and nature. That is not a limitation any more than being unable to make round squares.

objections.title: Science has shown nature is causally closed (course addition)
objections.whoRaises: Scientific naturalists
objections.objection: Physics shows that every physical event has a sufficient physical cause. There's no room for God to act, whether in ordinary events or miracles.
objections.reply:
1. The objection pictures God as one more cause competing for room in the causal chain — exactly the picture this chapter rejects.
2. On concurrentism, physical causes are real causes, and God is the source of their existence and power at every moment, not a rival force. Science describes the secondary causes; it doesn't and can't show they would exist or act on their own.
3. Laws describe the dispositions of natures; they say what things do when left to their natures, not that nothing beyond natures exists. A miracle is not a physical cause displacing another but the source of all natures elevating or suspending one.
4. ‘Every physical event has a sufficient physical cause’ is not a finding of any experiment but a philosophical thesis — and the proofs give reason to deny that physical things are sufficient for their own existence.
objections.pushback: If they cite conservation of energy, note that conservation laws describe closed systems; whether the universe as a whole depends on something beyond it is exactly what's in question, and a law describing how natures behave can't answer it.

misconceptions.myth: Omnipotence means God can do literally anything you can put into words, including contradictions.
misconceptions.correction: Omnipotence is the power to actualize any potential that can be actualized. ‘Round square’ or ‘stone too heavy for God to lift’ names no possible thing, so there is no power there to lack. God's not doing the contradictory is not a limit on his power.

misconceptions.myth: God knows the future by looking ahead and seeing it, like a very good forecaster or a spectator with a telescope.
misconceptions.correction: God is not in time and does not observe or learn. He knows everything by knowing himself as its timeless cause, as an author knows his story by knowing his own creative act. Strictly, he has no ‘fore’-knowledge at all.

misconceptions.myth: If God causes and knows everything, human freedom must be an illusion.
misconceptions.correction: God is related to us as an author to characters, not as a hypnotist to a victim. A cause of the whole order does not compete with causes inside it; by concurrence God gives our choices their reality and power instead of replacing them.

misconceptions.myth: The privation theory says evil isn't real.
misconceptions.correction: It says evil is a real lack of what ought to be there, as blindness is a real lack of sight. It explains what evil's reality consists in; it does not deny it. Absences can be catastrophic.

misconceptions.myth: Since God is the cause of everything and effects resemble causes, God must contain evil too.
misconceptions.correction: Proportionate causality concerns positive features. Evil is a privation, not a positive feature, so it need not be in God. Making a world with evil is making goods while not making certain other goods.

misconceptions.myth: An unchanging God must be cold and loveless.
misconceptions.correction: What is essential to love is willing the good of the beloved, not undergoing emotional change (which is what usually accompanies love in bodily creatures). God wills the existence and good of every creature; his love is not less than ours but its source.

misconceptions.myth: Classical theism claims to have God completely figured out — or, when cornered, just says ‘it's a mystery.’
misconceptions.correction: Both halves are wrong. We have real negative knowledge and literal analogical knowledge of God, so we comprehend him loosely. But simplicity guarantees we cannot comprehend him strictly — a conclusion the arguments themselves deliver, not an escape hatch.

misconceptions.myth: God created the world long ago and now keeps it going the way an owner maintains a machine; ordinary events happen by themselves.
misconceptions.correction: Creation is not a past event but a present, continuous causing of existence (conservation), and creatures act only with God's concurrence. Nothing ‘happens by itself’; there is no existential inertia.

misconceptions.myth: A miracle is God breaking the laws of nature, or intervening in a world that otherwise runs without him.
misconceptions.correction: Laws express natures and cannot be violated. A miracle elevates nature beyond any created power, or suspends an effect by God withholding his concurrence. And God doesn't ‘intervene,’ since he is already causing everything and is not a cause alongside others.

misconceptions.myth: Calling God ‘he’ means classical theists think God is male.
misconceptions.correction: Feser explicitly says God is sexless. ‘He’ marks that God is personal (not ‘it’) and that his relation to the world — active, unchanged, independent, distinct — resembles fatherhood more than motherhood.

explain.tweet: Once you know God is pure act, the rest follows: he's all-powerful (every power comes from him), all-knowing (he knows by causing), all-good (evil is a lack), free & loving. And he never ‘intervenes’ in nature — he's the author, not a character.
explain.elevator: The proofs got us to something that is pure actuality and the source of everything's existence. From that you can work out more. Whatever creatures have, God must have in a higher way, so he has intellect and knows everything — not by watching, but the way an author knows his story. Goodness is being fully actual, so pure actuality is perfect goodness. And because God is the author rather than a character, he doesn't compete with our freedom or with natural causes, and miracles aren't violations.
explain.twoMinute:
Here's the setup. The five proofs each ended at the same place: something purely actual, with no unrealized potential, that is existence itself and keeps everything else in being right now. The second half of Feser's chapter 6 asks what follows about that being.

First, **power**. If nothing can exist for an instant without God, nothing can *act* without him either, because acting presupposes existing. So every power anywhere is borrowed from him: that's omnipotence. It doesn't mean he can make round squares — those aren't things, so there's no power missing.

Second, **knowledge**. An effect can't contain what its cause lacks. Everything about every possible creature must be in God somehow — and since it isn't there as physical stuff, and there's no Platonic heaven of forms, it has to be there as ideas in a mind. And how does he know? Like an author who conceives a whole novel in one flash: he doesn't watch his characters, he knows them because he's making them. That's why his knowledge doesn't turn us into puppets. An author writing a free character is different from a character who hypnotizes another.

Third, **goodness**. A good triangle, a good tree, a good person: each is good to the extent it actually realizes what its nature calls for. Badness is a lack. So something that is pure actuality, lacking nothing, is perfectly good — and evil isn't something God puts in the world; it's a gap where a good is missing.

Fourth, **will and love**. God doesn't have to create; nothing inside or outside him forces it, and there isn't even a ‘best possible world’ to be forced toward. And love, at its core, isn't a feeling but willing someone's good. Creating things just is willing that they exist and flourish.

Finally, **God and the world**. God isn't one cause among others. The sun really melts the ice, but only because God is giving it existence and power at every instant — like your hand and the chalk both causing a blue square. That's why miracles aren't ‘interventions’: you can't intervene in what you're already doing. A miracle is more like a jazz musician improvising on his own tune.
explain.eli12:
Imagine someone who isn't just really strong or really smart, but is the reason anything exists at all — like the singer of a song that only exists while it's being sung.

If everything gets its existence from that singer, it gets all its abilities from him too. So he has all power. That doesn't mean he can draw a square circle — that's not a real thing, just words stuck together.

He also knows everything, but not by spying on us. Think of an author writing a story: she knows everything in it because she's the one making it up. And a character in her story can still choose freely — that's different from one character hypnotizing another.

He's completely good, because being good means being everything you're supposed to be, and he isn't missing anything. Bad things are like holes — something good that's missing, like a triangle with a gap in its side.

He loves us, because loving someone means wanting what's good for them, and giving us our existence is the biggest ‘wanting good for you’ there is.

And he doesn't have to ‘break into’ the world to do a miracle — he's already doing all of it, like a musician who can play an extra solo in his own song.
whiteboard: Write at the top: GOD = PURE ACT, SIMPLE, EXISTENCE ITSELF, SUSTAINS ALL NOW. Say: this is where the five proofs left us; today we ask what follows.
Draw three tools in a toolbox: PPC (effect is in cause), ACTION FOLLOWS BEING, ANALOGY. Say every derivation today uses one or more of these.
Draw two arrows meeting at God: one from ‘the world’ (backward route) and one from ‘pure act’ (forward route). Label them POWER, KNOWLEDGE, GOODNESS. Say: two independent roads, same result.
Draw a book with an author above it and a small figure with a hypnotist's spiral inside it. Say: God is the author, not a character — this defeats the free-will objections.
Draw a triangle with a gap in one side. Write GOOD = ACTUALITY, BAD = PRIVATION. Say: evil is what's missing, so it needn't be in God.
Write LOVE = WILLING THE GOOD (not feeling). Cross out ‘love requires change’ and label it ‘fallacy of accident.’
Draw three columns: OCCASIONALISM (only God acts) | CONCURRENCE | MERE CONSERVATIONISM (creatures act alone). Circle the middle, and sketch a hand holding blue chalk.
Draw a musical staff with a few notes and an improvised flourish. Write MIRACLE ≠ VIOLATION. Say: laws are the laws of natures; God elevates or suspends, never forces.
Finish with a thin cloud over God labeled ‘known truly, never fully.’ Say: simplicity makes God knowable by argument but not comprehensible by analysis.
explain.keyAnalogy: **God as the author of a story, not a character in it.** Feser returns to this image again and again, and it unlocks nearly the whole module. An author knows every detail of the story without observing it, because he is making it (omniscience as knowledge-by-causing). His writing a murderer who acts freely does not make the character unfree, whereas a hypnotist character would (freedom). Every event in the story, ordinary or extraordinary, is his work, so he never ‘intervenes’ — a new chapter in a second edition is not an interference but an addition (miracles). And characters really do things within the story, though only because the author is writing them (concurrence). Use it by first asking the listener to agree about the novel, then transferring each point. Flag the limits: characters are fictional while we are real, and God is not in time as an author is.

persuade.coreInsight:
The idea that makes this module click is that **God is not a being among beings or a cause among causes, but the source of being and causality as such**. Once you see that, the attributes stop looking like inflated human traits (a super-strong, super-smart, super-nice person) and the objections stop looking devastating: a cause of the whole order does not compete with freedom, does not have to watch the future, does not need to intervene, and does not need feelings to love.

The usual reason it fails to click is that people unconsciously picture God as the biggest item in the universe — a very powerful agent standing next to us. On that picture, every objection in this chapter is strong: his power crowds out ours, his foreknowledge fixes our choices, his love must be emotional, his miracles must be break-ins. The persuader's job is therefore mostly *negative*: to dislodge the ‘big guy upstairs’ picture by getting the listener to see what the proofs actually concluded to — pure act, subsistent existence — and then to show, one objection at a time, that each objection is aimed at a God classical theism never believed in.

audiences.startingPoint: Assumes God would be a hypothesis competing with physical explanations; sees miracles as violations of physics and ‘mystery’ as a cop-out.
audiences.approach: Lead with the chapter's account of **laws as the dispositions of natures** — something many philosophers of science now take seriously — and show that on this view nothing in physics is threatened: secondary causes are real and science studies them. Then introduce concurrence as the claim that physical causes don't explain their own existence or causal power at each moment. Use the physics parallel for incomprehensibility: wave-particle duality and curved spacetime are strange because they're far from ordinary experience, and so is the ground of being.
audiences.openingQuestion: When we say water freezes at 32°F, are we describing a rule imposed on water from outside, or what water is like?
audiences.avoid: Don't present God as the explanation of specific puzzling phenomena (gaps). Don't say miracles ‘break’ laws — that concedes the Humean framing Feser rejects.

audiences.who: Believer troubled by free will and predestination
audiences.startingPoint: Believes God is sovereign and all-knowing, and worries that this makes their own choices unreal or makes God responsible for their sins.
audiences.approach: Use the **author vs. hypnotist** contrast and the **father guiding the hand**. Show that the trouble comes from picturing God as one force pushing against another. Explain that God's knowledge is not foreknowledge but timeless knowledge-by-causing, and that concurrence means he gives your choice its very being rather than replacing it. On sin, bring in the privation account: the defect in a bad act is a lack, which is traceable to the creature, not a positive thing God inserts.
audiences.openingQuestion: When you read a novel, does it ever occur to you that the villain isn't responsible because the author wrote him?
audiences.avoid: Don't claim the analogies fully explain how divine causality and freedom fit; Feser himself stresses the limits of our comprehension. Don't dismiss their worry as silly — it is one of the hardest questions in the chapter.

audiences.startingPoint: Finds the classical, immutable God distant and unbiblical; believes love requires vulnerability and responsiveness.
audiences.approach: Take the concern about love seriously, then work through the **fallacy of accident**: ask what makes love real — feelings that come and go, or the steady will for the other's good? Point to tough love and love of enemies. Show that God's creating *is* his willing your existence and good, from moment to moment. Suggest that a God changed by the world would be one more being in the world, with needs, rather than the source of all good.
audiences.openingQuestion: Which kind of love do you trust more: love that depends on how the other person makes you feel, or love that wills your good no matter what?
audiences.avoid: Don't make immutability sound like indifference or inertia; stress that it is fullness of act, not the stillness of a statue.

audiences.who: Agnostic who thinks theology is all hand-waving
audiences.startingPoint: Suspects that ‘analogy’ and ‘mystery’ are ways of making claims unfalsifiable; wants clear arguments.
audiences.approach: Show the **structure**: each attribute is derived by explicit steps from prior results and stated principles, often by two independent routes. Walk through omniscience as an elimination argument (in God somehow; not as instances; no Platonic realm; therefore as ideas). Then show how incomprehensibility is itself a *derived* conclusion from simplicity, not a patch. Distinguish analogy (literal, proportional) from metaphor.
audiences.openingQuestion: If an argument proved that something has no parts at all, would you expect to be able to understand it by taking it apart?
audiences.avoid: Don't overclaim. Be candid that premises from earlier chapters (e.g., realism about universals, the case against Platonism) are doing work and can be examined.

audiences.who: Religious pluralist or ‘spiritual but not religious’
audiences.startingPoint: Thinks the divine is probably an impersonal force or the universe itself, and that all religions are equally valid paths.
audiences.approach: Use the chapter's case that God has **intellect and will** (so is personal) and is **distinct from the world** (against pantheism and panentheism, including the ‘it's all illusion’ version). Then explain how natural theology works as a filter on religious claims and how miracles would be the only credible sign of revelation.
audiences.openingQuestion: If the source of everything contains, in some way, everything in its effects, could it contain minds and knowledge while itself being mindless?
audiences.avoid: Don't slide from ‘natural theology rules out some views’ to ‘natural theology proves my religion.’ Feser explicitly says it establishes no particular revealed religion.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Suppose I grant your First Cause. That's a long way from an all-powerful, all-knowing, loving God. Where do you get all that?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: From what the First Cause is. The arguments ended at something that is pure actuality and keeps everything in existence at every moment. If nothing can exist without it for an instant, nothing can act without it either — acting presupposes existing. So every power in the universe is borrowed from it. That's what omnipotence means.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then can it make a stone it can't lift?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: A stone rising is always something that can happen, so God can always cause it. ‘A stone too heavy for God’ is like ‘a round square’ — the words don't describe any possible thing. There's no power there to be missing.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine. But a mind? Why not an impersonal power source?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because a cause can't give what it doesn't have in some way. Every feature of every possible thing has to be in God somehow. Not as physical features — he's immaterial — and not as a Platonic realm of forms, which doesn't hold up. The only other way patterns like ‘catness’ can exist is as ideas in an intellect.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Even if he has ideas, knowing everything about the future wrecks free will. If God knows I'll lie tomorrow, I can't not lie.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Knowing doesn't force. If I know you're sitting in the next room, that doesn't make you sit there. Why would knowing about tomorrow be different?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Because God doesn't just know it. He causes it. That's your own view.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Right, so take a crime novel. A character plots a murder for money and does it. Nobody says he's innocent because the author wrote the book. But if we learn another character hypnotized him, we'd say he wasn't free. The hypnotist is inside the story, interfering. The author isn't a character at all. God is the author, not the hypnotist.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Characters in novels aren't real, though.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Agreed, the analogy is imperfect. The logical point is that a cause of the whole order doesn't compete with causes inside it. God gives my choice its existence and power; he doesn't substitute his push for mine. Feser's other picture is a father guiding a child's hand to write a letter: the child's cooperation is real, but no letter without the father.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: And ‘all-good’? Look at the world. If causes contain their effects, God contains the evil too.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Only if evil were a positive thing. But badness is always a lack: a triangle with a wavy side, a tree with rotten roots, a will missing respect for others. God is the source of what's there, not of what's missing.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: He could have filled in what's missing.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Some goods are impossible without some badness. There's no courage without real danger. Even God can't make courage without danger any more than he can make a round square. The full problem of evil is a bigger conversation — Feser takes it up in the next chapter — but it doesn't show God contains evil.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Your God doesn't change. Something that can't be affected by me can't love me.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: What makes love real — the feelings, which come and go, or steadily willing someone's good? We call love that's only feelings shallow. Tough love and loving an enemy are real love because of the will. God wills your existence and every good you have, at every instant. That's love without needing to be stirred.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then does he ever do anything? Miracles? That would mean breaking his own laws.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Laws of nature describe what things do because of what they are. They can't be broken, only blocked or suspended. A miracle is God raising something beyond what any created nature can do, or withholding his concurrence so some effect doesn't happen, like the fire that didn't burn in the furnace story.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Still sounds like God reaching in and meddling.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: You can only meddle in something you're alongside. God is already causing everything, ordinary and extraordinary. It's like a jazz musician improvising on his own tune: every note was always his. Whether any particular miracle happened is a separate, historical question.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Convenient that whenever it gets hard, it's ‘analogy’ and ‘mystery.’

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: The mystery is a conclusion, not a patch. We understand things by breaking them into parts. The arguments show God has no parts. So they predict he'll be knowable truly but not exhaustively — the same way physics predicts that reality at its deepest levels will be strange. I'd be more suspicious if it all came out easy.

socratic: If a thing can't exist for even a moment on its own, could it have the ability to act on its own? Where would that ability come from?
Is there any task that the phrase ‘make a square circle’ actually describes? What would count as succeeding at it?
When an author writes a character who freely chooses evil, whose choice is it within the story — the author's or the character's?
Does knowing that someone is doing something ever make them do it? Does it matter whether the knowledge is of the present or the future?
What makes a triangle drawn with a ruler ‘better’ than one scrawled on a moving bus — your taste, or what a triangle is?
Is blindness something a blind eye has, or something it lacks? Does that make blindness any less real?
Would you rather be loved by someone whose feelings for you fluctuate, or by someone who always wills your good? Which is closer to the heart of love?
If for any world with x forests there could be one with x + 1, is there such a thing as the best possible world?
Can you interfere in something you are doing entirely yourself? Could a novelist ‘interfere’ in his own novel?
If something had no parts at all, what method would you use to understand it fully?
If creatures did nothing whatsoever, would we have any reason to think they exist — or any starting point for arguing to God?
If water reliably turned into chocolate mousse at 32°F, would it still be water?

traps.trap: Presenting God as a super-person — the greatest item in the universe with maximal power, knowledge, and niceness.
traps.fix: Keep anchoring every attribute in pure actuality and subsistent existence. Say explicitly that God is not a being alongside others but the source of being; the attributes are analogical, not scaled-up human traits.

traps.trap: Saying God ‘foresees’ or ‘sees ahead’ what we will do.
traps.fix: Use the author model: God knows by causing, from outside time, not by observing. Avoid temporal vocabulary for God's knowledge, or flag it as loose talk.

traps.trap: Answering the problem of evil fully when the chapter only establishes that evil is not in God.
traps.fix: Keep the claims distinct: here, privation and ‘evil is not a positive thing God makes’; the courage example shows compatibility; the full problem of evil belongs to chapter 7.

traps.trap: Describing miracles as God breaking or overriding natural laws, or ‘intervening.’
traps.fix: Use Feser's vocabulary: laws are the laws of natures; miracles elevate (supernatural) or suspend; God can't intervene in what he is already doing.

traps.trap: Using ‘mystery’ to end a conversation whenever an objection gets hard.
traps.fix: Show that incomprehensibility is derived from simplicity and is compatible with real, literal (analogical) knowledge. Answer the objection first; invoke the limits of comprehension only to explain why a residual strangeness is expected.

traps.trap: Overselling the analogies (author, father's hand, prism) as if they were explanations of the mechanism.
traps.fix: Feser repeatedly flags them as imperfect and suggestive. Present each as showing a logical possibility — that two claims don't conflict — and name where the analogy breaks.

traps.trap: Collapsing concurrentism into occasionalism (‘God does everything’) or into mere conservationism (‘God just keeps things around’).
traps.fix: State both halves every time: secondary causes are real (they contribute to the effect) and secondary (they act only with God's concurrence). Use the blue chalk.

traps.trap: Defending masculine language by implying God is male or that men are superior.
traps.fix: Begin with Feser's clear statement that God is sexless, then give the two reasons: personhood rules out ‘it’; the analogy of active, independent, distinct paternity fits God's relation to the world better than maternal continuity.

connections.note: The introduction promised that the proofs reach not a vague ‘first cause’ but the God of classical theism. This module cashes that promise for the personal attributes (power, knowledge, goodness, will, love) and for God's ongoing relation to the world.

The Aristotelian proof's purely actual actualizer, sustaining a hierarchical (per se) series here and now, is the basis for omnipotence (all actualizing power), for perfect goodness (goodness as actuality), and for conservation and concurrence. The ladder image recalls that the proofs began from real change.

The Neo-Platonic proof's absolutely simple One grounds incomprehensibility (nothing to analyze into parts), the account of God's knowledge as undivided (prism and dough), and the argument against the existential-inertia thesis (composites need a cause of their unity and being).

The Augustinian proof supplies the realism about universals and the rejection of Platonism that drive the elimination argument for a divine intellect; Feser also points back to chapter 3's forward-route argument for omniscience and its reply to Patrick Grim.

The Thomistic proof's subsistent existence itself grounds the forward route to omnipotence (what exists in the fullest way acts in the fullest way) and the real distinction of creatures from God that rules out pantheism.

The rationalist proof's necessary being and the principle of sufficient reason stand behind proportionate causality and agere sequitur esse; the footnote rejecting the world as the necessary being echoes that chapter.

Part A set out the three tools used throughout this module — proportionate causality, agere sequitur esse, the analogy of being — and derived unity, simplicity, immutability, immateriality, and eternity, plus the fallacy-of-accident reply that is reused here for freedom and love.

Chapter 7 answers general objections to the proofs; this module's picture of God as not ‘a cause among causes’ is key to answering ‘what caused God?’ and the charge that classical theism is a god-of-the-gaps.

The privation account of evil and the courage example here are the foundation for Feser's treatment of the problem of evil in chapter 7; the concurrence account also bears on objections about free will and divine action.

In the capstone, this module supplies the ‘so what’: how the conclusions of five different proofs converge on one personal, omnipotent, omniscient, good God who conserves the world, and how to present that convergence persuasively.

quiz.q: According to Feser, why can't God make a round square?
options: Because his power, though enormous, is finite
Because doing so would conflict with his perfect goodness
Because there is no such thing as a capacity to make a round square; the idea is self-contradictory
Because God freely chose to bind himself to the laws of logic
quiz.explanation: Omnipotence is the power to actualize whatever can be actualized. A round square is not a possible thing, so there is no power there to lack. The last option makes logic a self-imposed rule, which Feser does not claim.

quiz.q: In the ‘backward’ route to omnipotence, Feser combines the dependence of everything on God for existence with which principle?
options: Agere sequitur esse: since acting presupposes existing, what cannot exist on its own cannot act on its own
Proportionate causality: whatever is in the effect is in its cause
The principle that there is no best possible world
The analogy of proper proportionality
quiz.explanation: The key move is that existence is prior to action, so dependence for existence entails dependence for all power. Proportionate causality is the key principle for omniscience and goodness, not this step.

quiz.q: Besides God's immateriality, what further reason does Feser give for denying that creaturely features exist in God as instances?
options: God would then be composed of form and matter
Universals do not really exist
Instances are always imperfect copies
His own instances would need explaining like any others, so he would not be the ultimate cause of things having those features
quiz.explanation: If God merely instantiated redness, his redness would be one more instance needing explanation. The second option contradicts chapter 3's realism about universals, which the argument relies on.

quiz.q: Why does Feser conclude that the forms of all possible things exist in God as concepts in an intellect?
options: Because universals exist only in concrete things, and God is a concrete thing
Because they must be in God somehow (proportionate causality), cannot be there as instances, and there is no Platonic ‘third realm’
Because nominalism shows that universals are just words, and words require a mind
Because God perceives everything and perceptions are mental
quiz.explanation: It is an argument by elimination: instances, intellect, or third realm; not instances, no third realm, so intellect. Nominalism is rejected, not assumed, and God does not perceive.

quiz.q: How does God satisfy the ‘reliable process’ condition of the standard account of knowledge?
options: He observes all events with infallible perception
There is no more reliable way of determining that p is true than being the one who makes p true
He reasons flawlessly from axioms to conclusions
His beliefs are confirmed by the testimony of angels
quiz.explanation: Like an author who knows a character is in the story because he put her there, God knows because he causes. He has no perceptual organs and does not reason step by step.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, doesn't God's knowing all times in a single timeless act imply four-dimensionalism?
options: Because God knows only the present moment
Because four-dimensionalism has been refuted by physics
Because God's knowledge is observational, and observation takes time
Because he knows by being the cause, and knowing timelessly that he causes a temporal world doesn't make that world timeless
quiz.explanation: The inference would work only if God's knowledge were observational. The hunter who knows in an instant that he fired a bullet doesn't make the bullet motionless. Option C gets God's mode of knowing exactly backward.

quiz.q: What is the point of contrasting the crime novel's author with a hypnotist character?
options: Freedom is threatened by a cause acting alongside the agent within the same order, not by the cause of the whole order
Fictional characters lack free will, and so, perhaps, do we
God is more like the hypnotist, but a benevolent one
The author is really just one more character in the story
quiz.explanation: The hypnotist interferes as one character with another; the author interferes with no one because he is not in the story. God's causality is of the author's kind. Option B misreads an illustration of logical compatibility as a claim about fiction.

quiz.q: What are the prism and the lump of dough meant to illustrate?
options: How evil is a privation of good
How God conserves the world in being
How a simple God knows every finite kind by knowing himself as unlimited actuality
How miracles add something new to nature
quiz.explanation: White light contains all colors in a unified way; knowing it perfectly would include knowing every derivable color. So God, knowing himself as pure act, knows every limited way of being actual.

quiz.q: Which of these is a privation, in Feser's sense?
options: A triangle's lacking a fourth side
A tree's lacking wings
A stone's lacking sight
A tree's lacking strong roots
quiz.explanation: A privation is the absence of something a thing's nature calls for. Trees should have strong roots; triangles should not have four sides, trees need no wings, and stones need no sight.

quiz.q: How does Feser answer the objection that pain is a positive bad rather than a privation?
options: Pain is an illusion produced by the brain
Pain is always good, since it warns of danger
What is bad is not pain as such but what it signals or causes — as its warning function, satisfying post-workout aches, and pain asymbolia suggest
Pain is merely the privation of pleasure
quiz.explanation: Feser does not say pain is always good (B), only that it isn't bad without qualification. Its badness lies in the damage it indicates or the lost tranquility it produces.

quiz.q: Why does the objection from a murderer's positive intentions (Calder) fail, according to Feser following Alexander?
options: Because murder is not really bad
Because the privation theory claims only that the badness of an act consists in privation, not that the act has no positive features
Because murderers have no real beliefs or desires
Because intentions are not real mental states
quiz.explanation: The murderer's desire for money may even be good in itself; what is bad is the missing intention to seek money only in ways that respect the innocent. The theory never denied that bad acts contain positive elements.

quiz.q: Why doesn't the principle of proportionate causality imply that evil is in God?
options: Because evil is an absence, not a positive feature, and the principle concerns the positive features of effects
Because the principle applies only to material causes
Because God's causality is equivocal rather than analogical
Because evil has another ultimate cause besides God
quiz.explanation: Making a world with evil means making goods while refraining from making certain other goods, like leaving a triangle unfinished. Feser explicitly rejects restricting the principle to material factors.

quiz.q: What does Feser's courage example show?
options: Some goods cannot exist unless some badness is permitted, so permitting badness is compatible with perfect goodness
God himself lacks the virtue of courage
Courage exists only in heaven
Evil is a positive reality after all
quiz.explanation: Courage requires facing real danger of harm; a world with courage but no danger is as impossible as a round square. The footnote adds that the blessed keep the courage they acquired on earth.

quiz.q: Which example illustrates Barry Miller's notion of a ‘limit case’ (as opposed to a mere limit)?
options: The speed of light, the highest possible speed
A speed of zero, which is not a speed at all, yet is what the ordering of speeds points toward
The largest prime number
The average speed of all moving objects
quiz.explanation: A mere limit (the speed of light) differs from lower speeds only in degree. A limit case differs absolutely, as zero speed is no speed, yet the series points to it. God's will and goodness are limit cases in this sense.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, is there nothing internal to God compelling him to create lions rather than unicorns?
options: Because lions are better than unicorns
Because unicorns are impossible
Because nothing in any concept in the divine intellect necessitates that its instances exist or not
Because God lacks the concept of a unicorn
quiz.explanation: Both concepts exist in the divine intellect, and neither contains any necessity of existing or not existing, so before creation either world was equally possible.

quiz.q: What mistake does Feser find in the objection that a simple, purely actual God cannot be free?
options: It wrongly denies divine simplicity
It confuses omnipotence with omniscience
It assumes that God's will is compelled from outside
It commits a fallacy of accident, inferring from the fact that our free choices involve actualizing potentials that free choice as such must
quiz.explanation: The objection assumes simplicity; its error is treating an accompaniment of creaturely freedom as essential to freedom, just as it is an error to think all acting involves changing.

quiz.q: Which two assumptions of the Leibniz/Rowe argument does Feser reject?
options: That God is omnipotent and that he is omniscient
That God exists and that he is good
That one is always obliged to bring about the best one can, and that there is a best possible world
That creatures can be harmed and that God can be harmed
quiz.explanation: No one is wronged if God does not create (not God, not nonexistent trees), and there is no best world since there could always be x + 1 forests.

quiz.q: The perfect diamond that is perfect whether or not it cuts any glass is used to answer which objection?
options: That God cannot suffer with his creatures
That God's knowledge is observational
That miracles violate the laws of nature
Rowe's claim that if there is no best world, there can be no most perfect being
quiz.explanation: God's perfection follows from what he is (pure actuality), not from what he makes, as a diamond's perfection doesn't depend on which glass it cuts.

quiz.q: On Feser's account, what is essential to love?
options: Willing the good of the beloved
Being emotionally affected by the beloved
Needing the beloved
Desiring to possess the beloved
quiz.explanation: Emotions usually accompany our love, but treating them as essential is a fallacy of accident. Tough love and love of enemies show that the will is what makes love real.

quiz.q: Why can't we comprehend God in the strict sense?
options: Because we don't yet have enough empirical data about him
Because strict comprehension works by analyzing things into parts or into genus and specific difference, and God is absolutely simple
Because God deliberately conceals his nature
Because all language about God is metaphorical
quiz.explanation: God is hard to understand precisely because he is simple (partless). Feser insists analogical language is literal, not metaphorical, so option D is a misreading.

quiz.q: What is Feser's response to the thesis of ‘existential inertia’?
options: It contradicts Newtonian physics
It is true of material things but not of immaterial ones
It applies to God rather than to creatures
Its defenders never explain it, and nothing composite of act and potency or of essence and existence could have it
quiz.explanation: Composite, contingent things need a sustaining cause at every moment; merely suggesting existential inertia ignores rather than answers the arguments of earlier chapters.

quiz.q: Someone says: ‘The sun doesn't really melt the ice; God melts it whenever the sun is out.’ Which view is this?
options: Occasionalism
Mere conservationism
Concurrentism
Deism
quiz.explanation: Occasionalism denies creatures any causal efficacy; mere conservationism (and deism) makes creatures act independently of God; concurrentism affirms real secondary causes acting with God's concurrence.

quiz.q: In Freddoso's blue chalk example, what shows that the chalk is a genuine (though secondary) cause?
options: It moves by itself across the board
The effect would be different if red chalk or a pencil were used
It could exist without anyone holding it
It produces the square without the hand
quiz.explanation: A secondary cause is a true cause because it makes a real contribution to the character of the effect, and secondary because nothing happens without the primary cause (your hand).

quiz.q: How do Feser and Oderberg interpret a miracle like the fire's failing to burn Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego?
options: As a breach of the law that fire burns
As evidence that fire's nature was changed permanently
As a suspension: God refrains from conserving or concurring with some of the factors, so the normal effect does not arise
As a preternatural effect produced by angels
quiz.explanation: A breach (fire acting against its nature while all conditions are sustained) is impossible. God simply does not bring about certain things, like a musician omitting notes or a government temporarily revoking a law.

quiz.q: Why does Feser hold that laws of nature are metaphysically necessary (given that the relevant things exist)?
options: Because God decreed them and cannot change his mind
Because they are statistical regularities that have never failed
Because they express the natures of things, so a thing obeying different laws would have a different nature and be a different thing
Because physics has discovered they are mathematically unavoidable
quiz.explanation: Laws are laws of the natures of things: whatever reliably turned into chocolate mousse at 32°F wouldn't be water. The Humean regularity view (B) is exactly what Feser rejects.

quiz.q: In the module's reconstruction, which step secures that God's knowledge does not depend on observing the world?
options: Step 11, the principle of proportionate causality
Step 14, the rejection of a Platonic third realm
Step 17, the standard account of knowledge
Step 20, that God knows the world by knowing himself as its cause, since he is eternal, incorporeal, and immutable
quiz.explanation: Steps 11 and 14 establish that God has an intellect, and step 17 supplies the definition of knowledge, but only step 20 settles the *mode* of God's knowing: by causing, not by observing. That is what blocks the four-dimensionalism inference.

quiz.q: A friend says: “If God already knows what I'll order for lunch tomorrow, I'm not really choosing.” What would Feser reply first?
options: Knowing that someone does something doesn't make them do it — knowing you're sitting in the next room doesn't make you sit there, and knowing it ahead of time wouldn't either
God doesn't know particular facts like lunch orders, only general truths
Free will is an illusion anyway, so nothing is lost
God deliberately avoids knowing our future choices
quiz.explanation: Feser's first reply is that knowledge doesn't compel. He then adds that God's knowledge isn't really ‘fore’-knowledge, and that his causing our acts is like an author's, not a hypnotist's. Options B and D contradict omniscience.

quiz.q: The objection “an immutable God cannot love, since love means being affected” overlooks which distinction?
options: Privation vs. mere absence
Supernatural vs. preternatural
What usually accompanies an activity in us vs. what is essential to it
Breach vs. suspension of a law
quiz.explanation: Our love usually comes with emotional change, but its essence is willing the good of the beloved. Treating the accompaniment as the essence is the fallacy of accident.

quiz.q: The objection “if God causes all our acts, we aren't free” overlooks which distinction?
options: Formal vs. eminent containment
A cause within the order (a hypnotist) vs. the cause of the whole order (an author)
Natural vs. moral goodness
Loose vs. strict comprehension
quiz.explanation: Only a cause that acts as one agent alongside another, interfering with it, competes with that agent's freedom. God is the author of the whole story, not a character in it.

quiz.q: A theist says: “God keeps the eye in existence, but its seeing is entirely its own doing, independent of God.” Which view is this?
options: Occasionalism
Concurrentism
Pantheism
Mere conservationism
quiz.explanation: Conservation without concurrence is mere conservationism. Feser argues that, by agere sequitur esse, what could act independently of God could exist independently, so the view slides into deism.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, would occasionalism imply that God alone exists?
options: Because by agere sequitur esse, what could do nothing at all would not truly exist
Because God is present everywhere and so fills all space
Because occasionalists deny divine simplicity
Because creatures are literally parts of God
quiz.explanation: What a thing does reflects what it is. A ‘thing’ with no causal efficacy whatsoever would have no real being. But you know you exist and are not God, so occasionalism must be false.

quiz.q: Which image does Feser use for the way occasionalism and mere conservationism undermine the proofs' starting points?
options: An airplane on autopilot
A diamond cutting glass
A man who climbs a ladder and then blasts it out from under himself with a ray gun
White light passing through a prism
quiz.explanation: Both views abandon the premises (real, changing, composite things that cannot exist on their own) that led to God as First Cause. The autopilot image is used against the ‘intervention’ picture of miracles.

quiz.q: On the Aristotelian view Feser adopts, what is a law of nature?
options: An exceptionless regularity that has never been observed to fail
A rule God imposes on otherwise inert matter from outside
A mathematical equation with no connection to the natures of things
A description of the dispositions things have by virtue of their natures, which can be blocked or left untriggered
quiz.explanation: Laws express natures (water's disposition to freeze at 32°F), and a disposition can fail to manifest without any law being broken. Option A is closer to the Humean view Feser rejects.

quiz.q: Why would an angel's extraordinary feat not certify a revelation as coming from God, on Feser's account?
options: Because angels certainly do not exist
Because it would be merely preternatural — within created powers — while only a strictly supernatural effect must come from God
Because angels are parts of God
Because such feats would be subnatural defects
quiz.explanation: Angels, if they exist, are creatures with natures, part of the natural order broadly construed. Only an effect beyond every created nature can serve as God's own ‘seal.’ Feser's point doesn't depend on whether angels exist.

quiz.q: According to Feser, what is faith as Aquinas understands it?
options: Believing something because God has revealed it, where the fact that God revealed it needs evidential support
Believing without any evidence
Believing in the face of contrary evidence
A feeling of trust that has nothing to do with reason
quiz.explanation: Feser calls the ‘belief without evidence’ idea a very common misconception. Faith rests on God's authority, and that God has spoken must be established by evidence such as miracles.

quiz.q: Which religious claim would natural theology, as Feser describes it, show to be false?
options: That God became incarnate
That God is triune
That God is a finite, material being
That God has revealed a moral law
quiz.explanation: Natural theology proves God is immaterial, omnipotent, and omniscient, so a finite material god is ruled out. Claims like the Incarnation or Trinity are beyond natural theology's competence to prove or disprove.

quiz.q: In the analogy of attribution applied to power, which statement is correct?
options: The sun is the primary analogate, and God has power only by analogy with it
God and the sun have power in exactly the same sense
‘Power’ is used equivocally of God and the sun
God is the primary analogate as pure underived power, and the sun has power only as derived from him
quiz.explanation: The order of knowing runs from creatures to God, but the order of being runs from God to creatures: God just is underived causal power, and every creature's power depends on him at every instant.

quiz.q: How does Feser understand moral goodness?
options: As a kind of goodness unrelated to the goodness of triangles or trees
As the special case of goodness arising when free rational creatures choose to promote or frustrate the potentials they need to flourish
As whatever God happens to command
As whatever produces the most pleasure
quiz.explanation: Specimen goodness applies to everything; moral goodness enters with creatures that can freely choose. It is not a separate, unrelated notion, nor defined by arbitrary command or pleasure.

quiz.q: Why does Feser reject pantheism in this chapter?
options: Because the world contains too much evil to be God
Because the world is composite, potential, and contingent, with essence distinct from existence, whereas God is simple, purely actual, and necessary
Because pantheism is unscientific
Because pantheists deny that miracles can occur
quiz.explanation: The same features that made things require a divine cause make them distinct from that cause. Feser does not argue from evil or from science here.

quiz.q: What would Feser say to the suggestion that God himself might be the one having the ‘illusion’ of a changing, many-sided world?
options: That an omnipotent God could have any illusion he likes
That illusions are privations and so God has them
That this proves panentheism
That whatever has successive, differing, mistaken experiences is changeable, composite, and not omniscient, so it cannot be God
quiz.explanation: Having one experience and then another is change; having different experiences implies parts; being deceived implies ignorance. So the subject of the illusion is not the immutable, simple, omniscient God.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, is no one wronged if God does not create a world with trees?
options: Because what does not exist cannot be harmed or wronged, and God himself, lacking nothing, is not harmed either
Because trees have no moral worth
Because God has the right to do evil if he wishes
Because God is obliged to create trees anyway
quiz.explanation: This defeats the Leibniz/Rowe assumption that God must bring about the best he can. Creating trees without water might harm them, but only because they would then exist.

quiz.q: Why does Feser think the impersonal pronoun ‘it’ is inappropriate for God?
options: Because God is literally male
Because God has intellect and will, which are what make something a person
Because ‘it’ is ungrammatical in theological writing
Because God is a material being
quiz.explanation: God is sexless, but he is personal. The separate question of ‘he’ vs. ‘she’ is answered by the analogy with a father's active, independent, distinct role.

shortAnswer.q: Give both of Feser's routes to divine omnipotence, and explain why the paradox of the stone does not refute it.
shortAnswer.model:
**Backward:** everything other than God is composite and contingent and exists at each instant only because God causes it. Since action follows being and existing is presupposed by acting, what cannot exist independently cannot act independently. So all power derives from God and nothing is beyond his power.

**Forward:** God is subsistent existence, existing in the fullest way; to have power is to be able to actualize potential; so, by action follows being, he can act in the fullest way, and nothing could prevent him from actualizing any actualizable potential.

**Stone:** omnipotence covers whatever could exist or occur. A stone's rising can always occur, so God can always cause it; ‘a stone too heavy for God to lift’ is self-contradictory like ‘round square,’ so there is no capacity to lack.

Uses agere sequitur esse to extend dependence to action
Gives the forward route from subsistent existence and power as actualizing potential

Applies this specifically to the stone

shortAnswer.q: Reconstruct Feser's argument that there is an intellect in God.
shortAnswer.model: Everything that exists or could exist depends on God's causal action at every moment. By proportionate causality, whatever is in an effect is in its total cause in some way, so every feature of every possible thing must be in God somehow. Not as instances: God is immaterial, and if he merely instantiated redness his redness would itself need explaining, so he wouldn't be the ultimate cause. Chapter 3 showed universals are real and that, apart from concrete instances, they could exist only as concepts in an intellect or in a Platonic third realm, which does not exist. So they exist in God as concepts: God has intellect. Likewise states of affairs exist in him as propositions.
rubric: Dependence plus proportionate causality
Rules out existence as instances with both reasons
Invokes realism about universals and rejection of Platonism
Draws the conclusion by elimination
Extends to propositions/states of affairs

shortAnswer.q: How does God know the world, according to Feser, and how does this help with (a) four-dimensionalism and (b) free will?
shortAnswer.model:
God knows the world not by observing it but by knowing himself as its cause, in a single timeless act, as an author knows his story by knowing his own intentions. He is not in time, has no senses, and cannot learn.

(a) Four-dimensionalism would follow only if the knowledge were observational. Knowing from outside time that one causes a temporal world does not make the world timeless (the motionless hunter and the moving bullet).

(b) Knowledge as such does not compel (knowing you sit in the next room). And causation by God is like an author's writing a free character, not like a hypnotist character interfering; God is not a cause alongside us, so his causality doesn't rival our freedom.

Grounds this in eternity, incorporeality, immutability

shortAnswer.q: Explain the privation account of badness and answer two objections to it.
shortAnswer.model:
A thing is good as a specimen to the extent it actualizes what its nature calls for (the ruled triangle, the deep-rooted tree); badness is the absence of such actuality — a privation, the lack of something the nature calls for (a wavy side, weak roots — not a missing fourth side or missing wings). Goodness is primary, badness derivative, as blindness is the lack of sight.

**Evil's reality:** calling blindness a lack doesn't deny it's real; it explains what it is. **Pain:** pain isn't bad without qualification (it warns; post-workout pain can satisfy; asymbolia separates pain from unpleasantness); the badness lies in damage or disturbance. (Also acceptable: murderous intention — the positive desires may be good, the badness is the missing respect for rights; sadism — misdirected desire, a psychological deformity.)

shortAnswer.q: Why is God perfectly good, and why doesn't this make him the source of evil?
shortAnswer.model: Forward: goodness is actuality and badness unrealized potential; God is pure act with no potential, so he is purely good. Backward: by proportionate causality, all good in the world is in God as its source, so he is all-good. Evil is not in God, because the principle concerns positive features and evil is an absence: making a world with evil is making goods while refraining from others (the unfinished triangle). Refraining is no defect when there is good reason: the lecturer's incomplete triangle serves a larger good, and some goods, like courage, are impossible without real danger.
rubric: Forward route from pure actuality

Evil as absence, so not required in the cause
