shortAnswer.q: Why does God have a will, why is it free, and how does Feser answer Leibniz/Rowe?
shortAnswer.model: Natures incline toward their ends: unconsciously (trees), with sensory appetite (dogs), rationally (humans). God, having intellect, has the limit case of rational appetite, and since he grasps all possibles but causes only some, something analogous to willing. It is free: nothing external compels him (everything depends on him) and nothing internal (no concept, lion or unicorn, necessitates its instances). Leibniz/Rowe assume one must do the best one can and that there is a best world; but not creating wrongs no one (God needs nothing; nonexistent trees can't be wronged), and there is no best world (x + 1 forests). Rowe's rejoinder fails because God's perfection comes from what he is, not what he makes (the diamond).

shortAnswer.q: Can an immutable God love? Give Feser's argument.
shortAnswer.model: The objection says love requires being affected, and being affected is change. Feser calls this a fallacy of accident: our love usually involves emotional change, but what is essential to love is willing the good of the beloved. That's why love that is only fluctuating feeling is shallow, while love that keeps willing the other's good (tough love, love of enemies) is serious. Love is chiefly an act of will, which is active, not a passion. God has will, and creating is actualizing, which is willing that things exist with all the goods their natures call for (a tree's roots and photosynthesis). So God loves his creatures, without change.

Identifies the fallacy of accident

Conclusion: love without change

shortAnswer.q: In what sense can we comprehend God and in what sense not? Why is this not obscurantism?
shortAnswer.model: Loosely, yes: we understand the arguments; negative knowledge is real knowledge; positive predicates apply literally by analogy — attribution (God primary analogate of power, the sun secondary) and proper proportionality (tree, human, angel, and God each related to their own goodness; God's as the limit case). Strictly, no: full comprehension analyzes things into parts or genus and difference, and God is simple, so the positive content of our concepts thins out. Not obscurantism, because the limitation is derived from the arguments themselves, and physics likewise uses strange concepts (wave-particles, curved space) far from ordinary experience.

Analogy is literal; both types illustrated
Simplicity blocks strict comprehension via analysis
‘Hard to understand because simple’

shortAnswer.q: Compare occasionalism, mere conservationism, and concurrentism, and give Feser's case for concurrentism.
shortAnswer.model: Occasionalism: only God causes (God melts the ice on the occasion of sun). Mere conservationism: God sustains things, but they act independently. Concurrentism: creatures are real but secondary causes acting only with God's concurrence. Against occasionalism: by action follows being, what does nothing is nothing, so only God would exist; but you exist and are not God (you change, doubt, lack power); and it destroys the proofs' starting point (the ladder). Against mere conservationism: what can act independently can exist independently (deism), yet nothing composite can exist without conservation; it too kicks away the ladder. So concurrentism: the blue chalk (you cause the square, the chalk its blueness), the moon and sun, and — for freedom — the father guiding his son's hand.

shortAnswer.q: What is a miracle on Feser's view, why is it not a ‘violation of a law of nature,’ and what role could miracles play?
shortAnswer.model: Laws describe dispositions things have by nature (water freezing at 32°F), which can be blocked or untriggered; and since laws are the laws of natures, they are metaphysically necessary given the things exist, so violations are impossible. A miracle elevates a thing beyond what any created nature can account for — supernatural, not subnatural (defect) or preternatural (angelic) — so only God can cause it, and he doesn't ‘intervene,’ being no cause alongside others. Miracles can add (resurrection) or subtract (the furnace), the latter by God withholding conservation/concurrence: a suspension, not a breach. Their role: a divine seal confirming revelation, making them the bridge between natural and revealed theology and grounding faith in reason.

Metaphysical necessity and impossibility of violation

shortAnswer.q: Why does Feser think it is appropriate to call God ‘he’ even though God is sexless?
shortAnswer.model: God is immaterial and not an animal, so not literally male or female. But he has intellect and will, which define personhood, so ‘it’ is wrong. His relation to the world resembles a father's biological role more than a mother's: the father acts, is unchanged, is not physically dependent on mate or child, and is not physically continuous with the child during gestation; God is active in creating, unchanging, independent, and utterly distinct from the world. Maternal imagery would suggest a God changed by or continuous with the world, i.e., panentheism or pantheism.

shortAnswer.q: Why does Feser reject the thesis of existential inertia, and why can't the world itself be the necessary being?
shortAnswer.model: Existential inertia says some things, once they exist, keep existing on their own until destroyed, and so need no divine conserver. Feser raises two problems. First, its defenders never explain what feature of a material or contingent thing could give it this power; they merely suggest it. Second, no contingent thing could have it: everything other than God is composite — a mixture of act and potency, of essence and existence — and anything composite in these ways requires a sustaining cause here and now. Merely positing inertia ignores rather than answers those arguments. The world cannot be the necessary being because nothing composite, potential, or with essence distinct from existence can be necessary; and even a derived necessity (Aquinas's Third Way) presupposes God.

shortAnswer.q: Distinguish supernatural, preternatural, and subnatural events, and explain why the distinction matters for the role of miracles.
shortAnswer.model: A subnatural event falls short of a thing's nature — a defect, like a malformed organ. A preternatural event is extraordinary but still within the powers of some created nature, such as an angel (which, if it exists, is a creature conserved and concurred with by God). A supernatural event elevates something to a power no created nature can account for, and its cause lies outside the natural order altogether, so only God can produce it. The distinction matters because miracles are supposed to certify revelation: only an effect that nothing but God could cause can serve as God's ‘seal’ on a prophet's message. It also shows miracles are nothing like magic or advanced technology, which are just more natural causes.

shortAnswer.q: How can God's knowledge be one simple act and yet include knowledge of every finite kind of thing?
shortAnswer.model: Concepts can't be in God as many distinct thoughts, since he is simple; even a single giant conjunctive proposition would have parts. Feser's analogies: white light contains all colors in a unified way before a prism separates them; uncut dough contains countless cookie shapes virtually. God is unlimited actuality, and each creature is a limited way of being actual (actual as a stone, a tree, a dog). Creation is like the prism or cutter drawing out limited modes. Just as perfectly knowing white light would include knowing every derivable color, perfectly knowing himself as pure act includes knowing every limited way of being actual. The multiplicity lies in creatures, not in God. The analogy limps: creatures are not made out of God as cookies are out of dough.

shortAnswer.q: Why can't God ‘intervene’ in the world, and how do Feser's music, film, and book analogies capture what a miracle is?
shortAnswer.model: Talk of ‘intervention’ (like ‘violation’) suggests God forces things from outside, as a machinist tinkers with a machine. But God is not a cause alongside natural and preternatural causes; he is the precondition of there being any causal power at all and is already causing the ordinary course of things. To interfere you must be alongside what you interfere with (McCabe); you can't intervene in what you're doing yourself (Davies). The world isn't a plane on autopilot. Instead: God is a musician, and a miracle is a jazz improvisation on his own score; or a director, and miracles belong to the director's cut; or an author, and miracles are additions in a second edition. The originals are complete and good, so miracles raise them higher rather than fixing defects; subtractive miracles are like omitted notes or cut scenes.

shortAnswer.q: Explain how the analogy of proper proportionality lets us speak literally of the goodness of a tree, a human being, an angel, and God.
shortAnswer.model: In proper proportionality a term applies intrinsically and literally to several things because each stands in a proportionally similar relation (as the eye is to a tree, so the intellect is to the Pythagorean theorem, grounding ‘seeing’ in both). A tree is to its goodness as a virtuous human is to his, and as an angel is to his, even though the goodness differs: the tree's develops gradually and unconsciously; the human's gradually through choices, sometimes against disordered bodily desires; the angel's through choice but not over time or against bodily desire. God is to his goodness as these are to theirs, but his is more radically different still: he cannot fail to be good, being pure act — the limit case of goodness. So the predication is neither univocal (same sense) nor equivocal (unrelated), yet literal.

flashcards.back: Evil isn't in God and permitting it fits his goodness: evil is an absence, and some goods (courage) require permitted badness.

flashcards.front: What does step 34 claim and why?
flashcards.back: Neither simplicity nor goodness removes God's freedom: freedom as such needn't involve potency; no one is wronged by non-creation; there's no best world; perfection comes from what God is.

flashcards.front: What does step 42 claim and why?
flashcards.back: God conserves everything at every instant; nothing contingent has existential inertia, since composites of act/potency and essence/existence need a sustaining cause.

flashcards.front: What does step 50 claim and why?
flashcards.back: Given that the things exist, laws of nature are metaphysically necessary and can't be violated, since laws express natures.

flashcards.front: What does step 53 claim and why?
flashcards.back: Miracles may add or subtract; subtraction is God withholding conservation or concurrence — a suspension, not a breach.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘Concepts in God contradict simplicity.’ Reply?
flashcards.back: They aren't in God as distinct thoughts; like white light holding all colors, God's one self-knowledge contains every limited way of being.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘Good and bad are just preferences.’ Reply?
flashcards.back: The ruled triangle and the healthy tree are better specimens because of what triangles and trees are, not because of anyone's taste.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘Sadism is a positive delight in harm.’ Reply?
flashcards.back: Sadistic desire is misdirected desire, contrary to the concern for others social animals need — a psychological deformity, as blindness is a physical one.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘The world itself might be the necessary being.’ Reply?
flashcards.back: Nothing composite, potential, or with essence distinct from existence can be necessary; any derived necessity presupposes God.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘Pantheism is true; change and multiplicity are illusions.’ Reply?
flashcards.back: Whoever has the illusion has successive, differing, mistaken experiences — so is changeable, composite, contingent, and ignorant: not God.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘Faith is belief without evidence.’ Reply?
flashcards.back: Faith is believing because God revealed; that he revealed needs evidence, which only a miracle could supply. Faith is grounded in reason.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘Miracles mean God fixing a defective world.’ Reply?
flashcards.back: A miracle is like a jazz improvisation or director's cut: it raises something already complete and good to a higher level.
Pantheism: God is the world. Panentheism: God isn't the world but is in it and changed by it. Feser rejects both (God is distinct and immutable).

flashcards.front: Deism, and why mere conservationism collapses into it
flashcards.back: Deism: creatures carry on without God. By action-follows-being, what could act independently of God could exist independently.
Universals are mere names; only human concepts; or denizens of a mind-independent third realm. Chapter 3 rejected all three, leaving the divine intellect.

flashcards.front: Fideism — and why Feser's view isn't it
flashcards.back: Fideism rests belief on faith alone. Feser's position is rationalist: God's existence and attributes are demonstrated, though not fully comprehended.
A merely relational change (Socrates becoming shorter as Plato grows). God's becoming Creator is a Cambridge change: the real change is in the world.

flashcards.front: Genus and specific difference — why it matters here
flashcards.back: We understand natures by genus + difference (animal + rational). God has no such composition, so he can't be fully comprehended this way.
Humeans think water could turn to mousse at 32°F under different laws; for Aristotelians, anything that did so reliably just wouldn't be water.
Liquid water can exist below 32°F in unusual conditions — showing laws describe dispositions that can be blocked, not exceptionless regularities.

flashcards.front: Iced tea and the cue ball
flashcards.back: Feser's examples of occasionalism: God, not the sun, melts the ice; God, not the cue ball, sinks the eight ball.
Both concepts are in the divine intellect; neither requires its instances to exist, so nothing internal compelled God to create lions — his will is free.

flashcards.front: Why the Augustinian proof can't rescue occasionalism
flashcards.back: It starts from universals and necessary truths, not causality, so it doesn't give God as the source of all causal power — which occasionalism needs.

teachBack:
**The challenge:** Explain to a thoughtful friend who is *not* religious, in about eight minutes, how Feser gets from “a purely actual First Cause” to “an all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good, free, loving God who is not a cause among causes.”

**Constraints:**
- Use no technical Latin except, once, “action follows being,” and explain it in plain words.
- You must use exactly three analogies: the author of a novel (for knowledge and freedom), the unfinished triangle (for goodness and evil), and the blue chalk or the jazz musician (for concurrence or miracles). For each, say out loud where the analogy breaks.
- You must state and answer, in your own words, at least three objections: the stone, foreknowledge vs. free will, and ‘an unchanging God can't love.’
- End by explaining why God is knowable but not fully comprehensible, without using the word ‘mystery’ as a conversation-stopper.

**Check yourself:**
1. Did you derive each attribute from something already established, rather than just asserting it? Could you name the principle used at each step (dependence, action follows being, proportionate causality)?
2. Did you avoid saying God ‘foresees,’ ‘intervenes,’ or ‘breaks laws’?
3. Did you keep both halves of concurrence (creatures really cause; they cause only with God)?
4. Did you distinguish privation from mere absence with an example?
5. Could your friend repeat the author-vs-hypnotist point back to you? Ask them to. If they can't, re-teach that piece first — it carries most of the module.
videoPrompt: Audience: curious, intelligent adults with no philosophy background, some skeptical. Goal: show how, once the five proofs establish a purely actual First Cause that sustains everything, Feser derives God's other attributes and his relationship to the world. Emphasize, in order: (1) omnipotence — all power is borrowed from the source of existence; the stone paradox dissolves because contradictions aren't things; (2) omniscience — God knows like an author, by causing, not by watching; author vs. hypnotist for free will; (3) goodness as actuality and evil as privation, using the triangle and tree examples and the courage point; (4) God's free will, no best possible world, and love as willing good rather than feeling; (5) knowable but not fully comprehensible because simple; (6) concurrence — the blue chalk — versus occasionalism and deism; (7) miracles as elevation or suspension, never violation, with the jazz musician. Correct the misconceptions that God is a super-person, that he ‘foresees,’ and that miracles break laws. Tone: clear, warm, intellectually serious, never preachy.

readingGuide.beforeYouRead:
By this point in the book, Feser believes he has shown that there is a First Cause of everything: something that isn't made of parts, has no untapped potential, can't fail to exist, and keeps everything else in existence right now. But a skeptic can fairly say: “So what? That could be an impersonal force. Why call it *God*?” These pages are Feser's answer. He tries to show that this First Cause must be **all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good, free, and loving** — the God of traditional religion, not just a cosmic engine.

The second half of the section asks how such a God relates to the world. Does he just keep things around, or does he do everything himself? Can he work miracles, and would those ‘break’ the laws of nature? Along the way Feser takes on the most famous puzzles people raise about God: Can God make a stone too heavy to lift? If God knows the future, am I free? If God made everything, did he make evil? Can a God who never changes really love?

**What you'll be asked to accept.** Mostly, things Feser argued earlier: that the First Cause is purely actual and simple, that a cause can't give what it doesn't have (proportionate causality), and that what a thing does reflects what it is (“action follows being”). He also leans on chapter 3's claim that universals — shared patterns like ‘triangularity’ — are real. If you haven't read those chapters, this module's key-terms list will fill you in.

**Reassurance.** Some passages are genuinely hard, especially the free-will discussion (pp. 213–215), the privation theory of evil (pp. 218–222), and divine freedom (pp. 224–228). You don't need to master every footnote. Hold on to one idea and much of the section will fall into place: God is not the biggest thing in the universe competing with other things; he is the source of everything's existence, more like the **author of a story** than a character in it. Feser returns to that image again and again. The chapter also gets easier toward the end: the miracles section and the short appendix are mostly clear, concrete prose.

knowFirst.plain: Being completely ‘all there,’ with nothing waiting to happen or develop. Feser's First Cause is like this, and most of the chapter's conclusions follow from it.
A cause can't give what it doesn't have in some way. Feser uses it to argue that whatever is in the world must somehow be ‘in’ God.
Latin for ‘action follows being’: what something can do depends on what it is. If you can't even exist on your own, you can't act on your own.
God has no parts of any kind. ‘Simple’ here means ‘not made of pieces,’ not ‘easy to understand.’

Ways of using a word: exactly the same sense, totally different senses, or related senses. Words like ‘good’ and ‘powerful’ apply to God in the related (analogical) way — truly, but not exactly as they apply to us.

knowFirst.term: Privation (and the privation theory of evil)
knowFirst.plain: Missing something you're supposed to have, like blindness in an eye. Feser argues all badness is like this: a gap, not an extra ingredient.
Mistaking something that usually goes along with a thing for part of what the thing is. Feser uses it against the objections that God can't love or choose without changing.
God keeps everything in existence at every moment, not just at the beginning.
Created things really cause things, but only with God working through them at every moment — like chalk that really colors a square but only moves when a hand moves it.
God isn't one more force competing with others inside the world; he's the reason there are any forces at all. This idea unlocks most of the chapter.

questionsToHold: Each time Feser assigns God an attribute, what does he derive it from — the world as God's effect, or God's own nature as pure actuality? Can you spot both routes?
Where is an objection quietly treating God as a very powerful being inside the world, rather than as the source of the world's existence?
When Feser says God has intellect, will, or love, what exactly is being kept from the human version, and what is being stripped away?
How can badness be real if it is only an absence? Can you think of an absence that really hurts?
What would it take for creatures to be genuine causes if God is involved in everything they do?
If the laws of nature can't be broken, what room is left for a miracle?

map.what: Feser argues God is all-powerful, first because everything depends on God for its existence and therefore its power, then because what exists fully can act fully. He dissolves the paradox of the stone and explains why God can't sin.
map.tip: Read slowly the paragraph on ‘action follows being’ — it's reused throughout. The stone paradox is quick; read the footnote on Frankfurt for fun.

map.what: Using the ‘cause can't give what it lacks’ principle plus chapter 3's results, Feser argues that the patterns of all things exist in God as ideas, so God has a mind; then he shows God meets the standard conditions for knowledge, using the image of an author.
map.tip: The argument is an elimination: instances, mind, or Platonic realm. Write the three options in the margin. The cat-on-the-mat passage is easier than it looks.

map.what: How God knows: by knowing himself as cause, not by watching. Feser rebuts the claim that this makes time a ‘block,’ answers the foreknowledge-versus-free-will objection with the crime novel (author vs. hypnotist), and uses a prism and cookie dough to explain how a partless God knows many things.
map.tip: This is the hardest stretch. Reread pp. 213–215 (free will) twice. You can skim the footnotes; don't worry if the prism analogy feels loose — Feser says it's imperfect.

map.what: Feser argues that ‘good’ is objective — a good triangle, a good tree — and that badness is always a lack of what something should have (a privation).
map.tip: Make sure you can say why a triangle lacking a fourth side is fine but one with a wavy side is defective. That example carries the whole theory.

map.what: Four objections to the privation theory (evil's reality, pain, murderous intent, sadism) and replies; then the conclusion that God is perfectly good, why evil isn't ‘in’ God, and the courage example.
map.tip: Notice every reply has the same shape: something positive is present, but the badness is what's missing. The unfinished-triangle passage on p. 222 is key; read the courage footnote.

map.what: From the inclinations of plants, animals, and humans to something like will in God; why God's will is free (no outside or inside compulsion — lions vs. unicorns); and the objection that a simple, unchanging God can't choose.
map.tip: Footnote 61 (the ‘limit case’: zero speed isn't a slow speed) is worth reading closely. The Kretzmann–Richards footnote can be skimmed.

map.what: Leibniz and Rowe argue God must make the best world and so isn't free; Feser replies that no one is wronged by not being created and that there's no best world (always one more forest), then answers Rowe's rejoinder with a diamond.
map.tip: Separate the two assumptions Feser attacks, labeled (a) and (b). The diamond paragraph answers a different objection from the forests paragraph — keep them apart.

map.what: A short, clear argument that love is essentially willing someone's good rather than a feeling, so an unchanging God can love.
map.tip: Easy reading. Connect it back to ‘goodness is actuality’: creating things just is willing their good.

map.what: We can know God truly (by negation and analogy) but never fully, because we understand things by taking them apart and God has no parts. Feser compares this to physics' strange concepts.
map.tip: Review Part A's two kinds of analogy (attribution; proper proportionality) before reading. The tree–human–angel–God comparison on pp. 230–231 is the heart of it.

map.what: God keeps the world in existence at every moment; Feser rejects ‘existential inertia’ and argues the world is distinct from God (against pantheism and panentheism).
map.tip: Footnote 75 (the world as the necessary being) is short and useful. Make sure you can explain why ‘the world depends on God’ doesn't mean ‘the world is God.’

map.what: Three views of divine causation: occasionalism (only God acts), mere conservationism (creatures act on their own), and concurrentism (both, at different levels). Feser refutes the first two and illustrates the third with chalk, the moon, and a father guiding a child's hand.
map.tip: Draw three columns as you read. The ladder-and-ray-gun image appears twice — note both uses. Footnotes 78 and 79 are worth reading.

map.what: Why ‘violation of a law of nature’ is the wrong definition (laws express natures); what a miracle is (beyond any created nature); why God doesn't ‘intervene’; miracles that subtract (the fiery furnace) as suspensions; and miracles as the bridge to revealed religion.
map.tip: The block quotes from Ramelow, Oderberg, Davies, and McCabe carry the argument; read them carefully. The music, film, and second-edition analogies (pp. 243–245) are easy and memorable.

map.what: God is sexless, but ‘he’ is the least misleading pronoun because God is personal and his relation to the world resembles a father's role more than a mother's.
map.tip: A quick read. Focus on the list of parallels and why maternal imagery would suggest pantheism.

afterReading: Without notes, explain both routes to omnipotence in under a minute, then dissolve the paradox of the stone.
Reconstruct the elimination argument for an intellect in God: what are the three options for where universals exist, and why are two ruled out?
Explain the author-versus-hypnotist contrast to an imaginary friend who worries about free will, and name one limit of the analogy.
Give an example of a privation and of a mere absence, then say why proportionate causality doesn't put evil in God.
State the two assumptions Feser attacks in the best-possible-world argument, and his reply to Rowe's rejoinder.
Draw the three columns (occasionalism, concurrentism, mere conservationism) from memory and give Feser's argument against each extreme.
Explain the difference between a breach and a suspension of a law, using the fiery furnace.
Take the module's section checks and quiz; for any question you miss, reread the matching pages in the map above.
